## 2.3.2.1 Quality Target Product Profile
The Quality Target Product Profile (QTPP) provided in Table 1 describes the elements related to quality, safety and efficacy. 

### Table 1. Quality Target Product Profile and Associated Quality Attributes
| Product Quality Attribute | Target |
| Route of Administration and Dosage Form | Oral film-coated tablet |
| Dose Strength(s) | 20 mg |
| Potency | Meet pharmacopoeia requirements for identity, assay and content uniformity |
| In vitro Drug Release | Immediate release |
| Degradants and Impurities | Controlled in accordance with ICH Q3 and M7 guidelines; regional guidelines for nitrosamine impurities, as applicable |
| Microbiology | Meets harmonized compendial requirements for solid oral tablets |
| Shelf Life | 36 months at room temperature across all climatic zones |
| Container closure system(s) | HDPE Bottle with child-resistant closure and PA/AL/PVC blister |

### 2.3.2.1.1 Critical Quality Attributes 
Identification of critical quality attributes from the QTPP was based on the severity of harm to a patient (safety and efficacy) resulting from failure to meet the acceptance criteria for each quality attribute. Investigation during pharmaceutical development focused on those CQAs that could be impacted by a realistic change to the drug product formulation or drug substance or drug product manufacturing process (see Table 2). 

### Table 2 Critical Quality Attributes
| Quality attribute | Justification |
| Drug Product Description | Color, shape and appearance are not directly linked to safety and efficacy, but can indirectly impact through medication errors, patient compliance, dose identification, etc. The target is set to ensure product quality and patient acceptability. |
| Drug Product Identification | Though identification is critical for safety and efficacy, this CQA can be effectively controlled by the quality management system and will be monitored at drug product release. |
| Drug Product Uniformity of Dosage Units | Variability in content uniformity will affect safety and efficacy. Both formulation and process variables impact content uniformity, so this CQA will be evaluated throughout product and process development. |
| Drug Product Assay | Assay variability will affect safety and efficacy. Process variables may affect the assay of the drug product.   |
| Drug Product Dissolution | Failure to meet the dissolution specification can impact bioavailability.  Formulation, material attributes and process variables affect the dissolution profile.  |
| Drug Product Impurities | Impurities in the drug product can affect safety and are controlled to levels demonstrated to be safe per ICH Q3 and ICH M7, which enable routine manufacturing to ensure a robust supply for patients.  |
| Microbiological Quality | Control of microbiological quality ensures patient safety  |

## 2.3.2.2 Overall Development Strategy
SakuraBloom is an immediate-release 20 mg film-coated tablet, manufactured via wet granulation followed by compression and film coating.
The development followed a systematic Quality by Design (QbD) approach, in alignment with ICH Q8, Q9 and Q11. The drug substance (API), Sakuramil, is a poorly soluble, highly permeable BCS Class II compound manufactured with proprietary technology from Sakura Pharmaceuticals Company, LTD (applicant), the same company that developed the finished product. Development and manufacture of the drug substance and drug product were performed at contract development and commercial manufacturers, IROHA-Corp and Aparna Pharmaceutical Manufacturing, respectively. This facilitated alignment between API and drug product development and ensured consistent control of critical material attributes (CMAs) throughout the manufacturing chain (from drug substance to finished product).
For the drug substance, particle size was identified as a CQA influencing dissolution and uniformity of dosage units. Controls were implemented within the release specifications and maintained through development and commercial manufacturing (see 2.3.4.DS.C and 2.3.4.DS.M). Key control elements included limits for related substances (e.g., CP-9-1, CP-8), potentially mutagenic impurities (e.g., CP-6), and residual solvents (Methylene chloride). Types and grade of excipients were chosen based on excipient compatibility studies (see 2.3.4.DP.D.1 Components of the drug product).
For the drug product, a design space was defined linking drug substance particle size distribution (PSD), granulation endpoint (granule particle size), and compression force, supported by DoE studies. Fluid bed granulation was selected to avoid thermal degradation risks. In-process controls – covering moisture content, particle size distribution, hardness, weight, and assay – ensure manufacturing robustness (see 2.3.4.DP.M). In the final control strategy of the drug product, granule particle size and uncoated tablet hardness are controlled within a design space to ensure satisfactory dissolution. The developed in-house dissolution method (2.3.3 AP (Dissolution/UV}) is capable of differentiating between formulations manufactured using different PSD of the drug substance and predicting their in vivo performance in the pilot bioequivalence (BE) study. Film coating is controlled to ensure uniform appearance. Control strategies integrate in-process monitoring/RTRT and specification testing, ensuring the intended product quality at release and throughout shelf life (see 2.3.3.DP.C).

## 2.3.2.3 Overall Control Strategy Summary Representation 
Enhanced understanding has been obtained through development.  The Fishbone diagram (Figure 1) shows an overview of the drug product CQAs in the context of an integrated drug substance and drug product overall control strategy, including process design, CPPs, CMAs and critical IPCs. 

### Figure 1. Fishbone Diagram of Overall Control Strategy for Sakura Bloom.
[IMAGE:  Sakura_Bloom_OCS_Fishbone.png]
<Double click image to enlarge>
A simplified flowchart diagram depicting the overall control strategy illustrates which elements are responsible for ensuring that each CQA is met, and where the relevant parameters and material attributes are controlled in the overall control strategy (see Figure 2).  These diagrams demonstrates how the control strategy, which consists of the process controls and material controls for the raw materials, intermediates, and final product, ensures the quality, safety, and efficacy of the product throughout the product life cycle, and supports the concept of ongoing process verification and continual improvement.

### Figure 2. Overall Control Strategy for Sakura Bloom.
[IMAGE:  0_0]
<Double click image to enlarge>
The overall control strategy is also summarized in Table 3. The control strategy summary table illustrates which elements are responsible for ensuring that each CQA is met, and where the relevant parameters and material attributes are controlled in the overall control strategy. The first column lists the product attribute.  The second column lists the CQA.  The third column provides functional relationships between the CQA and the elements of the control strategy, and the fourth column lists the controls that appear in the PLCM/registration elements. The control types are categorized as follows:
- Design - Controls implicit in the design of the manufacturing process (e.g., sequence of
purification steps or order of addition)
- CMA - Controls on material attributes (including raw materials, starting materials,
intermediates, reagents, primary packaging materials, etc.)
- CPP - Critical process parameter
- IPC - In-process controls (including in-process tests and process parameters)
- Spec - Controls on the product specification (e.g., release testing/stability testing).
The fifth column provides a brief description of the control.  It should be noted that additional GMP controls are in place and are documented in the batch records and other GMP systems.

## Process description
A narrative description of the manufacturing process for sakuramil drug substance, including the critical process parameters and in-process controls, is provided here.  Supportive Information regarding  manufacturing process are provided in section [[3.2.DS.M.1 Description of Manufacturing process]].

| Manufacturing process step | Narrative description | Raw Materials/Quantities | Critical Process Parameters | In-process Controls |
| Step 1 | CP-4 is combined with methyl chloroformate, lithium-tert-butoxide, and tetrahydrofuran, then stirred. After that layers are settled and separated. Precipitates are filtered, rinsed with tetrahydrofuran and dried to yield CP-5 | Starting Material CP-4 (175-185 kg) Methyl chloroformate (55-120 L) Lithium-tert-butoxide (22-85 kg) Tetrahydrofuran (750-920 L) | N/A | N/A |
| Step 2 | CP-5 is combined with sodium borohydride, magnesium chloride, and methanol, then filtered after the reaction completes. No routine reprocessing is carried out, hence no further justification is given

# 2.3.4.DS.M.1 Development of manufacturing process and process controls

## Introduction
The development program for Sakuramil has utilized the principles outlined in ICH Q8, Q9 and Q11 and thus, Quality by Design. The Manufacturing Process Development section for Sakuramil is organized as follows:
1. Overall Process Development Summary
1. Risk Assessment
1. Description of Critical Material Attributes and Critical Process Parameters
1. Drug Substance CQAs
1. Summary of proposed Control Strategy for CMAs and CPPs

## 1 Overall Process Development Summary

## 1.2 Stages of Development and Evolution of the Manufacturing process
STAGE 1 – SELECTION OF SYNTHETIC ROUTE
STAGE 2 – LABORATORY SCALE PROCESS DEVELOPMENT
STAGE 3 – MANUFACTURING PROCESS SCALE UP, DRYING STEP OPTIMIZATION AND PRODUCTION OF DEVELOPMENT AND PRODUCTION BATCHES
More details on the different Stages are provided below in section

### 1.2.1 STAGE 1 – SELECTION OF SYNTHETIC ROUTE
Selection of the appropriate synthetic route was based on available literature data. The first goal was to select appropriate synthetic route, starting materials and raw materials which would enable the synthesis the targeted molecule.
Full details on changes during development can be found in section  2.3.4.DS.M.2 Changes during manufacturing process development
1.2.2.1 Definition of Raw Materials, Reagents and Starting Materials
1.2.2.1.1 Starting Materials
IROHA-corp. proposed that CP-4 and CP-8 serve as structurally distinct and suitable Starting Materials (SM), or “Regulatory Starting Materials” (RSM). The proposed “Regulatory Synthesis” is convergent, consisting of four synthetic steps, wherein significant molecular fragments are incorporated to create Sakuramil drug substance. The proposed “Regulatory Synthesis” was selected extensive based on laboratory and manufacturing experience established a high degree of process understanding. The appropriate specifications for SMs have been established to assure the quality of Sakuramil drug substance.
CP-4 that was manufactured by the three development routes, as outlined in section , have all produced Sakuramil drug substances that meet the current specifications. In addition, batches of CP-4 have been manufactured by a second supplier using second and third generation synthesis. All of these resulted in CP-4 and Sakuramil drug substance with similar impurity profiles and of high quality. There were not any impurities from all of these batches or route modifications of CP4  that resulted in any impurity above the 0.15 % level in Sakuramil drug substance. The potentially mutagenic impurity CP-3, originating from CP-4 synthesis, controlled at NMT 0.3% in CP-4 was shown to be purged in the drug substance to
CP-4 tested positive in the Ames assay classified as potentially mutagenic impurities. CP-3, although not directly tested, exhibited structural alerts in SAR databases and is therefore also controlled as potentially mutagenic. Fate and purge studies confirmed that CP-4 and CP-3 are effectively removed during the manufacturing process, resulting in levels 10% below TTC (37.5 ppm) in the final drug substance  Both impurities are controlled upstream on suitable intermediate with limit above TTC. Option 3 per ICH M7 guideline is used. These findings support the adequacy of the control strategy and justify the use of CP-4 as a suitable starting material. 
Justification for section of CP-4 Starting Material is provided in section [[2.3.4.DS.D Description (Sakuramil) [IROHA-corp] ]] 
Table 3-1 Critical material attributes and controls for CP-4
| Tests | Potential for variables to impact quality | Control Value¹ | Actual Value | Comments: Importance Designation |
| Related substancesCP-3 | Yes | NMT 0.3 %² | ≤ 0.01 – 0.04% | High risk: 0.3 % resulted in < 10 ppm in drug substance, The potentially mutagenic impurity CP-3 controlled at NMT 0.3% in CP-4 was shown to be purged in the drug substance to <TTC levels |
¹These acceptance criteria have changes with increased processing experience and understanding. While some of these lots do not meet current acceptance criteria, all lots have been successfully processed forward to produce drug substance of acceptable quality
²Fate and purge study supports up to 1 %. Fate and purge study: Elevated levels of this impurity is introduced to laboratory batches and then evaluated in the process to identify the fate of the impurity, and the purge factor of the impurity or reacted impurity.
Full details on designation of critical and non-critical material attributes of CP-4 are provided in section [[1.1 Starting Material 1 - CP-4]]  
CP-8 is generally produced through a three-step route. All potentially identified impurities originating from its synthesis are non-mutagenic and considered to be controlled according to ICH Q3 limits.  None of the  potential impurities affects API impurity profile, except two regio isomers (CP-8-25l and CP-8-24l) that were identified as high-risk material attributes due to their potential to form positional isomers of the Sakuramil drug substance. These isomers follow the same reaction pathway as the intended starting material and exhibit minimal purge during final crystallization. To ensure product quality, a specification limit of ≤ 0.05% for each isomer has been established as part of the control strategy.

| CP-8-24I | Yes | ≤ 0.05 % ² | ≤ 0.02 % | High riskReact like SM, little purge in drug substance |
¹Fate and purge study supports up to 3%.
²0.1 % supported by fate and purge study -> not more than 0.1 % in drug substance
Full details on designation of critical and non-critical material attributes of CP-8 are provided in section [[1.2 Starting Material 2 - CP-8]] 
Justification for selection of CP-8 Starting Material is provided in section [[2.3.4.DS.D Description (Sakuramil) [IROHA-corp] ]] 
1.2.2.2 Raw Materials
Raw Materials include all the solvents, reagent and catalyst used in the process. Specifications of all these raw materials have to meet the requirements for the manufacturing process.
Table 4-3 Overview of Critical Material attributes (CMA) of raw materials (RM)
| Material | Origin | Impact on CQA |

### 1.2.2 STAGE 2 – LABORATORY SCALE PROCESS DEVELOPMENT
Initial experiments in Stage 2 were oriented towards getting scientifically sound understanding of mechanistic background synthesize and isolation. The process was then optimized and the parameters evaluated on a laboratory scale. Parameters were generally varied to an extent sufficient to determine the proven acceptable ranges. Design of experiments (DoE) was used to build a model of operation and gain specific knowledge about the parameters affecting attributes which are important for process performance and quality of the product. The product isolation was also developed at this stage.

### 1.2.3 STAGE 3 – MANUFACTURING PROCESS SCALE UP, DRYING STEP OPTIMIZATION AND PRODUCTION OF DEVELOPMENT AND PRODUCTION BATCHES
After the laboratory development, where small scale laboratory process was confirmed, further development work was focused on commercial manufacturing process.
The process designed at the laboratory level was adjusted to the specific manufacturing equipment. Adjustment of the process demanded the redefinition and optimization of some process parameters, since some operations are scale and equipment dependent. Scale up effects and data required to define equipment and to set parameters for successful transfer from laboratory to industrial scale were identified.
Commercial Manufacturing Process is outlined in section [[2.3.3.DS.M Manufacture (Sakuramil) [IROHA-corp]]] 

## 2 Risk Assessment
Once the commercial manufacturing process for Sakuramil drug substance was established, increased understanding of the functional relationships between manufacturing process inputs (raw materials, SM, intermediates, etc.) and operating parameters (and their respective levels of criticality) and critical quality attributes of the drug substance was developed. This ultimately led to defining a design space and a control strategy for the manufacturing process.
Initially, a risk assessment process was undertaken to identify potentially critical process parameters and potential scale and equipment dependencies and assess their probable impact on drug substance quality (resulting in an understanding of their criticality and definition of inputs and operating parameters as high risk (critical), moderate risk (key) or low risk (non-critical)). In this risk assessment process, each step of the manufacturing process was considered individually. Firstly, the material attributes of the product for each step were considered with respect to their potential to impact a critical quality attribute of the drug substance. For drug substance processes, this is strictly an impurity exercise until the isolation of the drug substance, where physical characteristic are included. Next, process inputs and process operating parameters for each step were assessed with respect to their potential to impact the important impurity attributes for that step in the process.
This initial structured risk assessment utilized the knowledge that had been gained through development and scale up of the manufacturing process, and a mechanistic and kinetic understanding of the chemistry and the manufacturing process. After identifying the process inputs (raw materials, SM, intermediates, etc.) and process operating parameters and their potential links to drug substance critical quality attributes, an experimental plan was developed, prioritized and executed in order to (a) establish if the identified parameter does impact the quality attributes, and (b) to determine the extent of this impact and identify the design space / proven acceptable ranges (PAR) within which the process can be operated to produce drug substance that meets its specification.
All process-related impurities, including intermediates, diastereomers, and potentially mutagenic compounds, have been identified and assessed throughout the commercial manufacturing process of Sakuramil. CP-6 impurities above 0.1% are controlled based on demonstrated purge capability, and unspecified impurities are limited to NMT 0.1%. The process consistently achieves the desired impurity profile through robust crystallizations, which efficiently purge lipophilic intermediates and impurities.
Key material attributes impacting CQAs include:
- CP-7-1 and CP-9-1, formed in Steps 3 and 4, with low purge and controlled via process parameters.
- Unreacted CP-8, retained in the drug substance, requiring control in Step 4.
- Potentially mutagenic impurities (CP-3, CP-4, CP-5, CP-6) are purged below TTC levels.
- Nitrosamine risk is low due to absence of nitrosating agents, though vulnerable amines are present.
- Chirality is not impacted by the process and remains controlled.
- Residual solvents are effectively removed during crystallization.
- Elemental impurities, such as Pd, are controlled at the SM and intermediate level, with no need for control in the final drug substance.
Full details on commercial manufacturing process related impurities [[3.2.DS.M.2 Development of manufacturing process and process control]] 

## 3 Description of Critical Material Attributes and Critical Process Parameters

### 3.1 Design space development
A comprehensive design space was established for the Sakuramil manufacturing process based on risk assessments, multivariate experiments, and mechanistic understanding. Focus was placed on Steps 3 and 4, where critical quality attributes (CQAs) are most impacted.
Equivalents (2.0–7.5), sodium carbonate stoichiometry (0.75–4.0), and THF volume (3–15 L/kg), along with crystallization parameters such as cooling rate (0.15–0.5 °C/min), water content (10–50% w/w), ethanol volume (4–10 L/kg), and agitation rate. CP-7-1 remained below the 0.15% specification in all tested conditions, with no edges of failure observed.
In Step 4, residual CP-8 was the primary concern. DoE variables included CP-8 stoichiometry (0.9–2.0 equivalents), phase ratio (NaOH/DCM, 0.25–1.25), reaction concentration (0.25–5 L/kg), cooling rate (0.15–0.5 °C/min), and water content (20–35% w/w). Cooling rate and water content were identified as critical process parameters (CPPs), and when controlled, CP-8 levels remained below 0.10% in the drug substance. Overall, the design space ensures robust control of impurities for Sakuramil drug substance. Further Information on design space development is provided in section [[3 Design Space Development]].

# 4 Drug Substance CQAs
Based upon knowledge of the product (QTPP and CQA for drug product) and the process, several drug substance critical quality attributes (CQAs) were proposed. The links between drug substance CQAs on the one hand and critical process parameters (CPPs) and critical material attributes (CMAs) on the other hand were established.

### 4.1  Drug Substance Critical Quality Attributes
Critical Quality Attributes of Sakuramil Drug substance are: Identification, Assay, Purity Related substances, Purity Potentially mutagentic impurities, Purity Residual solvents, Purity Elemental impurities, as outlined in table below.

The synthesis of Sakuramil drug substance was evaluated regarding the manufacturing process impact on impurity control. Therefore, CQA of Sakuramil can be controlled by understanding and controlling the formation routes and fate and purge of impurities. The following related substances are found necessary to be controlled in Sakuramil drug substance specification: CP-9-1 with limit NMT 0.15% and CP-8 with limit of NMT 0.10%, meanwhile Individual unspecified impurities are limited at NMT 0.10%. 
The identification and control of potentially mutagenic impurities were done according to ICH M7 guideline. An in silico assessment was performed using DEREK Nexus and SARAH Nexus. The following impurities are found to be potentially mutagenic and control strategy was appropriately established in line with control options per ICH M7 guideline.  
CP-3, originating from SM CP-4, Class 3, Controlled as per ICH M7 Option 3; CP-3 is included in CP-4 specification with a limit of NMT 0.3%. Carry over results on three final API batches demonstrate levels of CP-3 below 30% of TTC.
CP-4, SM, Class 3, controlled as per ICH M7 Option 3; CP-4 is included in CP-6 specification with a limit of NMT 0.3%. Carry over results on three final API batches demonstrate levels of CP-4 below 30% of TTC.
CP-5, API synthesis, Class 3, controlled as per ICH M7 Option 3; Residual CP-5 is monitored and controlled as Individual unspecified impurity within intermediate CP-6 specification with a limit of NMT 0.1%. Carry over results on three final API batches demonstrate levels of CP-4 below 30% of TTC.
CP-6, API synthesis, Class 3, controlled as per ICH M7 Option 1; included  in Sakuramil drug substance specification with limit of NMT 37.5 ppm
For further details on ICH M7 assessment, please refer to [[ICH M7 Risk Assessment]].
Solvents used in the manufacturing process of Sakuramil drug substance are the following : methyl chloroformate, tetrahydrofuran, methanol, ethanol, n-hexane, methylene chloride. Potential residual solvents originating from starting materials are the following: toluene, heptane.Dichloromethane is used in the last step of the synthesis of Sakuramil and only residual dichloromethane is routinely controlled in the drug substance specification with a limit of NMT 600 ppm per ICH Q3C guideline. For all other solvents (ethanol, methanol, n-hexane, tetrahydrofuran, benzene, toluene) carry over results on three API batches  are present demonstrating levels below 10% of the corresponding ICH Q3C limit.
In line with ICH Q3D Guideline for Elemental Impurities, the Risk Assessment was performed in order to identify known and potential sources of elemental impurities in Sakuramil drug substance.
No class 1 elements are intentionally used and hence, not likely to be present in Sakuramil drug substance. Palladium (Pd) – class 2B element - is intentionally added in manufacturing process of SM1 CP-4, controlled in CP4 specification with NMT 10 ppm and therefore also considered in the risk assessment. Lithium (Li) – class 3 element – is intentionally added in form of the reagent Lithium-tert-butoxide. Results of carry over studies according to ICH Q3D guideline are provided in [[2.3.4.DS.C Control (Sakuramil) [IROHA-corp]]].

## 2.1 Control of related substances

### 2.1.1 Chiral Purity and Stereoisomer Control Strategy for Sakuramil
The stereoisomeric integrity of CP-4 and consequently of the final drug substance, Sakuramil is controlled to ensure high chiral purity. The first chiral center is introduced via CP-2 (designated as center “A”), a commercially available chiral building block sourced from the chiral pool. The second chiral center (designated as “B”) is established through a well-precedented, highly stereoselective cyclization reaction, yielding the intermediate CP-6.
Figure 1‑2      Chiral Control: Possible Enantiomers and Diastereomers
[IMAGE:  attachment:4db2b0e8-dc03-4d55-9ff7-fb1b72ed358b:image.png]
Enantiomer Control
The enantiomeric purity of CP-4 is governed by the enantiomeric specification of CP-2, which is controlled to ≤ 1.5% of the undesired enantiomer in accordance with vendor specification. Any enantiomeric impurity in CP-2 introduced at Step 1 would propagate as CP-9-E, an enantiomeric impurity in the final product. However, CP-9-E has been shown to purge effectively to below 0.10% through downstream crystallization steps involving CP-4, CP-6, CP-7, and Sakuramil.
To further substantiate this control strategy, a development study was conducted in which 5% of the off-enantiomer of CP-2 was deliberately introduced in Step A. The resulting material, processed through the full six-step synthesis, yielded Sakuramil with CP-9-E levels ≤ 0.1%, confirming the robustness of the purge. Information about analytical procedure used is available at [[3.2.AP Analytical Procedures (Enantiomeric impurity)[Purity][Sakuramil]]].
Diastereomer Control
Two theoretical trans diastereomers of CP-9 were considered:
- CP-9-D1: Could hypothetically arise from a disallowed cyclization pathway yielding a trans configuration between centers A and B. However, both experimental data and literature confirm that this pathway is not feasible.
- CP-9-D2: Would require both the incorrect enantiomer of CP-2 and the disallowed cyclization or racemization of center B. These conditions have been thoroughly investigated and ruled out as plausible.
Throughout development, no evidence of racemization at center B in CP-6, CP-7, or Sakuramil has been observed.
Analytical Confirmation and Purge Studies
To confirm the stereochemical control strategy, all three stereoisomers of Sakuramil and selected intermediates were synthesized and analyzed using dedicated, validated analytical methods. All manufactured batches of Sakuramil consistently demonstrated ≤ 0.1% of each stereoisomeric impurity.
No racemization or stereochemical erosion was observed during synthesis development, even under stress conditions applied in Steps 3 and 4. This aligns with literature and mechanistic understanding that both chiral centers are chemically stable and not prone to racemization.
A fate and purge study further demonstrated that spiking CP-6 with 1% of its enantiomer (CP-6-E) and diastereomer (CP-6-D) resulted in <0.1% (below the LOQ of 0.05%) of these impurities in the final drug substance.

### 2.1.1 Potentially mutagenic impurities  
The synthetic route for Sakuramil has been thoroughly evaluated for the presence and control of potentially mutagenic impurities (PMIs), in accordance with ICH M7 guidelines.
(Q)SAR Evaluation and Structural Alerts
Intermediates CP-6 and CP-4 have tested positive in both (Q)SAR systems, indicating potential mutagenic risk. Additionally, non-isolated intermediates CP-3 and CP-5 exhibit structural alerts in structure-activity relationship databases due to the presence of an aniline functionality, which is known to be associated with mutagenic potential.
Figure 1‑3      Potentially mutagenic Intermediates and Reactivity
[IMAGE:  attachment:034980fd-c181-404a-a18d-ffd2c87f018f:image.png]
Synthetic Design and Elimination Strategy
The commercial manufacturing process has been strategically designed to mitigate these risks. Specifically, CP-3, CP-5, and CP-6 are all consumed in Step 3 of the synthesis, where the aniline functionality is chemically eliminated. This transformation effectively removes the structural feature responsible for the mutagenic alerts.
Purge and Control Strategy
The reactivity of these intermediates, combined with the hydrophobic nature of downstream products CP-7 and CP-9 (Sakuramil), facilitates efficient purge of residual aniline-containing species. Crystallization steps in both Step 3 and Step 4 further enhance the removal of unreacted anilines and related byproducts.
This integrated control strategy has consistently ensured that PMIs remain within acceptable limits, either under the API specification or within the specifications for starting materials and intermediates.
Supporting Data and Risk Assessment
Comprehensive multivariate development data supporting this control strategy will be presented in this section.Detailed classification of potential and actual impurities according to ICH M7, together with batch results, is presented in  [[ICH M7 Risk Assessment]].

### 2.1.2 Nitrosamine impurities
The synthesis of Sakuramil has been evaluated for the potential formation and presence of nitrosamine impurities, in accordance with current regulatory expectations.
Identified Risk Factors
SM 1 CP-4 contains vulnerable amine. As there is no source of nitrites in Step 1 of Sakuramil manufacturing process there is no risk for formation of corresponding nitrosamine. However, in step 2 CP-5 intermediate, containing vulnerable amine moiety, is converted to CP-6 (also vulnerable amine). In this stage water is used under acidic conditions therefore risk for formation of the corresponding nitrosamines from CP-5 and CP-6 can not be fully excluded. Nevertheless, it is expected that potential nitrosamine of CP-5 would be converted during Step 2 to nitrosamine of CP-6. Therefore, it can be assumed that the levels of nitroso-CP-6, if present, would be significantly higher, than the levels of nitroso-CP-5 and therefore, only nitroso-CP-6 is relevant for further mitigation.
In conclusion, there is a potential risk for nitroso-CP-6 formation in the manufacturing process of Sakuramil drug substance, therefore testing of final drug substance batches is needed.
Conclusion and Control Strategy
While the overall nitrosamine risk in the synthesis of Sakuramil is low, the formation of nitroso-CP-6 remains a potential concern. 
As a result:
Confirmatory testing of three commercial batches of drug substance for N-Nitroso-CP-6 has been performed.  According to the analytical testing results it is demonstrated that the levels of N-nitrosamine impurity are below 10% of acceptable limit.  Therefore, there is no risk for the presence of N-nitrosamine impurity in Sakuramil drug substance and routine testing is not warranted. A detailed assessment, including analysis of risk factors related to manufacturing has been provided in Section 3.2.DS.C
- Nitrosating agents are not expected to be present in the final API.
- CP-6, which contains a secondary amine moiety, is included in the final API specification with a limit of NMT 37.5 ppm.
- Vulnerable amines are present in the final API and are considered in the overall risk assessment and control strategy.
Supporting data and justification will be provided in the multivariate development section and further elaborated in the ICH M7 Risk Assessment ((9+) Nitrosamine Risk Assessment)

### 2.1.3 Residual solvents
In the manufacturing process of Sakuramil, below listed Residual solvents are used.
Dichloromethane is used in the last step of the synthesis of Sakuramil. Residual dichloromethane is routinely controlled in the drug substance specification with a limit of NMT 600 ppm, by means of a headspace gas-chromatography according to USP <467>.
Solvents used in the manufacturing processes of Starting Materials are discussed in section 3.2.SM Starting Materials, where it was shown they are well controlled by starting material specification and are well purged during the manufacturing process. It can be concluded that these impurities do not affect the impurity profile of final drug substance and for this reason they do not need to be controlled with drug substance specification.
Potential residual solvents used in the manufacturing process but not specified in the final drug substance are Ethanol (ICH Class 3 solvent), Methanol (ICH Class 2 solvent), n-Hexane (ICH Class 2 solvent), Tetrahydrofuran (ICH Class 2 solvent) and Benzene (ICH Class 1 solvent) as a potential contaminant from other solvents like Ethanol or Methanol. Toluene (ICH Class 2 solvent) was additionally tested as it is used in the manufacturing process of CP-4.
Presence of these solvents was checked by verified GC analytical method per USP <467> in Sakuramil final drug substance. Information about the analytical procedure used is available at [[2.3.3.AP Analytical Procedures (Residual Solvents) [Residual Solvents][Sakuramil][CP-4]]].

### 2.1.3 Inorganic impurities
1.3.1 Elemental impurities
No metal catalyst is used in Sakuramil DS manufacturing process. Sakuramil DS is evaluated and meets the requirements of ICH Q3D guideline for elemental impurities. 
Screening results for Class 1 (Cd, Pb, As and Hg), Class 2A (Co, V and Ni), Class 2B (Pd), Class 3 (Li) and other elements (Mg and B) in Sakuramil drug substance demonstrate that the concentration of elemental impurities is below 30% of the permitted concentration limit for oral administration for all potentially present elements, therefore, no further controls are necessary. Information about the analytical procedure is available at [[3.2.AP Analytical Procedures (Elemental impurities)[Purity][Sakuramil]]].
Magnesium (Mg) and Boron (B) are only mentioned as “Other elements” in the ICH Q3D guideline for elemental impurities. Magnesium is an element that is also widely distributed in plant and animal food. The Permittable Daily Intake of Magnesium is generally considered with 350 mg Mg/day (FNB, 1997). Maximum daily dose of Sakuramil is 60 mg (= 0.06 g). Permitted concentration of Mg is calculated as 5.83 g/g.
The limit for Boron is calculated according to EMA/CHMP/619104/2013. Oral permitted Daily Exposure (PDE) for boron is 9.6 mg B/day. Maximum daily dose of Sakuramil is 60 mg ( = 0.06 g). Permitted concentration of B is calculated as 160 mg/g.
The limits used for the risk assessment represent permitted concentration limits for oral administration in µg/g for elemental impurities in drug substance when Option 1 (according to ICH Q3D) is selected.
Complete data results are in Module 3  [[Elemental risk assessment]] 
1.3.2 Potential residual inorganic reagents
Inorganic reagents used in the manufacturing process of Sakuramil drug substance (Sodium hydroxide (NaOH), Sodium borohydride (NaBH4), Magnesium chloride (MgCl2), Sodium carbonate (Na2CO3), Lithium-tert-butoxide (LiOtBu), Tetra-n-butylammonium bromide (TBAB) and Hydrochloric acid (HCl)) are potential sources of inorganic impurities in Sakuramil. The fate and purge of inorganic reagents in Sakuramil manufacturing process is provided in continuation.
The level of inorganic impurities that might be present in Sakuramil drug substance was determined by Residue on ignition test with a limit of NMT 0.2% (limit set in accordance with USP <281>). The analytical results of three batches of Sakuramil drug substance show that the content of inorganic impurities is far below 0.2%.

# 2.3.4.DS.C.3 Justification of specifications
Sakuramil is an active substance, which is not subject of an official compendium. The drug substance manufactured at IROHA-corp. meets the in-house requirements which are set based on knowledge acquired during development of Sakuramil drug substance. 
Skip-testing is not applicable for control of Sakuramil drug substance.

# 3.2.AP.1 Analytical Procedure Description

## 1.1 Principle
High-performance liquid chromatography (USP <621>)

## 1.2 Reagents
Reference substances: CP-9 standard
Buffer: Approx. 27.2 mg/ml KH2PO4 in water, pH 5.0 adjusted by addition of NaOH solution 2M.
KH2PO4: analytical grade
NaOH solution 2M: 80 mg/ml NaOH in water
Water: Water for injection
Acetonitrile: analytical grade
Diluent: Acetonitrile: Buffer (1:4)
Blank: Take 5 ml of Acetonitrile and dilute to 50 ml with Diluent

## 1.3 Chromatography
Column: length 250 mm, internal diameter 4.6 mm
Stationary phase: Silica C 18, 3.5 µm, e.g. Nucleosil 250-C 18, 3.5µm
System: isocratic
Mobile Phase: Acetonitrile / Buffer (40:60)
Flow rate: 1.0 mL/min
Oven temperature: 30 ± 1 °C
Sample injection: 10 µl
Detection: UV, 251 nm
Evaluation: Integration of the peaks referring to product; comparison of the retention times of test and reference solution.

## 1.4 Procedure
Test solution:
Approximately 0.1 mg/ml of sample to be examined in diluent.
Reference solution:
Approximately 0.1 mg/ml of CP-9 standard in diluent.

## 1.5 System Suitability Test
Theoretical plates: In the chromatogram of five replicate injections of reference solution, the number of theoretical plates is higher than 3200.
Reproducibility: In the chromatogram of reference solution, the relative standard deviation between peak areas of replicate injections (five injections) is not more than 0.73 %.

## 1.6 Calculation
The content of CP-9 is calculated according to the following formula:
[IMAGE:  Untitled.png]
AM =   Peak area value of CP-9 in the test solution
AS =   Peak area value of CP-9 in the reference solution
CS =   Weight of CP-9 (mg) in the reference solution
CM =   Weight of CP-9 (mg) in the test solution
V =     Assay of CP-9 standard, in %
Report the result “as is”.

# 3.2.AP.2 Analytical Procedure Validation/Qualification 
For determination of assay of Sakuramil an HPLC method was developed and validated by IROHA-corp. The method is validated in terms of specificity, linearity, range, accuracy, precision, intermediate precision, system suitability and stability of the test solutions.

## 2.1 Acceptance Criteria and Summary
In the present report, validation results of the assay test (HPLC) as described in DMF section [[2.3.4.AP Analytical Procedures (Assay/ID) [Assay/Identification] [Sakuramil]]] are compiled and evaluated.
For assay determination by HPLC, specificity, linearity, range, accuracy, precision, intermediate precision, system suitability and stability of the test solutions were considered as analytical performance characteristics according to current ICH guideline Q2(R2) Validation of Analytical Procedures.
Following acceptance criteria have been defined in a method validation protocol.
Table 2‑1 Acceptance criteria
| Validation Parameter | Acceptance Criteria | Results |
| Specificity / System Suitability Requirements | · Analyte peak of CP-9 is sufficiently separated from all other peaks; no peak is interfering with the CP-9 peak (Resolution ≥ 2.0) · Theoretical Plates (n=5): > 3200 · Reproducibility (n=5): ≤ 0.73 % | · Resolution = 12.1 · Theoretical Plates = 5686 · Reproducibility = 0.18 % |
| Solution Stability | Change in assay within specified time relative to the initial value:  ≤ 1.0 % | During the tested time period the relative change of CP-9 peak areas is within respective acceptance criterion (≤ 1.0 %). |
| Linearity | By visual inspection, the residuals/responses are randomly distributed                                    Correlation coefficient : R ≥ 0.998                              Y-intercept : ≤ 2.0 %                                          Residual standard deviation : ≤ 2.0 %                              | The residuals/responses are randomly distributed                                    Correlation coefficient = R 1.0459                              Y-intercept =  0.9997 %                                          Residual standard deviation = 0.060 %           |
| Range    | · Minimum 60 to 130 % target concentration          ·  If acceptance criteria for linearity are fulfilled, range of the method is demonstrated.  | The method has been validated for a range of 60% to 130% of the concentration examined (0.1 mg/ml of Sakuramil) |
| Precision | n ≥ 6; RSD ≤ 1.0 % | n = 6; RSD = 0.2 % |
| Intermediate Precision | n ≥ 12; RSD ≤ 1.0 % | n = 12; RSD = 0.3 % |
| Accuracy | Inferred from precision, linearity and specificity. •Acceptance criteria for these validation parameters are fulfilled.                                                    Maximum difference of individual results to mean result obtained from linearity data (n ≥ 6): Δ ≤ 1.0 % abs.                                                                 Individual recovery rates between 97-103 % | RSD (n=6) = 0.003 - 0.004 % Recovery between 99.9 and 100.1 % |
Evaluation of the results confirmed that this HPLC method is suitable for the intended use at IROHA-corp. laboratories. Validation parameters specificity, linearity, range, accuracy, precision as well as stability of the solutions could be demonstrated. Furthermore, the required system suitability criteria for theoretical plates and reproducibility fulfill the respective acceptance criteria. Therefore, also accuracy of the method could be confirmed under the actual conditions of use.

## 2.2 Experimental Details

### 2.2.1 Documentation
The raw data of this validation have been documented in the laboratory of IROHA-corp. where the experiments have been executed.

### 2.2.2 Validation Protocol
Validation experiments are carried out according to a previously approved method validation protocol.

### 2.2.3 Analytical Method(s)
The analytical instrument(s) and test conditions applied are described in section 3.2.AP.1 Analytical Procedure Description of [[3.2.AP Analytical Procedures (Assay/ID) [Assay/Identification][Sakuramil]]].

## 2.3 Results

### 2.3.1 Specificity / System Suitability Requirements

Furthermore, for evaluation of selectivity and potential carry-over, individual solutions of CP-8, CP-9-1 and CP-9 identification standard were injected. The system suitability requirements of theoretical plates and reproducibility calculated from 5 consecutive injections of the reference solution were examined and tabulated below.

### 2.3.8 Stability indicating Capability
Forced degradation studies on Sakuramil drug substance test sample was performed together with the method for determination of related substances, please refer to section [[3.2.AP Analytical Procedures (Related Substances)[Purity][Sakuramil]]]  for details and results. Forced degradation study showed that the chromatographic method for Assay is stability indicating.

## 2.4 Conclusion
Evaluation of the results confirmed that the HPLC method used for assay determination in Sakuramil is suitable for the intended use at IROHA-corp. laboratories. Validation parameter specificity, precision / repeatability, linearity, range, accuracy and intermediate precision as well as adequate stability of reference solution and test solution could be demonstrated. Furthermore, the required system suitability criteria of theoretical plates and reproducibility fulfill the respective acceptance criteria.

# 3.2.AP.1 Analytical Procedure Description
Analytical method is performed in-line with USP <467> Procedure A, compendial GC method.

# 3.2.AP.2 Analytical Procedure Validation/Qualification 
For the determination of residual solvents, a compendial GC method (USP <467> Procedure A) is used. The method is verified in accordance with USP <1467> Residual Solvents – Verification of compendial procedures and validation of alternative procedures. Verification of compendial methods for limit tests like Residual solvents includes the parameters specificity, detection limit (LOD) and solution stability.

## 2.1 Acceptance Criteria and Summary
In the present report, verification results of the determination of residual solvents test (GC) as described in USP <467> Procedure A are compiled and evaluated.
The method considers the specified residual solvent from Sakuramil drug substance. Specified residual solvent as per DMF section [[2.3.3.DS.C Control (Sakuramil) [IROHA-corp]]]  is Dichloromethane. Additionally, the method is used for determination of the IPC Ethanol (IPC #2).
The analytical procedure can be stated validated in accordance with ICH Q2(R2) and used for GxP release analysis of Sakuramil at IROHA-corp.
For determination of residual solvents by GC, specificity, limit of detection (LOD) and stability of the test solutions were considered as analytical performance characteristics according to USP <1467> Residual Solvents—Verification of Compendial Procedures and Validation of Alternative Procedures and current ICH guideline Q2(R2) Validation of Analytical Procedures. USP <1467> is focusing on Class 1 and 2 solvents, however, the same procedure was applied for Ethanol determination in order to ensure that the method is suitable under actual conditions of use.
Following acceptance criteria have been defined in a method verification protocol.
Table 2‑1 Acceptance criteria
| Verification Parameter | Acceptance Criteria | Results |
| Specificity / System Suitability Requirements | · Reagent blank does not produce any significant interference with any of the other peaks from solvents Dichloromethane and Ethanol.  · Separation of the solvent peaks in the standard solution from other peaks in the spiked sample solution (Resolution: NLT 1.0). | Resolution standard solution:  Dimethylformamide / Dichloromethane = 9.9 Dimethylformamide / Ethanol = 6.4 Ethanol / Dichloromethane = 5.8 Spiked sample solution:  Dimethylformamide / Dichloromethane = 10.1 Dimethylformamide / Ethanol = 6.3 Ethanol / Dichloromethane = 5.8 |
| Limit of Detection (LOD) | S/N ≥ 3 (n = NLT 3) | LOD = 6 ppm |
| Stability of Solutions | Detection limit for limit tests should be met throughout the testing period | For the spiked sample solution #B221157 the respective acceptance criteria of relative change are fulfilled for 28 hours for Dichloromethane and Ethanol. Standard solution: During the tested time period the relative change of Dichloromethane and Ethanol peak areas is within respective acceptance criterion (≤ 10 % relative change with respect to initial). |
Evaluation of the results confirmed that the GC method is suitable for determination of the residual solvents in Sakuramil drug substance tested at IROHA-corp. laboratories. Verification parameters specificity and limit of detection (LOD) fulfill the respective acceptance criteria.
Additionally, the stability of standard solution and test solution stored in the autosampler at RT (25°C) have been demonstrated. A holdup time of at least 28 hours was defined for both standard and test solution.

## 2.2 Experimental Details

### 2.2.1 Documentation
The raw data of this verification have been documented in the laboratory of IROHA-corp. where the experiments have been executed.

### 2.2.2 Verification Protocol
Verification experiments are carried out according to a previously approved method verification protocol.

### 2.2.3 Analytical Method(s)
The analytical instrument(s) and test conditions applied are described in USP <467> Procedure A.

### 2.3.1 Specificity / System Suitability Requirements

## 2.4 Conclusion
Evaluation of the results confirmed that the GC method used for determination of residual solvents Dichloromethane and IPC Ethanol in Sakuramil is suitable for the intended use at IROHA-corp. laboratories. Verification parameter specificity and limit of detection (LOD) fulfill the respective acceptance criteria.
Additionally, the stability of reference solution and test solution stored at RT have been demonstrated. A possible holdup time of at least 28 hours was defined for both standard solution and spiked sample solution.
The analytical procedure can be stated validated and used for GxP release analysis of Sakuramil at IROHA-corp.

# 3.2.AP.2 Analytical Procedure Validation/Qualification 
For determination of potentially mutagenic impurities of Sakuramil an HPLC method was developed and validated by IROHA-corp. The method is validated in terms of specificity, linearity, precision (repeatability, intermediate precision and system precision), limit of quantification (LOQ), limit of detection (LOD), range, accuracy, robustness, system suitability and stability of the test solutions.

## 2.1 Acceptance Criteria and Summary
In the present report, validation results of the determination of  potentially mutagenic impurities (HPLC) as described in DMF section [[2.3.3.AP Analytical Procedures (Potentially mutagentic Impurities) [Potentially mutagenic Impurities] [Sakuramil]]] are compiled and evaluated.
The method considers the specified impurity from Sakuramil drug substance as well as total impurities. The specified impurity as per DMF section [[2.3.3.DS.C Control (Sakuramil) [IROHA-corp]]] is CP-6.
The analytical procedure can be stated validated in accordance with ICH Q2(R2) and used for GxP release analysis of Sakuramil at IROHA-corp.
For determination of potentially mutagenic impurities by HPLC, specificity, linearity, range, accuracy, precision (repeatability, intermediate precision and system precision), limit of quantification (LOQ), limit of detection (LOD), system suitability and stability of the test solutions were considered as analytical performance characteristics according to current ICH guideline Q2(R2) Validation of Analytical Procedures.

### 2.3.14.2 Evaluation of Data
Evaluation was carried out by visual examination of chromatograms and purity graphical plot in addition by UV-diode array peak purity.
The impurities (> 0.10 %) as well as the observed degradation level calculated as decrease of the CP-9 peak area normalized to actual sample weight compared to the original sample chromatogram are quantified and reported.
Table 2‑29 Detector settings
| Detector parameter | DAD Value for impurities | DAD Value for Sakuramil (diluted 1:10) |
| Peak Purity Start Wavelength | λ = 210 | λ = 210 |
| Peak Purity End Wavelength | λ = 400 | λ = 400 |
| Peak Purity Threshold | 10 % | 0.1 % |
| Enable background subtraction | Yes | Yes |
| Peak spectrum bunch | With 5 spectra | With 5 spectra |
Evaluation of Recorded Spectra:
- Each of these spectra is compared with the average spectrum (n = 5) of the chromatographic peak. Correspondence is expressed via a similarity factor with values between 1000 (identical spectra) and 0 (no match).
- The plot of similarity factors along the chromatographic peak gives the similarity curve.
- A purity factor is calculated taking both the similarity and threshold values into account (values between 1000 and 0).
Calculation of the Peak Purity:
- The mean of all purity values gives the purity factor (= match factor).
- The match factor is calculated for the CP-9 peak as well as for impurity peaks > 0.10 %.
Acceptance Criteria Stability-Indicating Testing / Peak Purity:
- adequate selectivity is given
- observed level > 70.0 % → match factor ≥ 995.0
- observed level > 5.0 % → match factor ≥ 950.0
- observed level > 0.5 % → match factor ≥ 900.0
- observed level > 0.1 % → match factor ≥ 800.0

Sakuramil (#B221157) test sample was stressed at 90 °C for 14 days in closed glass vial inside a drying oven. Due to the intrinsic stability of the material only slight degradation in the order of approx. 1 % was observed.

## 2.4 Conclusion
Evaluation of the results confirmed that the HPLC method used for determination of related substances in Sakuramil is suitable for the intended use at IROHA-corp. laboratories. Validation parameter specificity, linearity, precision (repeatability, intermediate precision and system precision), limit of quantification (LOQ), limit of detection (LOD), range, accuracy and robustness as well as stability indicating capability fulfill the respective acceptance criteria.
Robustness of the method with regards to variation of following chromatographic conditions is given:
- column temperature: 23 to 30 °C
- flow rate: 1.1 to 1.3 mL/min
- pH of eluents: 4.8 to 5.0
- variation of column lot
Additionally, the stability of reference solution and test solution stored at RT have been demonstrated. A possible holdup time of at least 28 hours was defined for the reference solution and of maximum of 20 hours for the test solution, respectively.
Furthermore, following response correction factors in relation to Sakuramil (RCFs to be multiplied with) were determined:
CP-6=1.19
From evaluation of the data following system suitability test criteria were defined:
Resolution: In the chromatogram of the reference solution, the resolution between the peaks of CP-6 and CP-9 is not less than 1.5.
Reproducibility: In the chromatogram of reference solution, the relative standard deviation between peak areas of replicate injections (six injections) of CP-9 is not more than 1.0%.
The analytical procedure can be stated validated and used for GxP release analysis of Sakuramil at IROHA-corp.

Not applicable

# 3.2.AP.2 Analytical Procedure Validation/Qualification 
For determination of related substances of Sakuramil an HPLC method was developed and validated by IROHA-corp. The method is validated in terms of specificity, linearity, precision (repeatability, intermediate precision and system precision), limit of quantification (LOQ), limit of detection (LOD), range, accuracy, robustness, system suitability and stability of the test solutions.

## 2.1 Acceptance Criteria and Summary
In the present report, validation results of the determination of related substances test (HPLC) as described in DMF section [[2.3.3.AP Analytical Procedures (Related Substances)[Purity][Sakuramil]]]  are compiled and evaluated.
The method considers all specified impurities from Sakuramil drug substance as well as unspecified impurities. Specified impurities as per DMF section [[2.3.3.DS.C Control (Sakuramil) [IROHA-corp]]]  are CP-8 and CP-9-1.
The analytical procedure can be stated validated in accordance with ICH Q2(R2) and used for GxP release analysis of Sakuramil at IROHA-corp.
For determination of related substances by HPLC, specificity, linearity, range, accuracy, precision (repeatability, intermediate precision and system precision), limit of quantification (LOQ), limit of detection (LOD), system suitability and stability of the test solutions were considered as analytical performance characteristics according to current ICH guideline Q2(R2) Validation of Analytical Procedures.

### 2.3.13 Stability indicating Capability
To demonstrate that the methods used for determination of related substances and assay in Sakuramil are stability indicating, forced degradation studies were performed on Sakuramil test sample (#B221157). The objective of these experiments was to provoke the formation of degradation products under various stress conditions and to demonstrate that these impurities are adequately separated using the described HPLC systems. Determination of related substances is performed according to procedure described in section [[2.3.3.AP Analytical Procedures (Related Substances)[Purity][Sakuramil]]]. Determination of assay is performed according to procedure described in section [[2.3.3.AP Analytical Procedures (Assay/ID) [Assay/Identification][Sakuramil]]].

### 2.3.13.2 Evaluation of Data
Evaluation was carried out by visual examination of chromatograms and purity graphical plot in addition by UV-diode array peak purity.
The impurities (> 0.10 %) as well as the observed degradation level calculated as decrease of the CP-9 peak area normalized to actual sample weight compared to the original sample chromatogram are quantified and reported.

|  | Impurities | Sakuramil (diluted 1:10) |

| Peak Purity End Wavelength | λ = 400 | λ = 400 |

| Enable background subtraction | Yes | Yes |
| Peak spectrum bunch | With 5 spectra | With 5 spectra |
Evaluation of Recorded Spectra:
- Each of these spectra is compared with the average spectrum (n = 5) of the chromatographic peak. Correspondence is expressed via a similarity factor with values between 1000 (identical spectra) and 0 (no match).
- The plot of similarity factors along the chromatographic peak gives the similarity curve.
- A purity factor is calculated taking both the similarity and threshold values into account (values between 1000 and 0).
Calculation of the Peak Purity:
- The mean of all purity values gives the purity factor (= match factor).
- The match factor is calculated for the CP-9 peak as well as for impurity peaks > 0.10 %.
Acceptance Criteria Stability-Indicating Testing / Peak Purity:
- adequate selectivity is given
- observed level > 70.0 % → match factor ≥ 995.0
- observed level > 5.0 % → match factor ≥ 950.0
- observed level > 0.5 % → match factor ≥ 900.0
- observed level > 0.1 % → match factor ≥ 800.0

### 2.3.13.12 Conclusion of forced degradation study
Forced degradation study results showed that the chromatographic methods for determination of related substances and assay are stability indicating with respect to the described conditions. No relevant increase of related substances was observed when the substance was exposed to light stress (conditions according to ICH Q1B). Thus, the product can be considered photostable. No interference of degradation products with known by-products was detected (apart from conditions in presence of copper(III) ions). The largest unknown degradation product was observed at oxidative conditions (12.48 % at RT 5.50).

## 2.4 Conclusion
Evaluation of the results confirmed that the HPLC method used for determination of related substances in Sakuramil is suitable for the intended use at IROHA-corp. laboratories. Validation parameter specificity, linearity, precision (repeatability, intermediate precision and system precision), limit of quantification (LOQ), limit of detection (LOD), range, accuracy and robustness as well as stability indicating capability fulfill the respective acceptance criteria.
Robustness of the method with regards to variation of following chromatographic conditions is given:
- column temperature: 23 to 30 °C
- flow rate: 1.1 to 1.3 mL/min
- pH of eluents: 4.8 to 5.0
- variation of column lot
Additionally, the stability of reference solution and test solution stored at RT have been demonstrated. A possible holdup time of at least 28 hours was defined for the reference solution and of maximum of 20 hours for the test solution, respectively.
Furthermore, following response correction factors in relation to Sakuramil (RCFs to be multiplied with) were determined:
CP-9-1=  1.23
CP-8=      2.01
From evaluation of the data following system suitability test criteria were defined:
Resolution: In the chromatogram of the identification solution, the resolution between the peaks of CP-8 and CP-9, and CP-9-1 and CP-9 is not less than 1.5.
Reproducibility: In the chromatogram of reference solution, the relative standard deviation between peak areas of replicate injections (six injections) of CP-9 is not more than 1.0%.
Forced degradation study results showed that the chromatographic methods for determination of related substances and assay are stability indicating with respect to the described conditions.
The analytical procedure can be stated validated and used for GxP release analysis of Sakuramil at IROHA-corp.

### 3.2.AP.1 Analytical Procedure Description
Purpose and scope
This procedure is used to detect and quantify ICH-M7 alerting, process-related impurities CP-3, CP-4 and CP-5 in the drug substance (Sakuramil) for confirmatory testing to verify the purge argument that supports Option 3 per ICH M7.
Analytical principle
Quantification is performed by reversed-phase LC coupled to mass spectrometry (LC–MS/MS) using electrospray ionization in positive mode and multiple-reaction monitoring (MRM). The LC separation provides selectivity against matrix components; MS/MS provides sensitivity at sub-ppm levels.
Typical conditions (representative; exact tuned values are recorded in the method record AP-MI-LCMS-01)
- Column: C18, ~100 × 2.1 mm, ~1.7–3 µm.
- Mobile phases: A = water with ~0.1% formic acid; B = acetonitrile with ~0.1% formic acid.
- Gradient: initial 5–10% B to 90–95% B in ~8–10 min; total run ≤ 15 min.
- Flow/temperature/injection: ~0.30 mL·min⁻¹ / 35–45 °C / 2–10 µL.
- Detection: MRM transitions individually optimized for CP-3, CP-4, CP-5; qualifier/quantifier ion-ratio acceptance ±20% of calibrator at comparable response.
- Internal standard (IS): a stable-isotope-labelled or suitable structural analogue; single-point IS normalization is used for drift and matrix-effect correction.
Solutions and sample preparation
- Stock standards: ~0.1 mg/mL of each impurity in acetonitrile.
- Mixed working standards: prepare at ~0.3×, 0.5×, 1.0×, and 1.5× of the reporting level (see below).
- Sample: dissolve API to ~10 mg/mL in water:acetonitrile (1:1, v/v), spike with IS, vortex, and filter (0.22 µm PTFE or PVDF; filter-compatibility verified).
- Matrix-matched calibration: performed in API matrix (blank API demonstrated free of targets) to mitigate matrix effects.
System suitability
Prior to analysis:
- S/N at the LOQ standard ≥ 10 (each analyte).
- Peak tailing ≤ 2.0 for all targets; IS-normalized area RSD for five replicate injections ≤ 10%.
- MRM ion-ratio criteria met for standards and samples (±20% window).
Reportable units and limits
Results are reported as µg/g (ppm) relative to API. The analytical reporting level is set at or below the M7 acceptable-intake-based limit (AI/MDD), and, for this product, has been fixed at ≤ 10 ppm (individual) to align with the purge-verification strategy; the method is designed to achieve LOQ ≤ 30% of the reporting level (≤ 3 ppm) and typically achieves ≤ 1 ppm for all three impurities.
> Note on control strategy: > > > CP-3 (formed in situ), CP-4 (starting material) and CP-5 (in situ intermediate) are controlled upstream (e.g., CP-4 spec NMT 0.3%, CP-6 spec NMT 0.1%) and by demonstrated purge to < 10 ppm in the final API. Confirmatory testing of the first three commercial API batches and periodic verification (skip-lot) are performed with this LC–MS/MS method. >

### 3.2.AP.2 Analytical Procedure Validation/Qualification
Validation was performed in line with ICH Q2(R2) terminology and principles and, where relevant, the method design/knowledge elements of ICH Q14 (e.g., deliberate variability studies to establish a robust operating region). Unless stated otherwise, acceptance criteria follow common practice for M7 trace analysis: LOQ ≤ 30% of the reporting level; trueness 80–120% (≥ 70–130% at LOQ); repeatability RSD ≤ 15% (≤ 20% at LOQ); coefficient of determination (R) ≥ 0.99. A full data package is available in report AP-VAL-MI-Sakura-01.
Selectivity/Identification capability
- No interfering peaks at the retention times of CP-3, CP-4, CP-5 or IS in reagent blank, placebo, or API matrix.
- MRM qualifier/quantifier ion ratios in samples met ±20% acceptance versus standards at similar responses, confirming identity.
Calibration model and working range
- Matrix-matched calibration over 0.3× to 1.5× of the reporting level using ≥ 5 levels (plus LOQ).
- Weighted (1/x) linear regression; R ≥ 0.99 for all analytes; back-calculated levels within ±15% (±20% at LOQ).
Detection capability (LOD/LOQ)
- LOQ established by S/N ≥ 10 and precision/trueness criteria; achieved LOQs ≤ 1 ppm for CP-3, CP-4, CP-5 (≤ 10% of the 10-ppm reporting level).
- LOD estimated as ~⅓ of LOQ (S/N ≥ 3).
Trueness (recovery) and precision
- Trueness: triplicate spike-recoveries at LOQ, 0.5×, 1.0× across three API batches: 98–107% (LOQ: 90–110%).
- Repeatability: six independent preparations at the reporting level: RSD ≤ 6%.
- Intermediate precision: different day/analyst/instrument: RSD ≤ 10% at the reporting level; ≤ 15% at LOQ.
System suitability acceptance criteria (for routine use)
- S/N (LOQ) ≥ 10; IS-normalized peak-area RSD (n=5) ≤ 10%; retention-time RSD ≤ 2%; ion-ratio within ±20% of calibrator.

### Table 1 Uniformity of dosage units (NIR) (RTRT)
| Method Attribute | Conditions |
| Technique | Analytical procedure principle: ·       Near infrared absorption spectrometry. ·       The spectrum for each test tablet is collected following the acquisition of the background spectrum from the empty reference position on the sample wheel. ·       Select not less than 100 uncoated core tablets for testing. |
| Quantification analysis | The measured NIR spectra are evaluated by the QUANT method and single results for each tablet with the associated Mahalanobis distance is calculated. |
| Statistical Spectral Quality Test | The Mahalanobis distance limit is used automatically by the software to determine whether the characteristics of the sample fall within the range of variation for which the model was calibrated and validated. |
| System suitability | Must be performed and passed daily before any GxP acquisition, for the specific measurement channel (i.e. external transmission) to be used that day. |

## 1 Potentially mutagenic impurities – ICH M7 Risk Assessment
Risk Assessment has been carried out according to ICH M7 guideline including classification of impurities with respect to mutagenic and carcinogenic potential based on literature data or in silico (Q)SAR assessment of impurities (using DEREK Nexus, SARAH Nexus). Results are provided in table below.
CP-6 (including enantiomer and diastereomer) and CP-4 (including enantiomer) have been tested positive in both (Q)SAR systems. The intermediate CP-5 and precursor intermediate CP-3 (non-isolated intermediates) exhibit positive structural alerts in a structure activity relationship database with the same aniline functionality. However, due to design of the manufacturing synthesis, these three intermediated and CP-4 are reacted in Step 3 to eliminate the aniline functionality responsible for the potential mutagenic characteristics. The reactivity of these potentially mutagenic impurities and intermediates together with the hydrophobicity of formed CP-7 and CP-9 (Sakuramil), in addition to, the Steps 3 and 4 crystallizations have excellent purge of the resulting unreacted drug aniline and byproducts, have consistently enabled control of these potentially mutagenic impurities in Sakuramil drug substance to a total of four (CP-6, CP-5, CP-4 and CP-3) of ≤ 37.5 ppm (37.5 ppm is the concentration limit of potentially mutagenic impurities of Sakuramil based on the highest dose). Concentration limit is calculated by dividing TTC by Maximum daily dose. TTC value is 1.5 µg/day as per ICH M7 guideline. Maximum daily dose of Sakuramil is 40 mg (= 0.04 g).
The aniline group that is responsible for the mutagenicity is classified by IARC (International Agency for Research on Cancer) as Group 3 according to ICH M7 guideline with a lifetime permissible daily exposure (PDE) of 720 µg/day.
Solvents, inorganic acids or salts are not covered by this risk assessment as these are controlled by other ICH guidelines.

### 1.1 Methodology
Hazard assessment of impurities in the Sakuramil synthesis involved:
- Initial analysis of actual and potential impurities by conducting database and literature searches for carcinogenicity and bacterial mutagenicity data
- Classification of impurities with respect to mutagenic and carcinogenic potential based on literature data
- (Q)SAR assessment of impurities for which literature data are not available using
  1. DEREK Nexus (Lhasa Ltd.)
  1. SARAH Nexus (Lhasa Ltd.)
- Classification of impurities with respect to mutagenic and carcinogenic potential based on (Q)SAR predictions and expert knowledge

### 1.4 Rational for classification
Class 5 substances
Substances were shown to be negative for mutagenicity with both (Q)SAR systems. Based on the consensus (Q)SAR predictions, substances were deemed to lack mutagenic potential and were therefore considered as class 5 substances. For ethyl chloroformate and methyl chloroformate predictions to be negative for mutagenicity were used as a basis for classification.
Class 3 substances
Substances that were positive in both (Q)SAR systems. All of them containing an aniline group. As per Table for Classification of substances, Class 3 substances show alerting structure and are unrelated to the structure of the drug substance. 

### 2 Control Strategy
All of these substances are controlled either within Sakuramil drug substance specification, Starting Material CP-4 specification or Intermediate CP-6 specification. 
CP-3 is controlled in CP-4 Starting Material specification with a limit of NMT 0.3%, CP-4 is controlled in CP-6 Intermediate specification with a limit of NMT 0.3%, CP-5 is controlled as unspecified impurity in CP-6 Intermediate specification with a limit of NMT 0.1% as per Option 3 and CP-6 is controlled in the active substance specification with a limit of NMT 37.5 ppm as per Option 1. Therefore it is ensured that all potentially mutagenic impurities are well controlled in accordance with ICH M7.

The following compendial excipients are used for the formulation of Sakura Bloom 20 mg Film-coated tablets. They comply with the quality requirements of the listed compendial monographs.

### Table 1-1 List of Excipients and compendial status
| Description | Function | Control  |
| Lactose monohydrate/Lactose hydrate | Diluent | Ph. Eur., USP/NF, JP |
| Cellulose, microcrystalline/ Microcrystalline cellulose | Diluent | Ph. Eur., USP/NF, JP |
| Croscarmellose sodium | Disintegrant | Ph. Eur., USP/NF, JP |
| Hydroxypropyl cellulose | Binder | Ph. Eur., USP/NF, JP |
| Magnesium stearate | Lubricant | Ph. Eur., USP/NF, JP |
| Water, purified/Purified water (Note 1) | Solvent for coating suspension | Ph. Eur., USP/NF, JP |
Note 1: Purified water is used in the manufacturing. The water is removed during processing.
Adventitious Agents Safety Evaluation
Lactose monohydrate is the only excipient of animal origin.  The declarations of lactose compliance with EMA Note for guidance on minimizing the risk of transmitting animal spongiform encephalopathy agents via human and veterinary medicinal products, EMA/410/01 rev.3, 2011/C 73/01 are available in Figure 1 and Figure 2 of section [[3.2.EX Compendial excipients]]. Based on the statements provided by the suppliers and to the best of our knowledge, there is no risk of transmitting Transmissible Spongiform Encephalopathies (TSE) through the excipients.
Additional details pertaining to the lactose monohydrate of animal origin are shared in Table-1 of section [[3.2.EX Compendial excipients]].
The magnesium stearate used is of vegetable origin. 
Relevant certificates of analysis and copy of monographs are made available under [3.2.EX.1].

### Table 1-1 Summary
| Principle | The visual comparison of the colour of a film made from both the test substance and in-house reference substance. |
| Equipment | 1.     Device for film production 2.     White cardboard 3.     Propeller-type stirrer or blender |
| Procedure | Dispersion: Disperse 20 mg of test substance in 60 ml of de-ionized water. 15 mL of the dispersion are needed to prepare a film on a UGC-2 card.  Prepare a dispersion also for the in-house reference substance in the same manner. |
| Evaluation | Compare the colour of the film against a film of the in-house reference substance. The test substance is deemed acceptable if the colour of the film matches that of the authentic reference substance. |
| Alternative | The dispersion may also be prepared using an “Eppendorf” reaction vessel and a Vortex with 10 mg of test substance. |

# 1. Excipient controls - Justification of specifications

## 1.1 Compendial excipients
The excipients used in the formulation of Sakura Bloom 20 mg Film-coated tablet are compendial and comply with the references mentioned in Table-1-1 in section [2.3.3. EX].
All compendial excipients comply with the quality requirements of the applicable pharmacopoeial monographs and justification of the compendial specifications is therefore not provided. For the tests appearing in the compendial monograph of the excipients, no re-validation of analytical procedures is deemed necessary.
Adventitious Agents Safety Evaluation
Lactose monohydrate used in Sakura Bloom 20 mg Film-coated tablet is the only excipient of animal origin. The declarations of lactose compliance with EMA Note for guidance on minimizing the risk of transmitting animal spongiform encephalopathy agents via human and veterinary medicinal products, EMA/410/01 rev.3, 2011/C 73/01 are available in Figure 1  and Figure 2 of section [[3.2.EX Compendial excipients]]. Based on the statements provided by the suppliers and to the best of our knowledge, there is no risk of transmitting Transmissible Spongiform Encephalopathies (TSE) through the excipients.
Additional details pertaining to the lactose monohydrate of animal origin are shared in Table-1 of section [[3.2.EX Compendial excipients]].

pages.text:
# 1. Excipient controls - Justification of specifications

## 1.1 Film-coating premix
The basic coating premix red is a combination of ingredients established for use in medicinal products and is commercially available.  A monograph for the premix itself does not appear in any pharmacopoeia, however, the ingredients of the basic coating premix red meet compendial requirements and international standards. 
The test for total ash, identity by IR and for identity of iron of the basic coating premix red meet the requirements of pharmacopoeia and/or international standards, validation of this analytical procedure is deemed unnecessary. Similarly, validation of analytical procedures performed by visual examination is not deemed necessary.

### Information on the characterization
The primary working standard batch SAKU_20220114, prepared at laboratory scale using the same manufacturing process as described in section 2.3.3.DS.M, has been fully characterized and validated for use in analytical testing. Its comprehensive characterization, including mass spectrometry, ^1H NMR, and ^13C NMR, confirms its suitability as a working standard. This batch serves as the CP-9 working standard for HPLC-based identification, assay, related substances, and potentially mutagenic impurities testing, ensuring consistency and reliability in analytical evaluations.

## Information on the characterization
The CP-9 identification standard, batch no. SAKU_ID_Std_04, was prepared in-house by spiking a selected batch of Sakuramil with known impurities CP-9-1 and CP-8. This mixture is used for the determination of related substances by HPLC. The identification standard and its constituent impurities were fully characterized using in-house analytical methods, including mass spectrometry, ^1H NMR, and ^13C NMR. This confirms the suitability of the CP-9 identification standard for its intended analytical application.

## 2.3.4.AP.1 Analytical Procedure Justification
A high performance liquid chromatography method with UV detection has been developed for the identification by comparing relative retention time and UV-spectrum with a reference standard and allowing an accurate determination of the assay and impurity. 

## 2.3.4.AP.2 Analytical Procedure Validation/Qualification
This summary includes the tested performance characteristics, acceptance criteria, and results of validation. The results of the validation demonstrate that the HPLC method is sufficiently specific, accurate, and precise to determine the identity of sakuramil. The test method performance was evaluated based on ICH Q2(R2) and meets all validation criteria as listed in the table below.

| Range (60% - 130%) | R ≥ 0.998 Res SD ≤ 2.0 % | 0.997 0.060 |

| Precision (n=6) | RSD ≤ 1.0 % | 0.2 % |

## 2.3.4.AP.1 Analytical Procedure Justification
Analytical method for determination of residual solvents is performed in-line with USP <467> Procedure A, compendial GC method. Adjusted compendial procedures has been validated.

## 2.3.4.AP.2 Analytical Procedure Validation/Qualification
For determination of residual solvents by GC, specificity, limit of detection (LOD) and stability of the test solutions were considered as analytical performance characteristics according to USP <1467> Residual Solvents—Verification of Compendial Procedures and Validation of Alternative Procedures and current ICH guideline Q2(R2) Validation of Analytical Procedures. USP <1467> is focusing on Class 1 and 2 solvents, however, the same procedure was applied for Ethanol determination in order to ensure that the method is suitable under actual conditions of use.

## 2.3.4.AP.1 Analytical Procedure Justification
A High Performance liquid chromatography procedure with gradient program and UV detection has been developed to separate the 2 specified impurities CP-8 and CP 9-1 from the active substance. Stress studies have shown that the active peak and both impurities remain pure and are not co-eluting with other degradation products. The method allows the quantification of the impurities down to 0.03 %.
