# 3.2.DS.M.1 Description of Manufacturing process
Manufacturing process description for each process step along with corresponding CPPs, IPCs and their control ranges/acceptance criteria at each step are given below. Description includes also quantities of raw materials used. 

### Step 1 (CP-4 to CP-5)
CP-4 (175-185 kg), Methyl chloroformate (55-120 L) are combined. Lithium-tert-butoxide (22-85 kg) is added and stirred. To the mixture, tetrahydrofuran (750-920 L) is added and stirred. The layers are settled and separated. The resulting precipitates are filtered, rinsed with tetrahydrofuran and dried at temperatures up to 50°C to yield CP-5. Yield: Approximately 200 kg of Intermediate CP-5. About 91% in theory
Table 1‑1 Material stoichiometry in the synthesis of CP-5
|  | Name of material | Ratio [mol/mol] |
| Input | Starting Material CP-4 | 1 |
|  | Methyl chloroformate | 1.8 – 5.4 |
|  | Lithium-tert-butoxide | 0.45 – 2.0 |
|  | Tetrahydrofuran | 5 – 12 |
| Output | In situ Intermediate CP-5 | 1.3 |
Table 1-2: CPPs and IPCs of Step 1
| Critical Process Parameters | In-process Controls |
| N/A | N/A |

### Step 2 (CP-5 to CP-6)
CP-5 (195-210 kg), Sodium borohydride (480-2120 kg), Magnesium chloride (22-35 kg) and methanol (105-320 L) are combined. Upon reaction completion, the mixtures is filtered, and to the filtrate hydrochloric acid (54-59 L) is added and stirred. The layers are settled and separated. The organic layer is concentrated by distillation with ethanol for the solvents exchange (final concentration 1000 L). Water (25 to 35% weight per weight of ethanol) is added and the mixture is stirred at 14 to 26°C. The resulting crystalline precipitates are filtered, rinsed with ethanol, and dried at temperatures up to 50°C to yield CP-6. Yield: About 235 kg of Intermediate CP-6, About 87% in theory
Table 1‑3 Material stoichiometry CP-6
|  | Name of material | Ratio [mol/mol] |
| Input | In situ Intermediate CP-5 | 1 |
|  | Sodium borohydride | 2.6 – 10.5 |
|  | Magnesium chloride | 0.35 – 1.1 |
|  | Methanol | 0.7 – 3.2 |
|  | Hydrochloric acid | 0.1 – 0.2  |
|  | Ethanol | 6.8 |
|  | Water | 1.6 – 2.2 |
| Output | Intermediate CP-6 | 1.2 |
Table 1-4: CPPs and IPCs of Step 2
| Critical Process Parameters | In-process Controls |
| N/A | N/A |

### Step 3 (CP-6 to CP-7)
CP-6 (220-240 kg), tetrahydrofuran (598-3059 L), sodium carbonate (41.8-43.1 kg) are combined. Ethyl chloroformate (159-592 L) is added and the mixture is heated at temperature up to reflux. Upon reaction completion, the mixtures is filtered, and the filtrate is quenched with a sodium hydroxide solution (112-119 L) while maintaining a temperature below 30°C. To the mixture, n-hexane (52-55 L) is added and stirred, and then the layers are settled and separated. The organic layer is concentrated by distillation with ethanol for the solvents exchange (final concentration 1400L). Water (25 to 35% weight per weight of ethanol)is added and the mixture is stirred at 14 to 26°C. The resulting crystalline precipitates are filtered, rinsed with ethanol, and dried at temperatures up to 50°C to yield CP-7. Yield:  About 253 kg of Intermediate CP-7, About 89% in theory
Table 1‑5 Material stoichiometry CP-7
|  | Name of material | Ratio [mol/mol] |
| Input | Intermediate CP-6 | 1 |
|  | Tetrahydrofuran | 2.6 – 13.3  |
|  | Sodium carbonate | 0.75 - 4 0  |
|  | Ethyl chloroformate | 2.0 – 7.5 |
|  | Sodium hydroxide | 0.1 – 0.3  |
|  | n-Hexane | 0.2 – 0.3  |
|  | Ethanol | 3.5 – 8.7 |
|  | Water | 0.8 – 3.1 l/kg |
| Output | Intermediate CP-7 | 1.1 |
Table 1-6: CPPs and IPCs of Step 3
| Critical Process Parameters | In-process Controls |
| CPP #3.1:  Water addition in the crystallization (% by weight with respect to ethanol)  Acceptance range: 25 – 35 % | N/A |

### Step 4 (CP-7 and CP-8 to final drug substance)
CP-7 (240-260 kg) and CP-8 (200-220 kg)) are combined in methylene chloride (720-760 L). Tetra-n-butylammonium bromide (49-52 kg) and aqueous sodium hydroxide solution (720-760 L) are added while maintaining the mixture at temperatures between 12 and 25°C. Upon reaction completion, methylene chloride (805-815 L) and water (98-105 L) are added, the mixture is separated, and the organic layer is washed with diluted hydrochloric acid. The organic layer is concentrated and displaced by distillation with ethanol (final concentration 1800L). Water (20 to 35% weight per weight of ethanol) is added to the mixture. This addition of water in the crystallization is considered as CPP #4.1 with an acceptance range of 25 to 35% weight per weight of ethanol. Ethanol content is monitored by IPC #1. After cooling, the mixture is stirred at 14 to 26°C. Cooling rate is considered as CPP #4.2 with an acceptance criteria of 0.15 – 0.5 °C / min and tested in IPC #2. The resulting crystalline precipitates are filtered, rinsed with ethanol, and dried at temperatures up to 50°C to yield CP-9 (Sakuramil). Yield: Approximately 350 kg of Sakuramil About 90% in theory.
Table 1‑7 Material stoichiometry Final drug substance
|  | Name of material | Ratio [mol/mol] |
| Input | Intermediate CP-7 | 1 |
|  | Starting Material CP-8 | 0.86 |
|  | Methylene chloride | 2.6 – 5.4  |
|  | Tetra-η-butylammonium bromide | 0.1 – 1. 0 |
|  | Sodium hydroxide | 4.0 – 9.3 |
|  | Hydrochloric acid | 0.1 – 0.2  |
|  | Ethanol | 4.5  |
|  | Water | 1.2 – 1.8 |
| Output | Final drug substance CP-9 | 1.44 |
Table 1-8: CPPs and IPCs of Step 4
| Critical Process Parameters | In-process Controls |
| CPP #4.1: Water addition in the crystallization (% by weight with respect to ethanol)  Acceptance range: 25 – 35 %    | IPC#1: Ethanol  Acceptance criteria: ≤ 5000 ppm  LOD ≤ 6 ppm  Method: USP <467> Procedure A |
| CPP #4.2: Cooling rate (°C/min)  Acceptance range: 0.15 – 0.5°C / min | IPC #2:  Cooling rate  Acceptance criteria: 0.15 – 0.5°C / min  Method: Temperature measurement with temperature measurement device |

# 3.2.DS.M.2 Development of manufacturing process and process control

## 1 Description of Critical Material Attributes from Starting Materials

### 1.1 Starting Material 1 - CP-4
CP-4 has been manufactured by IROHA-corp. (China) and HETO-corp. (Germany). CP-4 manufactured at commercial scale has been converted to Sakuramil drug substance that has been used in Phase 3 clinical trials and ICH drug substance stability studies. The quality of CP-4 is tightly controlled in accordance with the commercial specification in section [[2.3.3.SM.C Control [CP-4] [Sakuramil] [CP-6]]] .
Justification for section of CP-4 Starting Material is provided in section [[2.3.4.SM.D Description [CP-4][Sakuramil][CP-6]]]. 
The desired impurity profile of CP-4 is achieved through the use of a reproducible process and a robust crystallization using a combination of ethanol and water as the final solvent mixture.
All process related impurities present in the SM, CP-4, at levels greater than 0.1 % have been identified and appropriate limits and controls have been established based on demonstrated purge data, design space knowledge, and scale and equipment considerations in the subsequent synthetic steps. Individual unspecified impurities are controlled in lots of CP-4 to levels of NMT 0.5 %. CP-4 is not a source of impurities (≥ 0.15%) in the drug substance.
Stability evaluation of CP-4 has demonstrated that CP-4 is stable with no observations of significant degradation. An informal study of the stability of CP-6 under conditions of 30°C/65% RH through 18 months showed no degradation product increase or impurity change greater than 0.1 %.
Table 1‑1        Risk designation for CP-4 specification parameters
| Tests | Potential for variables to impact quality | Control Value¹ | Actual Value | Comments: Importance Designation |
| Description | No | White to pale yellow crystals or crystalline powder | White to pale yellow crystals or crystalline powder | Low risk |
| Identity – IR | No | The IR spectrum of the sample is comparable to that of the reference standard (IR) | Meets Test | Moderate risk |
| Related substances CP-3 | Yes |  NMT 0.3 %² |  ≤ 0.01 – 0.04% | High risk: 0.3 % resulted in < 10 ppm in drug substance |
| Individual unspecified impurity | Yes | NMT 0.1 % | ≤ 0.05 – 0.2 % | Moderate risk |
| Total impurities | Yes | NMT 0.5 % | 0.1 – 0.2 % | Moderate risk |
| Enantiomeric purity | Yes | NMT 1.5 % | ≤ 0.01 – 0.04 | Moderate risk |
| Residual solvents Toluene |  No |  NMT 890 ppm |  ≤ 89 ppm |  Moderate risk |
| Palladium (Pd) | No | NMT 10 ppm | < 1 ppm | Moderate risk |
| Assay | No | 98.0 - 102.0 % | 97 – 103 % | Moderate risk |
¹These acceptance criteria have changes with increased processing experience and understanding. While some of these lots do not meet current acceptance criteria, all lots have been successfully processed forward to produce drug substance of acceptable quality
²Fate and purge study supports up to 1 %. Fate and purge study: Elevated levels of this impurity is introduced to laboratory batches and then evaluated in the process to identify the fate of the impurity, and the purge factor of the impurity or reacted impurity.

### 1.1.1 Importance assessment for CP-4 material attributes
Fate and purge of related substances in CP-4 in the manufacturing process of Sakuramil drug substance is shown in the figure below.
CP-4 and CP-6 have tested positive in the Ames Assay. The intermediate CP-5 and intermediate precursor CP-3 exhibited positive structural alerts in a structure activity relationship database, therefore will be controlled as potentially mutagenic impurities (CP-4 and CP-6) as well.
Figure 1‑1      Fate and Purge of Related Substances in CP-4 in the Manufacturing Process of Sakuramil
[IMAGE:  Untitled.png]

### 1.1.2 Control items for CP-4 high risk material attributes:
CP-4 is designated a high risk material attribute and the specification is established at NMT 0.3 % in the intermediate specification of CP-6. CP-4 is one of the four potentially mutagenic impurities in the process to manufacture Sakuramil drug substance; and all four of these impurities will be controlled in either the API specification or SM/Intermediate specification. It should be noted that CP-5 and CP-3 (two other potentially mutagenic impurities) are controlled under the unspecified impurity specification as NMT 0.1 % in CP-6 as shown in the table above. However, even at this level of 0.1 % for each of these two impurities, the level in Sakuramil drug substance for CP-5 and CP-3 is typically seen well below 1 ppm combined. The reactivity of the functional center responsible for the potentially mutagenic activity (aniline) combined with the purge factors for these two impurities is 100 times greater than in CP-4. In addition, 37.5 ppm was chosen as a target in Sakuramil drug substance based on the additive effect and combined control strategy for the last potentially mutagenic impurity: CP-6. This upstream critical control point for CP-4 is part of the combined control for all potentially mutagenic impurities as summarized below.
Summary of Potentially mutagenic Control Strategy
Control Strategy for CP-4, CP-5, CP-3:
In CP-6: Important MA CP-4 (≤ 0.3 %) + CP-5 and CP-3 (≤ 0.1 % each) = ≤ 10 ppm total for these three in Sakuramil drug substance as demonstrated by risk assessment outlined here [[2 Risk Assessment]] and supported by carry over studies in section [[ICH M7 Risk Assessment]]. 
Control Strategy for CP-6 (Intermediate):
< 10 ppm in Sakuramil when process through Steps 3 & 4 design space (specification for CP-6 as a CQA in Sakuramil drug substance: ≤ 25 ppm)
Therefore: CP-3 is controlled in CP-4 Starting Material specification, CP-4 is controlled in CP-6 Intermediate specification and CP-5 is controlled as unspecified impurity in CP-6 Intermediate specification as per Option 3. CP-6 is controlled in drug substance specification as per Option 1. Therefore it is ensured that all potentially mutagenic impurities are well controlled in accordance with ICH M7.  

### 1.1.3 Control items for CP-4 moderate risk material attributes:
Identity, assay, unspecified impurities, and total impurities have not been identified as important material attributes.
However, they are important when managing current suppliers or evaluating additional supplier of CP-4. These tests serve as an opportunity to identify any potential new sources of impurities that were not possible to evaluate during the course of development. In addition, the downstream methods for CP-7 and for Sakuramil drug substance are excellent additional orthogonal methods used as well to manage and mitigate risk of unknown impurities introduced from CP-4.

### 1.1.4 Control items for CP-4 low risk material attributes:
The enantiomer (CP-4-E) is a low risk material attribute. As discussed above, chirality is controlled in the CP-2 and the process and intermediates have no impact on the chiral control. In addition, the process has significant purge of all isomers as well as methods that are specific for, and confirmed, the correct enantiomer of Sakuramil (specifications for intermediate and the drug substance are specific for all chiral isomers). Manufacturing of the enantiomer would therefore not go undetected early in the process. Nevertheless, enantiomeric purity is controlled within CP-4 specification as it is the next step after introduction of the “chiral pool” of CP-2.

### 1.2 Starting Material 2 - CP-8
While the starting material CP-8 exhibited positive structural alerts in a structure activity relationship database, it was determined to be negative in the Ames assay. The Ames report is attached in 3.2.DS.C. Therefore, CP-8 is controlled in Sakuramil drug substance as an unspecified impurity with a limit of NMT 0.10%.
CP-8 has been manufactured by IROHA-corp. (China) and abcr Gmbh. (Germany) using the same manufacturing processes. CP-8 manufactured at commercial scale has been converted to Sakuramil drug substance that has been used in Phase 3 clinical trials and ICH drug substance stability studies. 
The quality of CP-8 is tightly controlled in accordance with the commercial specification in section [[2.3.3.SM.C Control [CP-8] [Sakuramil]]] 
Justification for section of CP-8 Starting Material is provided in section [[2.3.4.SM.D Description [CP-8][Sakuramil]]] 
All process related impurities present in the SM, CP-8, at levels greater than 0.1 % have been identified and appropriate limits and controls have been established based on demonstrated purge data, design space knowledge, and scale and equipment considerations in the subsequent synthetic steps. Individual unspecified impurities and total impurities are controlled in lots of CP-8 to levels of NMT 0.1 %. Related impurities CP-8-25l and CP-8-24l are controlled to levels of NMT 0.05%. CP-8 is controlled in the drug substance to the level of NMT 0.10%.
Stability evaluation of CP-8 has demonstrated that CP-8 is stable with no observations of significant degradation. 
Table 1‑2        Risk designation for CP-8 specification parameters
| Tests | Potential for variables to impact quality | Control Value¹ | Actual Value | Comments: Importance Designation |
| Description | No | White to pale yellow crystals or crystalline powder | White to pale yellow crystals or crystalline powder | Low risk |
| Identity – IR | No | The IR spectrum of the sample is comparable to that of the reference standard (IR) | Meets Test | Moderate risk |
| Related substances CP-8-OH  | No |  ≤ 1 %1 |  ≤ 0.2% |  Low risk No reaction |
| CP-8-CHO | No | ≤ 1 %1 | ≤ 0.2% | Low risk No reaction |
| CP-8-25I | Yes | ≤ 0.05 % ² | ≤ 0.02 % | High risk React like SM,  little purge in drug substance |
| CP-8-24I | Yes | ≤ 0.05 % ² | ≤ 0.02 % | High risk React like SM,  little purge in drug substance |
| Individual unspecified impurity | No | NMT 0.1 % | ≤ 0.1 % | Moderate risk |
| Total impurities | No | NMT 1.0 % | ≤ 0.1 – 0.3 % | Moderate risk |
| Assay | No | ≥ 97% | 99.7 – 100 % | Moderate risk |
¹Fate and purge study supports up to 3%.

### 1.2.1 Importance assessment for CP-8 material attributes
Fate and purge of related substances in CP-8 in the manufacturing process of Sakuramil is shown in the figure below.
Figure 1‑2      Fate and Purge of Related Substances in CP-8 in the Manufacturing Process of Sakuramil
[IMAGE:  Untitled.png]

### 1.2.2 CP-8 important material attribute:
The two regio-isomeric benzylbromides are high risk material attributes as designated in the table above. The high risk material attribute justification is warranted due to the fact that they produce to isomers of the drug substance. These two isomers react mechanistically the same as the SM and have very little purge in the final crystallization to isolate Sakuramil drug substance.
Therefore, the specification (and thus the control strategy) is established as ≤ 0.05% for each to ensure the quality of Sakuramil drug substance.

### 1.2.3 Control items for CP-8 moderate risk material attributes:
Identity, assay, unspecified impurities, and total impurities have not been identified as important material attributes.
However, they are important when managing current suppliers or evaluating additional supplier of CP-8. These tests serve as an opportunity to identify any potential new sources of impurities that were not possible to evaluate during the course of development. In addition, the methods for Sakuramil drug substance are excellent additional orthogonal methods used as well to manage and mitigate risk of unknown impurities introduced from CP-8.

### 1.2.4 Control items for CP-8 low risk material attributes:
CP-8-OH and CP-8-CHO are not important material attributes. Both of these impurities do not react in the final step and have significant purge factors in the final isolation of drug substance. Fate and purge have demonstrated that 3 % is easily purged to ≤ 0.1 % unspecified level in drug substance.
The non important tests will be maintained within the purchase specification for CP-8 and the manufacturing sites quality systems.

## 2 Risk Assessment

### 2.1 Commercial manufacturing process related impurities (including intermediates and diastereomers)
All impurities that may be included in the manufacturing process of Sakuramil drug substance are shown in the following figure of Impurity cascade for Sakuramil.
All process related impurities present in CP-6 at level greater than 0.1% have been identified, and appropriate limits may be established based on demonstrated purge data in subsequent synthetic steps. Individual unspecified impurities are controlled in CP-6 to levels of NMT 0.1 %. CP-6 related impurities are not a source of significant levels of impurities in the drug substance. The desired impurity profile of CP-6 and Sakuramil are consistently achieved through a reproducible process and robust crystallizations. Because of the lipophilic nature of all the intermediates and Sakuramil (as a result of the trifluoromethyl functional group) the crystallizations have historically demonstrated an unprecedented, highly efficient purge of previous intermediates and impurities such that the quality of CP-6 and Sakuramil are historically independent of major and minor changes. This purge stands true for all process related impurities, diastereomers, potentially mutagenic intermediates, and starting material related impurities.
Figure 2‑1    Impurity Cascade for Sakuramil
[IMAGE:  Untitled.png]
Note: Dashed arrow – without structure change. Solid arrow – Reaction with structure change

### 2.2 Manufacturing Process impact on CQA of Sakuramil drug substance
Table 2‑1        Impact on SM and Manufacturing Steps on drug substance CQA
| CQA | Tests | CP-4 (SM) | CP-8 (SM) | Step 1 | Step 2 | Step 3 | Step 4 |
| ID | IR, HPLC | No | No | No | No | No | Yes |
| Potency | Assay | No | No | No | No | No | Yes |
| Purity | Related Substances | No | Yes | No | No | Yes | Yes |
| Purity | Potentially mutagenic Impurities | Yes | No | Yes | Yes | Yes | Yes |
| Purity | Nitrosamine Impurities | Yes | Yes | No | Yes | Yes | No |
| Purity | Metal impurities | Yes | No | No | No | No | No |
| Optical Activity | Stereoisomers | Yes | No | Yes | No | No | No |

### 2.2.1 Material Attribute (MA) to be evaluated: Related substances
The following figure shows the impurities deriving from the manufacturing steps which could highly potentially impact CQA of Sakuramil. In step 3, ethyl homolog CP-7-1, the single impurity in the entire manufacturing process, is formed. CP-7-1 reacts and it converted to CP-9-1 in Step 4 and ultimately remains in the drug substance. CP-9-1 has very little purge in the crystallization in Step 4. Therefore, it is required to identify the process parameters which impact the formation and purge of CP-7-1 in Step 3.
In Step 4, unreacted SM CP-8 remains in the drug substance. Therefore, it is required to identify the process parameters which impact the formation and purge of CP-8 in Step 4.
SM CP-4, a potentially mutagenic impurity used in Step 1, is discussed in the section for potentially mutagenic impurities.

### 2.2.2 Material Attribute (MA) to be evaluated: Potentially mutagenic Impurities
SM CP-4, and CP-3, CP-5 and CP-6, potential impurities in SM, are potentially mutagenic impurities. It is required to investigate the process parameters which impact the purge of these impurities.

### 2.2.3 Material Attribute (MA) to be evaluated: Nitrosamine Impurities
Vulnerable amines are present in the drug substance, therefore it is required to investigate the risk on formation of N-nitrosamines. Nitrosating agents are not likely to be present in the drug substance. 

### 2.2.4 Material Attribute (MA) to be evaluated: Chirality (Stereoisomers)
As stated in 1.2.6, no racemization has been observed in the manufacturing process of Sakuramil drug substance. As chirality is controlled in accordance with the vendor specifications of CP-2 as well as in the specifications of SM CP-4, and the manufacturing process and intermediates do not impact the control of chirality, it is not an important MA.

### 2.2.5 Material Attribute (MA) to be evaluated: Residual Solvents
Class 2 solvents THF, Methanol and n-Hexane are used in the manufacturing process, but because of several solid-liquid separation operations in the crystallization in Step 3 and Step 4, these solvents have not been detected in the development stage.
A Class 2 solvent dichloromethane is used in the reaction step in Step 4, but as it is designated to be submitted for crystallization after dichloromethane is evaporated after completion of the reaction, dichloromethane also has not been detected in the development stage. Therefore, it is not considered an important MA.
A Class 3 solvent Ethanol is used in all of the manufacturing steps (except Step 1) and it is defined a critical parameter as the content of Ethanol may influences the formation of ethyl homolog impurity (CP-7-1).

### 2.2.6 Material Attribute (MA) to be evaluated: Elemental impurities
Pd catalyst is used in the manufacturing process of the SM CP-4 in Step A. Therefore, Pd content has been included in the specification for SM as well as intermediate CP-6. As the level of metal does not increase in the manufacturing process of Sakuramil drug substance, it does not need to be controlled in final drug substance, however it is considered a important MA.

## 3 Design Space Development
For the purposes of defining the design space for the Sakuramil manufacturing process, the impact of the process on the critical quality attributes of Sakuramil was investigated in combination with quality risk management processes and tools. A design space for the commercial manufacture of Sakuramil has been established relative to its critical quality attributes and critical process inputs (material and process parameters). As there are no critical parameters in Step 1 and Step 2 that would not result in critical parameters in the final steps 3 and 4, this Design Spaces focuses on the final steps.
The following sections (Step 3 to Step 4) provide a summary of the risk based assessment of each step, the experimental work conducted, an assessment of the results and the resultant design space for each step, leading to the overall design space for the manufacturing process.

### 3.1 Focus area multivariate protocols, experimental summaries, and conclusions that set up the Design Space for Sakuramil drug substance
Introduction
Once the commercial route to Sakuramil was. established as described in the process development history section above, a greater understanding of the functional interrelationships of the manufacturing process parameters on the critical quality attributes of the dt.ug substance was established and this ultimately led to definition of the design space for the manufacturing process.
Initially, a risk assessment process was undertaken to identify all process parameters (including MA and in-process controls) and assess their probable impact on drug substance quality. In order to do this, each step of the manufacturing process was divided into focus areas (FA) and evaluated individually. Step 3 and Step 4 were each divided into FA1 - FA6. Evaluated FA are shown in Table 1-5. This initial risk assessment was conducted by means of Cause and Effect (C&E) Matrix. Examples of process parameters assessed are shown in Table 1-6.
First, the material attributes of the product for each step were assessed against their potential to impact a critical quality attribute of the dt.ug substance. Next, process parameters for each step were assessed against their potential to impact the important material att1·ibutes for that step product. The evaluation points were calculated and risks were classified into three levels (high, medium and low). This initial structured risk assessment utilized the knowledge that had been gained through development and scale up of the manufacturing process, and a mechanistic understanding of the chemistry of reactions and work up procedures.
The quality attributes that gain the highest priority to evaluate were the impurities generated and controlled by the process.

Table 3‑2        Examples of Process Parameters Assessed at Initial Risk Assessment

After the risk assessment was completed for the manufacturing process, the focus areas where impurities were generated and/or controlled were identified as the foundation of the design space requiring more process understanding to assess the impact on the critical quality attributes of Sakuramil drug substance. An experimental plan was developed for each of these focus areas to evaluate process parameters and quality attribute links. They were prioritized and executed in order to (a) examine if the identified parameters do impact the quality attributes, and (b) to determine the extent of this impact and identify the proven acceptable ranges (PAR) within which the process can be operated to produce Sakuramil drug substance that meets the specification.
The focus areas identified for the Sakuramil process are summarized in Table 1-7 and Table 1-8.

### 3.1.1 Step 3

### 3.1.1.1 Multivariate designs for Step 3 reaction
In Step 3, the aniline of CP-6 is reacted with ethyl chlorofo1mate to give the carbamate CP-7. Following the reaction, the mixture is quenched with a sodium hydroxide solution to consume any excess ethyl chlorofo1mate and hexane is added. The hexane layer is separated, exchanged with ethanol, and CP-7 is c1ystallized from an ethanol/water mixture.
Two focus areas were studied for the Step 3 process: the reaction and the crystallization.
Figure 3‑1    Step 3 Process
[IMAGE:  Untitled.png]
Reaction:
Impurity quality attributes, parameters, and ranges for the Step 3 reaction study:
Only one impurity, ethyl homolog (CP-7-1 ), has been observed in batches of CP-7 that is fanned in the Step 3 process that could potentially impact this critical quality attribute of Sakuramil. This impurity is formed through the reaction of ethyl chloroformate with the nitrogen of the methyl carbamate; and then subsequent loss of the methyl carbamate (or loss of methyl carbamate and the alkylation with ethyl chloroformate). Step 3 is the source of CP-7-1 formation and it is the single impurity in the entire manufacturing process demonstrated to have little purge in the Step 3 and Step 4 crystallizations that give Sakuramil drug substance.
Figure 3-2    CP-7-1, Ethyl Homolog
[IMAGE:  Untitled.png]
In addition, total "other" impurities were monitored while probing the ranges in the experimental design to identify if (I) Any new impurities m-e being generated, and (2) Any levels of known trace impurities already controlled in the standard process increase ( < 0.1 % ).
From the risk assessment, parameters that could potentially influence the levels of CP-7-1 (and total "other" impurities) in CP-7 were identified. This assessment identified that the stoichiometry of ethyl chloroformate and the base(s), and volume of THF were the process parameters that had the highest risk of impacting these quality attributes of CP-7. An experimental strategy was designed to determine the effects of this process parameter on controlling these quality attributes, improve process understanding and robustness, and establish the design space for the Step 3 manufacturing process.
Scale and equipment consideration: (Prior to multivariate design to establish the design space)
Neither the Sodium Carbonate particle size nor the agitation speed had any observable effect upon the reaction rate and product purity profile, indicating that poor mixing upon scale-up should not be a significant concern. Although the rate of the biphasic ethyl chloroformate quench is sensitive to agitation, there were no byproducts or safety concerns to indicate any potential issues upon scale-up related to mixing.
Through the course of development there has not been any observed scale and or equipment limitation, which is supplied by chemical knowledge. However, additional stressing experiments are executed to understand if there is any impact on prolonged time difference between laboratory and manufacturing times on the quality attributes. In addition, the multivariate experiments mimic the "worst case" scenario of the proposed commercial equipment and its limitations.
Note: The "worst case" scenario means the laboratory simulation of heating and cooling profiles, etc. of the worst conditions that may occur in the commercial manufacturing facility. For example, whether by-products or degradation products increase or not is confirmed by conducting the reaction at the temperature 10°C higher than the set reaction temperature or for a longer time than the set reaction time, or with reagents in a larger quantity than the set charge-in quantity.
Parameters and ranges explored in the DoE:
A central composite DoE was designed and executed using the following:

Because the ethyl homolog has very little opportunities for purge in the process, it will be the MA that limits the boundaries of the unit operation design space for Step 3.
The specification of the ethyl homolog derivative in Sakuramil drug substance is 0.15%. The acceptance criteria for the multivariate experiments for the ethyl homolog in the Step 3 reaction and crystallization will be the same as 0.15%; since derivatives from ethyl analogs are only slight purge in Steps 3 & 4 crystallizations of the downstream.
Conclusion for Ethyl Homolog, CP-7-1
- In all experiments using carbonate, the level of CP-7-1 was measured to be significantly less than 0.15% (0.15% is the specification for CP-9-1, the ethyl homolog resulting from CP-7-1 in Sakuramil drug substance). In addition, the level of CP-7-1 measured in the reaction mixture after 36 hours at the process temperature of 66°C (a worst case scenario) was well below 1.0% as well. Step 4 of the Sakuramil process is not a source of formation of CP-7-1 and the crystallizations of Steps 3 and 4 demonstrate slight purge of this impurity and downstream analog CP-9-1. Therefore, the design space proposed for Step 3 is very much in control of the formation of CP-7-1 ; well within the critical quality attribute specification limit set for CP-9-1 of 0.15% set in Sakuramil drug substance.
- There was no deviation from acceptance criteria and no Edges of Failure (EoF) were observed in the parameter multivariate experiments and/ or the stressing experiments.
Sodium Carbonate is a non critical parameters as shown below.
- For the carbonate series, all three factors are important with the cross interaction term between ethyl chloroform and base to play the biggest role. In general the low amount of carbonate, high concentrations, at high ethyl chloroformate levels lead to increased amount of ethyl homolog. Carbonate appears to generate larger amounts of ethyl homolog under the extreme conditions. However at the standard condition of 2.5 eq ECF, the reaction is extremely clean through out the design space.
- It should be noted that the highest ethyl homolog values (~ 0.3%) were obtained after holding at reflux for 36 hours, yet some of these reactions were essentially complete at less than 6 hours. So scale and equipment time differences are not factors for controlling the generation of the ethyl homolog.

Scale-up and development experience have shown that these impurities purge well in the Step 3 crystallization below the quality specification for CP-7 and Sakuramil drug substance.

Additional Observations:
- The standard operating conditions for both bases, in general, generate the highest level of "other" impurities within the design space. This suggests that the standard workup condition should be sufficient purging the other impurities through out the design space.
- Phosphate experiments: Based on the analysis, the level of other impurity does depend strongly on concentration. In general, the level of other impurities decreases with a high amount of base and low levels of ethyl chloroformate.

### 3.1.2 Step 4

### 3.1.2.1 Step 4 reaction
In Step 4, CP-7 is reacted with CP-8 in dichloromethane to give crude Sakuramil drug substance. The crude reaction mixture is quenched, extracted, and exchanged with ethanol; and Sakuramil drug substance is crystallized from an ethanol and water mixture.
Figure 3‑10    Impurity quality attributes strategy for Step 4:
[IMAGE:  Untitled.png]
Fate and purge data combined with reaction development indicate the level of CP-8 in the crude reaction mixture at levels of 1.2 % risk meeting the 0.10% specification in drug substance. Therefore, monitoring the reaction completion and using CP-8 as the limiting reagent must be seriously evaluated for criticality and control options. The risk assessment combined with prior development knowledge believes this is high risk to uncover multiple edges of failure and be a limiting factor of the design space.
MA of CP-8: A batch was chosen with the "high levels" of impurities in CP-8 for multivariate experimentation to highlight the ability of the design space to control impurities from this starting material. These data complement actual fate and purge data to help evaluate risk and determine acceptable levels and criticality.
Reaction:
In the reaction between CP-8 and CP-7, CP-8 is used as the limited reagent. A PAT method (REACTR) will be used in the reaction to evaluate the disappearance of CP-8. In addition, total "other" impurities were monitored while probing the ranges in the experimental design to identify if 1. Any new impurities are being generated, and 2. Any levels of known trace impurities already controlled in the standard process increase (< 0.1 %).
From the risk assessment, parameters that could potentially influence the levels of CP-8 (and total impurities) in drug substance were identified. This assessment identified that the stoichiometry of CP-8, phase ratio, and reaction concentration were the process parameters that had the highest risk of impacting the potential quality attributes of drug substance. An experimental strategy was designed to determine the effects of this process parameter on controlling these quality attributes, improve process understanding and robustness, and establish the design space for the Step 4 manufacturing process. NaOH concentration and TBAB catalyst eq. are non critical. Development range demonstrated no impact on quality or rate. Historical data / prior knowledge around phase transfer reactions are supports.
Scale and equipment consideration: (Prior to multivariate design to establish the design space)
As with many phase transfer reactions, the reaction rate will be severely impacted if the aqueous and organic phases are not adequately dispersed; however, product purity does not appear to suffer even after 24 hours under poor mixing conditions, indicating that the reaction is robust enough to withstand any mixing issues that may be encountered on scale ( e.g. temporary loss of agitation).
Figure 3‑11    Relations between Agitation Rates and Remaining CP-7 (CP-703458)
[IMAGE:  Untitled.png]
Figure 3‑12    Relation between Agitation Rates and Reactor Temperature Profile
[IMAGE:  Untitled.png]
As expected, mixing has a very strong influence upon the rate of the phase transfer reaction, which proceeds faster at higher agitation speeds. If adequate dispersion of the aqueous and organic phases is not achieved, as was the case at 200 rpm in this series of experiments, the reaction may not be complete even after 24 hours. Even though only 70% conversion was reached after 24 hours at 200 rpm, reaction completion was achieved in 1.5 hours after increasing the agitation rate to disperse the phases.
Despite these results, the reaction appears robust enough such that in all of the experiments, product purity profiles were typical for all of the complete reactions, and issues with purity related to mixing are not anticipated upon scale-up.
Continued stressing experiments were executed to understand if there is any impact on prolonged time difference between laboratory and manufacturing times on the quality attributes. This will be confirmed in the design space of the reaction and crystallization. In addition, the multivariate experiments mimicked the "worst case" scenario of the proposed commercial equipment and its limitations (example; the heating and cooling profile was executed over hours with the same ability as the manufacturing facility).
Parameters and ranges explored in the DoE:
Design: An efficient 3-parameter hybrid response surface design for coupling reaction. Because the level of CP-8 can be controlled within spec (≤ 0.1 %) in the downstream crystallization, the whole study ranges for coupling reaction is the design space.

- In all experiments the highest level of CP-8 was less than 1 %. (1.2% is the specification for CP-8 that purges to 0.1 % in the crystallization step.)

- There was no deviation from acceptance criteria and no Edges of Failure (EoF) were observed in the parameter multivariate experiments and/or the stressing experiments. At the high end of the three parameters studied in a multivariate, analysis, the level of CP-8 was at I%. The acceptance criteria for CP-8 is 1.2%. The combination of these three parameters all at high levels is unrealistic for manufacturing; therefore warrants non critical designations.

## Development History

### 1 Route A: First Generation Synthesis
Figure 1‑1      Route A: First Generation Synthesis
[IMAGE:  Untitled.png]
- Disadvantages
  - Resolution discards 50% of the wrong enantiomer: not reasonable for high volume products
- Safety: Use of hazardous reagents/chemistry
  - Trifluromethylbromoaniline (potential HF generation)
    - N-vinylcarbamate (polymerizes and generates impurity)
  - Azide chemistry (explosive)
- Suppliers for this route are limited due to the hazards associated to this chemistry

### 2 Route B: Second Generation Synthesis
Figure 1‑2      Route B: Second Generation Synthesis
[IMAGE:  Untitled.png]
Improvements from Route A
- Use safer and reliable technology that reduces the use of hazardous reagents
- Elimination of resolution step
- Technology that can be nm in a general 1m1pose plants
- More efficient capacity utilization for large volume product
- Multiple vendors and the supplier option
Process highlights that needed to be addressed for commercialization
- Step CP-6 to CP-7
  - Reaction done in DCM with IPE as the isolation solvent
  - Pyridine use as base for the reaction with ethyl chloroformate
  - Reaction done at a low temperature to reduce decomposition
  - Reaction typically resulted in 2% unreacted starting material
- Step CP-7 to Sakuramil
  - Potassium t-butoxide reacts with methylene chloride when CP-7 is absent, potential safety issue identified.
  - Potassium t-butoxide must be titrated to reaction to avoid fo1mation of impurities difficult to purge
  - Two solid charges / worker exposure potential.
  - Large volumes of DCM also needled
  - The process requires a significant excess of CP-8 (1 .4 eq.) an expensive reagent classified as a sensitizer (P-4).
  - The reaction typically leaves 1 to 2.5% of starting material

### 3 Route C: Third Generation Synthesis
Figure 1‑3      Route C: Third Generation Synthesis
[IMAGE:  Untitled.png]
Key Improvements to Commercial Process
- Step CP-6 to CP-7
  - Reaction done in THF with Ethanol/water as the isolation solvent
  - Pyridine was substituted by sodium carbonate
    - No stability issue
    - Reaction typically resulted in ≤ 0.5 % unreacted starting material
  - Step CP-7 to Sakuramil
    - Reaction is done using 50% NaOH and a phase transfer catalyst
    - DCM still needed but with significantly volumes reductions
    - No stability or incompatibility issues between reagents/solvents
    - The process requires only 1.03 equiv of CP-8 (vs. 1.4 eq. Old process) an expensive reagent classified as a sensitizer (P-4).
    - The reaction typically leaves ~ 0.5% of starting material

# 1 Declaration
Red KIRSCH2358 is a red film-coating for tablets. It is a mixture of Hypromellose (USP/NF, Ph. Eur., JP), Macrogol 6000 (USP/NF, Ph. Eur., JP), Titanium Oxide (USP/NF, Ph. Eur., JP), Red ferric oxide (USP/NF, JP).
Properties: Red powder

# 2 Pharmacopoeia status
As mentioned above, the raw materials used in Red KIRSCH2358 are tested and certified according to the current pharmacopoeias.

# 3 Test specifications
| Test Code | Title of Test, Principle | Requirements |
| Description |  |  |
| 10001.01 | Appearance by visual examination | Red powder |
| Identification |  |  |
| 20443.01 | Identity by IR (ATR) | Complies with a reference spectrum from an authentic reference substance |
| 25301.01 | Identity of colourants | Complies favorably to authentic reference substance |
| 24221.01 | Identity of iron | Positive |
| Tests |  |  |
| Ph. Eur. | Total ash | 47.05 – 56.15% |

# 4 General remarks
| Equipment | After examining its suitability, other equipment than mentioned in this Testing Monograph may also be used. Volumes and masses may be adapted, provided the resulting concentrations lie within the validated range. |
| Reagents | Reagent grade chemicals are used unless otherwise indicated. Deionized or distilled water should be used unless otherwise indicated. |
| Authentic reference substance | Red KIRSCH2358 |

# 5 Tests

## 5.1 Appearance by visual examination (10001.01)
| Principle | Visual examination |
| Procedure | Examine the colour and form of the substance on a white base in daylight. Compare with the authentic substance. |
| Substance required | Ca. 1 g |

## 5.2 Identity by IR (ATR) (20443.01)
Procedure: Determine as indicated in Ph. Eur. Current edition.

### Figure 5-1           Comparison spectrum for Red KIRSCH2358
[IMAGE:  Untitled.png]
Reference substance, batch: BML5344

## 5.3 Identity of colourants (25301.01)
| Principle | The visual comparison of the colour of a film made from both the test substance and authentic reference substance. |
| Equipment | 1.     Device for film production, e.g. Spring Blossom 0.008” (Evergreeny.AG.) 2.     White cardboard, e.g. UGC-2 card, 4” × 5” White Cardboard (Boacaard Corp.) 3.     Propeller-type stirrer or blender |
| Procedure | Dispersion: Add 60 ml of boiling de-ionized water into a blender and, while operating at low speed, slowly add 20 g of test substance. After all test substance is added, increase the speed to high and maintain until the test substance is completely dispersed (about 5 minutes). Transfer the dispersed test substance into an amber container and then place into an ice bath for about 30 minutes. Prepare a dispersion also for the authentic reference substance in the same manner, or a use a previous prepared standard film if less than one year old. Film: Pour about 15 ml of the dispersion onto the dull side of the UGC-2 card and spread evenly with the Spring Blossom applicator. Allow the film to dry at room temperature, protected from light. |
| Substance required | 10 – 20 mg |
| Evaluation | Compare the colour of the film against a film of the authentic reference substance. The test substance is deemed acceptable if the colour of the film matches that of the authentic reference substance. |
| Alternative | The dispersion may also be prepared with 10 g test substance and 30 ml water, using an “Eppendorf” reaction vessel and a Vortex. |

## 5.4 Identity of iron (24221.01)
| Principle | Colour reaction |
| Procedure | According to USP/NF – Monograph “Ferric oxide” Test: Identification Instead of the solution of ferric oxide described in USP/NF, use a solution with the same concentration of Red KIRSCH2358. |
| Substance required | 0.5 g |

## 5.5 Total Ash (Ph. Eur.)
| Procedure | Determine as required in Ph. Eur. current edition |
| Substance required | 1 g |

# 3.2.DP.M.1 Description of manufacturing process

## 1 Representative description of manufacturing process

### Pre-Blending
1. Blend 52.000 kg of cellulose, microcrystalline, 26.000 kg of croscarmellose sodium, 353.600 kg of lactose monohydrate/Lactose hydrate and 52.000 kg of Sakuramil drug substance into a diffusion mixer (bin blender).
1. Dissolve 15.600 kg hydroxypropyl cellulose in purified water using a vessel with stirrer to prepare a granulation liquid free from lumps.

### Granulation and blending
1. Load the pre-blended material from Step 1 into a fluid bed granulator and add granulation liquid from Step 2 using an inlet air volume of 40-45 m³/min, an inlet air temperature of 75-85°C and a spray rate of 900 – 1100 g/min,  to achieve wetting of pre-blended material and formation of granules. 
1. Dry the obtained granules using dryer integrated within the fluid bed granulator unit with inlet air temperature ranging between 75-85 °C until loss on drying of 1 - 2% is achieved.
1. Sieve the dried granules from Step 4 using a screening mill.
1. Sieve 5.200 kg of magnesium stearate through a screen (screen size 0.85 mm) and add it to the granules from Step 5.
1. Blend the mixture from step 6 for 20 revolutions during 10 min using a diffusion mixer (bin blender) to obtain the final blend.

### Tablet compression
1. Compress the final blend from step 7 using a tablet press at 20-30 revolutions with a compression force of 6-14 kN to obtain the tablet cores.

### Film coating
1. Prepare a homogeneous suspension of the Basic coating premix, red in purified water in a suitable sized vessel.
1. Film-coat the tablet cores from Step 8 using the film coat suspension from Step 9 in a coating pan using an inlet air temperature of 70 - 80 °C, inlet air volume of 40-45 m³/min and a pan rotation speed of 2.0-6.0 rpm at stable conditions with a gradual increase of set target spray rate from 280 to 420 g/min. Collect the film coated tablets in a suitable container.

### Inspection
1. Collect 10 tablets to perform Description test method with RTRT and Identification Test method with RTRT.

### Packaging
1. The film-coated tablets are either primary packaged.
1. The primary packaged product is then packed in a cardboard based secondary pack.

# 3.2.DP.M.2 Development of manufacturing process and process controls

# 3.2.DP.M.6 Process validation or evaluation studies

### 1. Summary
The manufacturing process of Sakura Bloom 20 mg Film-coated tablets has been validated using three production-scale batches which have been processed in the same manufacturing facilities, using the same process and the same equipment as for the batches intended for marketing.
All three batches consistently meet the quality control specifications. The results of routine and extended in-process control (IPC) testing have demonstrated that the manufacturing process is robust and consistently yields a product capable of meeting the pre-defined quality characteristics.

### 2 Introduction
Sakura Bloom 20 mg Film-coated tablets are produced according to standard manufacturing processes: Wet granulation, milling, drying of granulates, blending, mixing, compression and film-coating and is controlled by process parameter settings and in-process control testing performed during the manufacture. The detailed process used for the preparation of the drug product is described in Module 2 of this submission.

### 3 Batches used for validation
The production scale batches of Sakura Bloom 20 mg Film-coated tablets used for validation at Aparna Pharmaceutical Manufacturing Pte. Ltd., Bangladesh are summarized in Table 3-1. The batch size is approximately 520 kg corresponding to 2,600,000 tablets.

| ABC456  | Aparna Pharmaceutical Manufacturing Pte. Ltd., Bangladesh | May 2022 | B221217, B221218, B221219, B221220 |
| ABC789 | Aparna Pharmaceutical Manufacturing Pte. Ltd., Bangladesh | Jun 2022 | B221221, B221222, B221223 |

### 4 Manufacturing equipment

| 8. Compression | Tablet press |
| 10. Film-coating | Perforated coating pan |

### 5 Critical process steps and parameters
The manufacture of Sakura Bloom 20 mg Film-coated tablets consists of standard pharmaceutical operations and is controlled by in-process-control testing performed during manufacture. The potentially critical steps have been evaluated at various stages throughout the development process.
An overview of the steps and parameters that have been investigated during process validation is provided in Table 5-1 below.

During validation an extensive sampling and testing program, consisting of routine in process controls (IPC) and additional testing, was conducted. The sampling strategy as well as the applied criteria for the testing during validation is summarized in Table 5-2, Table 5-3 and Table 5-4.

### 8 Analytical data of validation batches
Analytical release results of the three validation batches are provided in Section ‘Controls’. All test results consistently complied with the final release specifications.

# 9 Conclusion
The data gathered during the process validation show that the manufacturing process of Sakura Bloom 20 mg Film-coated tablets is robust and consistently yields drug product which meets the predetermined quality characteristics. Moreover, the chosen in-process tests have been shown to be suitable for monitoring the manufacturing process.
The conclusion from the presented data is that the process conditions and values chosen for the processing parameters are acceptable to support the commercial manufacture of the product.
CQAs of Sakura Bloom Tablets are ensured by CMAs that are maintained by routine production. The control strategy in production of Sakura Bloom Tablets operates the following maintenance program to verify the model.
Daily check:
- Trend analyses of CQA and CMA are performed for every batch produced, and the changes are confirmed to be within an acceptable range.
- If the trend is out of the acceptable level, a comparison is made between the model and conventional testing methods. If the model has some problems, it should be revised. If the model has no problems, the relationship between CPP and CMA is considered to be broken. Thus, control of CPP is reviewed so that CMA has an appropriate value.
Periodical check:
- A comparison is made between the values calculated by the model and those obtained by the conventional testing methods at a certain production interval. If the difference between the two is out of the acceptable level, the model should be revised.

| Procedure |  |

## 1 Test method (NIR) (RTRT)
Principle        Near infrared absorption spectrometry (NIR method)
| Equipment, procedure and spectrum acquisition parameters | The equipment, the acquisition parameters and the number of tablets analyzed are identical to those used for the test  “Uniformity of dosage units by content uniformity by NIR”. |
| Mathematical treatment | The spectral data are pre-treated by the NIR software IDENT. |
| ID method | IDENT identifies those reference spectra which are closest equivalent to the test spectrum, and determines the deviations between these spectra and the test spectra. |
| Digitally signed IDENT method for the identification of Sakuramil | SM82145_Vil_A.FAA Updated version of the IDENT method will be named as follows: SM82145_Vil_A.FAA   (CCNN = site, X = current version) |
| Type of Model | Partial Least Squares Regression (PLSR) |
| Acceptance criteria | The ‘hit quality’, i.e. the spectral distance between the test spectrum and the average spectrum of the reference library, must be smaller than the validated method-related threshold which depends on the variability of the reference spectra. |
|  | For further details see Validation Report VR82145x(AS1234)  (x = current version) |

### Figure 1 NIR spectra of Sakura Bloom 20 mg Film-coated tablet
[IMAGE:  Untitled.png]

# 3.2.AP.2 Analytical Procedure Validation/Qualification 
The validation report describes the parameters to be tested, the working instructions and the acceptance criteria. The working instructions also include a section about the method specific parameters.
This method is foreseen for In Process Control and release testing. The validation was executed in the facilities of Aparna Pharmaceuticals Manufacturing Pte. Ltd.
Validation strategy
The validation was subdivided into two steps:
In the first step the spectral reference library was validated internally by fulfilling the acceptance criteria.
After successful internal validation, the specificity of the database was validated using samples that were not used to generate the database and were only available after the approval of the validation protocol. In addition, all validation spectra of previous validations including the challenges of previous validations were used. Furthermore, the method was tested with further batches of each dosage strength.
Since this method is only concerned with the qualification of Sakura Bloom 20 mg Film-coated tablets, specificity is the only validation parameter to be considered.
Detailed validation report is available in [[[Placeholder] VR_SB_20_2021_Addendum_ Method validation:  Identity by NIR]]

# 3.2.AP.1 Analytical Procedure Description
Principle
Isocratic Reverse Phase HPLC with UV detection at 218 nm
| Reagents |  |
| Water | Double deionized and filtered, e.g. Milli-Q |
| Acetonitrile | HPLC grade, e.g. Merck no. 1.00030, or equivalent |
| Potassium dihydrogen phosphate, anhydrous | ACS reagent grade, Aldrich Chemical no. 22130-9, or equivalent |
| Ammonium hexafluoro­phosphate | ACS reagent grade, Sigma-Aldrich Chemical no. 216593, or equivalent |
| Phosphoric acid 85 % | e.g. Merck no. 1.00573, or equivalent |
| Phosphate buffer solution (pH 3.0 ± 0.1) | Add 1.7 g of potassium dihydrogen phosphate, anhydrous into 1 L of water and mix to dissolve. Adjust this solution to pH 3.0 ± 0.1 with phosphoric acid. Add 8.0 g of ammonium hexafluorophosphate (NH₄PF₆) and mix well to dissolve.  |
| Note | It is recommended to filter this final solution through a 0.45 µm filter. |
| Solvent | Water + acetonitrile + phosphoric acid 900 + 100 + 1 (v/v/v) e.g. Pipette 1.0 mL of phosphoric acid into 900 mL of water, add 100 mL of acetonitrile and mix well. |
| Equipment |  |
| Apparatus | Suitable HPLC system equipped with a pump, auto-sampler, UV detector capable of monitoring absorbance at 218 nm and a column heater. |
| Column | Waters, Atlantis, dC₁₈, 3 µm, 100 Å |
|  | Length 150 mm, internal diameter 4.6 mm, or equivalent column |
| Filter for test solution | Nylon 0.45 µm pore size, Titan or equivalent |
| Chromatographic conditions |  |
| Mobile phase A | Phosphate buffer solution + water 400 + 600 (v/v)  Mix together 400 mL of phosphate buffer solution and 600 mL of water. |
| Mobile phase B | Phosphate buffer solution + acetonitrile 400 + 600 (v/v) Mix together 400 mL of phosphate buffer solution and 600 mL of acetonitrile. |
| Mobile phase C | Mobile phase A + Mobile phase B 550 + 450 (v/v) or Phosphate buffer solution + water + acetonitrile 400 + 330 + 270 (v/v/v) |
| Isocratic conditions | Mobile phase A: 55 %  Mobile phase B: 45 % or Mobile phase C: 100 % |
| Column temperature | 40°C |
| Flow rate | 1.8 mL/min |
| Detection | UV, 218 nm |
| Injection volume | 10 µl of the test and reference solutions, equivalent to about 2.5 µg of Sakuramil drug substance in the reference solution |
| Run time | 3 minutes |
| System suitability test (SST) |  |
| SST solutions |  |
| ·         Blank chromatogram | Solvent |
| ·         Repeatability | Reference solution |
| ·         Tailing factor | Reference solution |
| Requirements |  |
| Blank chromatogram | No interfering peak at the retention time of Sakuramil drug substance in the chromatogram |
| Repeatability | Srel ≤ 2.0 % (peak area of Sakuramil drug substance in the reference solution, n = 6) |
| Tailing factor | T ≤ 2.0 (peak of Sakuramil drug substance in the first injection of the reference solution) |
| Note | Calculations in accordance with Ph. Eur. 2.2.46 “Chromatographic Separation Techniques” or USP <621>, “Chromatography, System Suitability”. Adjustments of chromatographic conditions to meet the system suitability requirements may be necessary. |
| Procedure | Select not less than 30 units. Individually test 10 units (film-coated tablets or cores respectively). If the requirements are not met, continue testing to level 2 (or further units). |
| Test stock solution | Place 1 unit into a 200 mL volumetric flask. Dilute to volume with solvent, stir for 45 minutes with a suitable magnetic stir bar. Centrifuge a portion of this suspension in order to get a clear supernatant or filter through a 0.45 mm Nylon filter (Titan or equivalent), discarding the first 3 mL of filtrate. |
| Test solution  (for Sakuramil) | Use test stock solution “as is”. (Conc. = 0.25 mg Sakuramil/mL). |
| Note | Alternatively a qualified dilutor system can be used, provided the resulting concentration lies within the validated range. |
|  | Test solutions are stable for 3 days, if stored at ambient conditions. |
| Reference solution | Weigh about 25 mg of Sakuramil drug substance, accurately to 0.01 mg, reference substances into a 100 mL volumetric flask, dissolve in and dilute to volume with solvent. Mix well. |
| Note | The reference solution is stable for 9 days, if stored at ambient conditions or in a refrigerator. |
| Evaluation | Determine the peak area for Sakuramil in the chromatogram of test solution. Also determine the peak area for Sakuramil in the chromatogram of the reference solution. |
| Calculation for Sakuramil | Percent content, CUV, of Sakuramil, based on the declared content  (= individual contents xi) |
$$CUv = \frac {PATV × mRV × VT × CRV}{PARV × VR × mDV}$$
Where:
| PATV | Peak area of Sakuramil in the chromatogram of test solution |
| mRV | Mass of Sakuramil reference substance in mg |
| VT | Volume of the test stock solution in mL (200) |
| CRV | Declared content of Sakuramil reference substance in percent |
| PARV | Peak area of Sakuramil in the chromatogram of the reference solution |
| VR | Volume of the reference solution in mL (100) |
| mDV | Declared Sakuramil content in mg per unit (50) |

Principle   
Measurement of the amount of drug substance dissolved in a dissolution apparatus 2

Determination by UV detection
Procedure
| Reagents |  |
| Water | Demineralized (purified), e.g. from Millipore Q |
| Hydrochloric acid, 35% | A.C.S. grade or equivalent |
| Equipment |  |
| Spectrophotometer | e.g. Perkin Elmer Lambda 25 UV-Vis Spectrophotometer, Agilent UV-Vis Spectrophotometer with plotter or equivalent |
|  |  |
| Filter | PVDF glass fiber (e.g. Millipore multigrade 0.45 µm) or Whatman Roby 25/GF55 0.7 µm or Millipore APFD 1.0 µm or equivalent |
|  |  |
| Dissolution conditions | Paddle method according to Ph. Eur. 2.9.3 “Dissolution test for solid dosage forms”, USP <711> “Dissolution” and JP 6.10 “Dissolution Test” |
| Speed of rotation | 50 ± 2 rpm |
| Test medium | 4.0 N McIlvaine buffer Dilute 80 mL 0.1M HCl in 820 mL demineralized water. Test medium has to be degassed before use (e.g. Helium flow). Or transfer 9.0 mL concentrated hydrochloric acid (35%) in 10 L demineralized water. Test medium has to be degassed before use (e.g. Helium flow or vacuum). Other concentrated hydrochloric acid solutions or alternative volume can be used for the preparation of the test medium as long as the final concentration of diluted McIlvaine buffer (pH 4.0). |
| Volume of test medium | 900 mL |
| Temperature | 37 ± 0.5°C |
| Number of units tested | Examine the prescribed number of units according to the Acceptance Table 1 of Ph. Eur. and USP or Acceptance Table 6.10-1 of JP (minimum of 6, 1 per vessel) |
| Procedure |  |
| Test solution  | The test can be carried out either by a manual procedure or by a semi-automated dissolution system. # 3.2.AP.2 Analytical Procedure Validation/Qualification 
The dissolution method (Dissolution by UV) for Sakura Bloom 20 mg Film-coated tablet is described in validation protocol VP_SB_22_2021 has been validated for full development. Details are reported in:
[[22940ba1-bbd1-814d-9e00-fb9b311dd0c7]] 

# 3.2.AP.3 Analytical Procedure Development
The method was designed to ensure biorelevant in vitro performance and consistent results across manufacturing batches.

## 1. Solubility and Media Selection
Sakuramil is a white solid with low aqueous solubility at room temperature (0.05 mg/mL in water). Solubility varies significantly with pH:
- pH 1.2 (0.1 N HCl): < 0.1 mg/mL
- pH 4.5 (acetate buffer): 5.0 mg/mL
- pH 6.8 (phosphate buffer): 3.2 mg/mL
- pH 8.0 (0.1 N NaOH): 5.1 mg/mL
These results confirm sink conditions at physiological pH and justify the selection of McIlvaine buffer pH 5.0 as the dissolution medium.

## 2. Apparatus and Test Conditions
Comparative testing using USP Apparatus I (Basket) and II (Paddle) was performed. Apparatus II (Paddle) at 50 ± 2 rpm provided consistent and reproducible results with minimal variability. Use of sinkers was evaluated and found unnecessary. Filter compatibility was assessed, and a suitable material was selected to ensure sample clarity without adsorbing the drug substance.
The standard volume recommended by the USP for the dissolution testing of immediate release products is 900 mL; therefore, this dissolution volume was selected.
During the development phase, sampling timepoints of 5, 10, 15, 20, 30, and 45 were set to adequately characterize the ascending and plateau phases of the dissolution curves. More than 85% of the drug is released within the duration of the dissolution test.
[IMAGE:  attachment:10a6a9a7-30d7-4b13-a084-c37a6da246dd:image.png]
[IMAGE:  attachment:243125dd-a6fa-41f9-b6d6-a434547e0af8:image.png]

## 3. Discriminating ability of the dissolution method
The method’s discriminatory capability was confirmed by testing batches with deliberate formulation, and process variations. The procedure successfully detected differences in dissolution behavior, validating its suitability for stability studies and quality control.
[IMAGE:  attachment:24155775-30cc-4438-a64e-47e27a097e7e:image.png]
[IMAGE:  attachment:4601e31b-9634-4bdf-824e-444223fb9273:image.png]

## 4. Deaeration
Deaeration of the medium was evaluated and found to have no impact on dissolution results under the selected conditions. Therefore, deaeration is not required for routine testing.

## 5. Target Q Value
In accordance with pharmacopoeial guidance, the target Q value was defined as not less than 80% of the labeled amount dissolved within the specified time frame. This specification was supported by data from the batches used in the clinical trials and confirmed during method validation.
[IMAGE:  attachment:29d4fdb4-69ce-4e84-8a6d-7ca63453f020:image.png]

## 6. Final Method Conditions
The finalized method is based on ultraviolet absorption spectroscopy and follows the principles outlined in Ph. Eur. 2.9.3, USP, and JP 6.10. The test is performed using Apparatus II (Paddle) at 50 ± 2 rpm in 900 mL of McIlvaine buffer (pH 5.0), prepared by dissolving sodium phosphate dibasic dihydrate and citric acid in 800 mL of demineralized water, adjusting pH with HCl or NaOH, and completing the volume to 1 L with distilled water. The dissolution temperature is maintained at 37 ± 0.5 °C.
A minimum of six units are tested, one per vessel, in accordance with the acceptance criteria of Ph. Eur., USP, and JP. UV detection is used to determine the absorbance of the test solutions, with reference solutions prepared at approximately 0.25 mg/mL of Sakuramil. Absorbance values are measured using a suitable spectrophotometer, and comparative evaluation is performed when applicable.

## 7. Conclusion
The dissolution method developed for
Sakura Bloom 20 mg
is scientifically justified, robust, and compliant with international pharmacopoeial standards. It demonstrates reproducibility, discriminatory power, and suitability for routine quality control, comparative dissolution studies, and regulatory submissions. The incorporation of UV detection and McIlvaine buffer at pH 5.0 ensures reliable performance and sensitivity across batches, supporting product quality throughout its shelf life.

# 3.2.AP.1 Analytical Procedure Description
Dissolution under RTRT is controlled in three-dimensional design space so that the dissolution is about 90% (feedback control of spray rate by FBRM, compression force control by compression force controller).
1) Particle size of drug substance affecting dissolution is a specification item for drug substance which is performed by Laser diffraction particle size distribution analyzer.
2) Granule particle size is monitored using Focused Beam Reflectance Measurement (FBRM).
3) Uncoated tablet hardness is controlled by tablet hardness tester.
The particle size of drug substance is measured as a specification testing in the process of drug substance, by a laser diffraction-scattering type particle size distribution measuring device. Without preparing samples for measurement, the powder of drug substance is measured for particle distribution by the dry method (specification testing of drug substance). Regarding the particle size of the granulation, the particle size at the end of granulation, which is obtained by a FBRM method is used. The uncoated tablet hardness is measured in 200 tablets (10 tablets × 20 time points) sampled over time.
Dissolution test was performed for the drug product manufactured under the conditions allocated by DoE, and the affect of each factor on the dissolution rate were investigated. The test results were subjected to multidimensional analysis. For the formula for the sum of each factor which is multiplied by a coefficient, the coefficients that make the residual sum of squares minimum were calculated (the formula is shown below).
The dissolution rate calculated by the dissolution model at the time point of 30 minutes is 80% or higher.
[IMAGE:  Untitled.png]

# 3.2.AP.3 Analytical Procedure Development

### 1. Objective
To develop a Real-Time Release Testing (RTRT) method for monitoring and predicting the dissolution behavior of pharmaceutical solid dosage forms using ultraviolet (UV) spectroscopy.
---

### 2. Principle
UV spectroscopy measures the absorbance of UV light by a drug substance in solution. The absorbance at specific wavelengths correlates with the concentration of the dissolved active pharmaceutical ingredient (API), enabling real-time monitoring of dissolution.
---

### 3. Critical Quality Attributes (CQAs)
- Primary CQA: Dissolution rate
- Supporting CQAs:
  - API concentration in solution
  - Absorbance at characteristic UV wavelengths
  - pH and temperature of dissolution medium
---

### 4. Process Analytical Technology (PAT) Tools
| PAT Tool | Purpose |
| UV Spectrophotometer | Real-time monitoring of API concentration in dissolution medium |
| pH and Temperature Probes | Control and monitor dissolution conditions |
| Flow-through Cell or Fiber Optic Probe | In-situ sampling and measurement |
---

### 5. Predictive Modeling Approach
- Model Type: Calibration curve or multivariate regression (e.g., PLS)
- Input Variables: Absorbance values at selected wavelengths, time, pH, temperature
- Output Variable: Dissolution profile (concentration vs. time)
- Model Basis: Beer-Lambert Law:
  A=ε⋅c⋅lA=ε⋅c⋅l
  where:
  - AA: absorbance
  - εε: molar absorptivity
  - cc: concentration
  - ll: path length
---

### 6. Method Development Steps
1. Wavelength Selection: Identify optimal wavelength(s) for API detection.
1. Calibration Curve: Prepare standard solutions and generate absorbance vs. concentration curve.
1. Dissolution Testing: Conduct dissolution studies with in-line UV monitoring.
1. Model Building: Correlate real-time absorbance data with dissolution profiles.
1. Validation: Validate the method per ICH Q2(R2) for accuracy, precision, linearity, and robustness.
1. Implementation: Integrate UV probe into dissolution apparatus for RTRT.
---

### 7. Regulatory Considerations
- Follow USP <711> for dissolution testing and USP <857> for UV-Vis spectroscopy.
- Ensure proper calibration and maintenance of UV equipment.
- Validate the method for specificity, especially in the presence of excipients or degradation products.
