pages.text:
The Risk Assessment considers the potential presence of nitrosamine impurities in Sakuramil drug substance based on the manufacturing process as defined in section [[2.3.3.DS.M Manufacture (Sakuramil) [IROHA-corp]]]. 
The risk evaluation is performed using quality risk management principles, as outlined in ICH Q9 Quality Risk Management guideline.
The risk assessment has evaluated the following items as potential sources of nitrosamines or their precursors in line with root causes described in EMA/409815/2020.
Risk factors related to the manufacture of the active substance:
1. Use of nitrite salts and esters (e.g. NaNO2, alkyl nitrites), or other nitrosating agents (e.g. nitroso halides, nitrosonium salts, nitrogen oxides, nitro alkanes, halogenated nitro alkanes, Fremy’s salt, nitroso sulfonamides), in the presence of secondary or tertiary amines within the same or different steps of the manufacturing process. Sources for secondary or tertiary amines can also be starting materials, intermediates, reagents, solvents (e.g. DMF, DMAc and NMP) and catalysts, which contain amine functionality, amine impurities (e.g. quaternary ammonium salts) or which are susceptible to degradation to reveal amines.
1. Nitrite formation by oxidation of hydroxylamine or nitrite release from nitro-aromatic precursors (e.g. by fluoro de-nitration), in the presence of secondary or tertiary amines within the same or different steps of the manufacturing process.
1. Use of disinfected water (chlorination, chloro-amination, ozonisation) in the presence secondary or tertiary amines within the same or different steps of the manufacturing process.
1. Oxidation of hydrazines, hydrazides and hydrazones by hypochlorite, air, oxygen, ozone and peroxides in the manufacturing process or during storage
1. Use of contaminated raw, recovered or recycled materials (e.g. solvents, reagents and catalysts) in the API manufacturing process.
1. Use of contaminated starting materials and intermediates supplied by vendors who use processes or raw materials which may contain residual nitrosamines or nitrosating agents.
1. Carry-over of nitrosamines deliberately generated (e.g. as starting materials or intermediates) during the manufacturing process.
Risk factors also related to finished product:
1. A particular risk of formation of nitrosamines should be noted for active substances that contain a nitrosatable amine functional group. Several examples have been reported where the amine functionality was shown to be vulnerable to nitrosation and formation of the corresponding N-nitroso impurity (i.e. NO-API). Secondary amines appear particularly vulnerable to this reaction, although some cases with tertiary amines have also been observed.
  1. Does the API, or one of its known impurities, have a nitrosatable nitrogen functionality?
  1. May nitrites be present in one of the used excipients?
1. Degradation processes of active substances, including those induced by inherent reactivity (e.g. presence of nitro-alkyl, oxime, or other functionality) or by the presence of an exogenous nitrosating agent. 
1. Oxidation of hydrazine or other amine-containing functional groups present in active substances or their impurities/degradants (e.g. from hydrazones and hydrazides), either in active substance manufacturing processes or during storage. 
1. Use of certain packaging materials.
1.  Reaction of amines leaching from quaternary ammonium anion exchange resins (e.g. used for purification steps) with nitrosating agents present in the liquid phase. In addition, disinfection procedures such as e.g. chlorination, chloro-amination and ozonisation can lead to significant N-nitrosamine generation as by-products in case vulnerable amines are present. Given the source of contamination, risk is related to the concentration of the reactive agent(s) and thus, to the volume of water in or used to dilute a particular product. The same risks could be associated with active substances or finished  products manufactured using water purified using similar resins.
Risk factors related to GMP aspects:
1. Cross-contamination due to different processes being run successively on the same manufacturing line.
1. Carry-over of impurities between process steps due to operator-related errors or insufficiently detailed batch records such as inadequate phase separations during work-up procedures.
1. Use of contaminated recovered or recycled materials (e.g. solvents, reagents and catalysts) where the recovery is outsourced to third parties who are not aware of the content of the materials they are processing. Recovery processes carried out in non-dedicated equipment should also be considered.

## Risk Assessment
Sakuramil manufacturing process is outlined below:
Figure 1  Synthetic route of Sakuramil drug substance
[IMAGE:  Untitled.png]
Risk factors related to the manufacture of the active substance

### 1 Use of nitrite salts and esters (e.g. NaNO2, alkyl nitrites), or other nitrosating agents (e.g. nitroso halides, nitrosonium salts, nitrogen oxides, nitro alkanes, halogenated nitro alkanes, Fremy’s salt, nitroso sulfonamides), in the presence of secondary or tertiary amines within the same or different steps of the manufacturing process. Sources for secondary or tertiary amines can also be starting materials, intermediates, reagents, solvents (e.g. DMF, DMAc and NMP) and catalysts, which contain amine functionality, amine impurities (e.g. quaternary ammonium salts) or which are susceptible to degradation to reveal amines.
Risk for the presence of nitrosamines identified?
□ Yes
□ No
■ N.A.
Justification: According to the manufacturing process of Sakuramil drug substance vulnerable / nitrosatable compounds are present in the manufacturing process. Starting material CP-4, and intermediates CP-5 and CP-6 contain vulnerable/secondary amine moiety. Nevertheless, nitrite salts, esters or other nitrosating agents are not used in the manufacturing process of Sakuramil drug substance; therefore, isa risk of nirosamin formation identified in the text below.    

### 2 Nitrite formation by oxidation of hydroxylamine or nitrite release from nitro-aromatic precursors (e.g. by fluoro de-nitration), in the presence of secondary or tertiary amines within the same or different steps of the manufacturing process.
Risk for the presence of nitrosamines identified?
□ Yes
□ No
■ N.A.
Justification: Hydroxylamines and nitro-aromatic compounds are not used in the manufacturing process of Sakuramil drug substance; Therefore, the formation of N-nitrosamines due to nitrite formation by oxidation of hydroxylamine or nitrite release from nitro-aromatic precursors is considered as not applicable.   

### 3 Use of disinfected water (chlorination, chloro-amination, ozonisation) in the presence secondary or tertiary amines within the same or different steps of the manufacturing process.
Risk for the presence of nitrosamines identified?
□ Yes
□ No
■ N.A.
Justification: Disinfected water is not used in the manufacturing process of Sakuramil drug substance; therefore, formation of N-nitrosamine impurities due to water disinfection is considered as not applicable.   

### 4 Oxidation of hydrazines, hydrazides and hydrazones by hypochlorite, air, oxygen, ozone and peroxides in the manufacturing process or during storage.
Risk for the presence of nitrosamines identified?
□ Yes
□ No
■ N.A.
Justification: Hydrazines, hydrazides and hydrazones are not used in the manufacturing process of Sakuramil drug substance; therefore, the risk for formation of N-nitrosamines due to oxidation of hydrazines, hydrazides and hydrazones is considered as not applicable.    

### 5 Use of contaminated raw, recovered or recycled materials (e.g. solvents, reagents and catalysts) in the API manufacturing process.
Use of contaminated raw materials (e.g. solvents, reagents and catalysts).
Risk for the presence of nitrosamines identified?
□ Yes
■ No
□ N.A.
Justification: According to Sakuramil drug substance manufacturing process description the following solvents/reagents/catalysts are used: Methyl chloroformate, Sodium borohydride, Magnesium chloride, tetrahydrofuran, hydrochloric acid, methanol, sodium carbonate, Ethyl chloroformate, ethanol,  methylene chloride, sodium hydroxide solution, tert-butyl ammonium bromide.
Solvents (tetrahydrofuran, methanol, ethanol, methylene chloride) are used clean, not recovered or recycled, and therefore bear negligible risk of contamination with N-nitrosamines.
Inorganic reagents (Sodium borohydride, Magnesium chloride, hydrochloric acid sodium carbonate, sodium hydroxide solution) are used clean, not recovered, or recycled, and therefore bear negligible risk of contamination with N-nitrosamines.
Organic reagents (Methyl chloroformate, Ethyl chloroformate, tetr-Butyl ammonium bromide) are also used clean, not recovered, or recycled and also bear negligible risk of contamination with N-nitrosamines.
Use of contaminated recovered or recycled materials (e.g. solvents, reagents and catalysts).   
Risk for the presence of nitrosamines identified?
□ Yes
□ No
■ N.A.
Justification: There are no recovered or recycled materials used in the manufacturing process of Sakuramil  drug substance manufacturing process. Therefore, formation of N-nitrosamine impurities due to contaminated recovered or recycled materials is considered as not applicable.   

### 6 Use of contaminated starting materials and intermediates supplied by vendors who use processes or raw materials which may contain residual nitrosamines or nitrosating agents.
Risk for the presence of nitrosamines identified?
■ Yes
□ No
□ N.A.
Justification: 
The following starting materials are used in the manufacturing process: SM1 CP4 and SM2 CP-8. Sodium nitrite is used in the synthesis of SM2 CP-8 (1-bromo-3,5-bis(trifluoromethyl)benzene) as indicated by the route of synthesis of that Starting Material below.
[IMAGE:  Untitled.png]
In the proposed manufacturing process of SM2 CP-8 (1-bromo-3,5-bis(trifluoromethyl)benzene) is prepared in a two-step synthesis starting from Br2. In the second step NaNO2 is used as a reagent to generate CP-8 from the intermediate 2-bromo-4-fluoroaniline HBr. The manufacturer from CP-8 Starting Material confirmed that vulnerable amines and vulnerable amine precursors are not used in the SM2 synthesis, therefore the risk for formation of N-nitrosamines and contamination of SM2 with nitrosamines is negligible. Nevertheless, since sodium nitrite is used it has to be assessed if some residual nitrite might be present in SM2 CP-8 and carried over into the Sakuramil drug substance manufacturing process. Considering the route of synthesis, there is no secondary or tertiary amine to form N-nitrosamine impurities in presence of sodium nitrite. Primary amines like the intermediate 2-bromo-4-fluoroaniline HBr  are not capable of formation of N-nitrosamine in presence of sodium nitrite. Furthermore, considering the route of synthesis of Sakuramil drug substance after introduction of CP-8 (Step 4), there is a basic condition at low temperature of 12-25 °C. Both conditions do not support formation of N-nitrosamine impurities. Therefore, the overall risk is for formation/presence of nitrosamines due to SM2 CP-8 is evaluated as negligible.
[IMAGE:  Untitled.png]
SM 1 CP-4 contains vulnerable amine. As there is no source of nitrites in Step 1 of Sakuramil manufacturing process there is no risk for formation of corresponding nitrosamine. However, in step 2 CP-5 intermediate, containing vulnerable amine moiety, is converted to CP-6 (also vulnerable amine). In this stage water is used under acidic conditions therefore risk for formation of the corresponding nitrosamines from CP-5 and CP-6 can not be fully excluded. Nevertheless, it is expected that potential nitrosamine of CP-5 would be converted during Step 2 to nitrosamine of CP-6. Therefore, it can be assumed that the levels of nitroso-CP-6, if present, would be significantly higher, than the levels of nitroso-CP-5 and therefore, only nitroso-CP-6 is relevant for further mitigation.
In conclusion, there is a potential risk for nitroso-CP-6 formation in the manufacturing process of Sakuramil drug substance, therefore testing of final drug substance batches is needed.

### 7 Carry-over of nitrosamines deliberately generated (e.g. as starting materials or intermediates) during the manufacturing process.
Risk for the presence of nitrosamines identified?
□ Yes
□ No
■ N.A.
Justification: N-nitrosamines are not deliberately generated during the manufacturing process of Sakuramil drug substance. Therefore, the risk for the formation of nitrosamines due to this root cause is considered as not applicable.
Risk factors also related to the finished product

### 8     A particular risk of formation of nitrosamines should be noted for active substances that contain a nitrosatable amine functional group. Several examples have been reported where the amine functionality was shown to be vulnerable to nitrosation and formation of the corresponding N-nitroso impurity (i.e. NO-API). Secondary amines appear particularly vulnerable to this reaction, although some cases with tertiary amines have also been observed.    

### 8a  Does the API, or one of its known impurities, have a nitrosatable nitrogen functionality?   
Risk for the presence of nitrosamines identified?
□ Yes
■ No
□ N.A.
Justification: Sakuramil drug substance does not contain vulnerable/nitrosatable amine functionality.  

### 8b May nitrites be present in one of the used excipients?   
Risk for the presence of nitrosamines identified?
■ N.A.
Justification: N/A. This should be evaluated by DP manufacturer. 

### 9 Degradation processes of active substances, including those induced by inherent reactivity (e.g. presence of nitro-alkyl, oxime, or other functionality) or by the presence of an exogenous nitrosating agent. 
Risk for the presence of nitrosamines is evaluated as:
□ Yes
□ No
■ N.A.
Justification: Sakuramil drug substance does not contain any functional group as nitro-alkyl, oxime, or other functionality that could form N-nitrosamine upon degradation. Therefore, the risk for the formation of nitrosamines due to this root cause is considered as not applicable.   

### 10 Oxidation of hydrazine or other amine-containing functional groups present in active substances or their impurities/degradants (e.g. from hydrazones and hydrazides), either in active substance manufacturing processes or during storage. 
Risk for the presence of nitrosamines is evaluated as:
□ Yes
□ No
■ N.A.
Justification: Oxidation of hydrazine or other amine-containing functional groups are not present in Sakuramil final drug substance.  

### 11 Use of certain packaging materials.
Risk for the presence of nitrosamines is evaluated as:
□ Yes
□ No
■ N.A.
Justification: No certain packaging materials are used. 

### 12     Reaction of amines leaching from quaternary ammonium anion exchange resins (e.g. used for purification steps) with nitrosating agents present in the liquid phase. In addition, disinfection procedures such as e.g. chlorination, chloro-amination and ozonisation can lead to significant N-nitrosamine generation as by-products in case vulnerable amines are present. Given the source of contamination, risk is related to the concentration of the reactive agent(s) and thus, to the volume of water in or used to dilute a particular product. The same risks could be associated with active substances or finished products manufactured using water purified using similar resins.
Risk for the presence of nitrosamines is evaluated as:
□ Yes
□ No
■ N.A.
Justification: No quaternary ammonium anion exchange resins are used. No disinfection procedures are applied. Therefore, the risk for the formation of nitrosamines due to this root cause is considered as not applicable.
Risk factors related to GMP aspects

### 13 Cross-contamination due to different processes being run successively on the same manufacturing line.
Risk for the presence of nitrosamines is evaluated as:
□ Yes
□ No
■ N.A.
Justification: There is no risk on cross-contamination with alkylamines, nitrite or nitrosamines due to the use of multipurpose equipment as adequate cleaning procedures according to ICH Q7: Good Manufacturing Practice Guide for Active Pharmaceutical Ingredients are in place. Therefore, the risk for the presence of nitrosamines due to cross-contamination due to the use of multipurpose equipment is considered as not applicable.   

### 14 Carry-over of impurities between process steps due to operator-related errors or insufficiently detailed batch records such as inadequate phase separations during work-up procedures.
Risk for the presence of nitrosamines is evaluated as:
□ Yes
□ No
■ N.A.
Justification: This is ensured through internal procedures. 

### 15 Use of contaminated recovered or recycled materials (e.g. solvents, reagents and catalysts) where the recovery is outsourced to third parties who are not aware of the content of the materials they are processing. Recovery processes carried out in non-dedicated equipment should also be considered.
Risk for the presence of nitrosamines is evaluated as:
□ Yes
□ No
■ N.A.
Justification: Recovered or recycled materials are not used in the manufacturing process of Sakuramil drug substance; therefore, the formation of N-nitrosamine impurities is not feasible.
Based on the risk evaluation presented above there is a risk for formation/presence of nitroso-CP-6 in Sakuramil drug substance. Therefore, further mitigation is necessary.

Potential risk for the presence of nitroso-CP-6 in Sakuramil drug substance is identified, therefore three batches of drug substance were tested.

## RISK OUTCOME
Based on the risk evaluation conducted and mitigation measures, the risk for presence of nitrosamines is evaluated as:
■ no risk identified
☐ risk identified
The risk evaluation indicates that there is a potential presence of N-nitroso-CP-6 impurity in Sakuramil drug substance. However, according to the analytical testing results it is demonstrated that the levels of N-nitrosamine impurity are below 10% of acceptable limit.  Therefore, there is no risk for the presence of N-nitrosamine impurity in Sakuramil drug substance.

Nitrosating agents: Nitrosating agents are not likely to be present in the final API.

### Reasons for designating CP-4 as regulatory starting material in the manufacturing process of Sakuramil are as follows:
1. CP-4 is a significant structural fragment incorporated in the structure of the Sakuramil drug substance.
CP-4 contains the main core structure of Sakuramil: one of the trifluoromethyl as well as the amine residues.
1. It is a substance of defined chemical properties and structure.
1. CP-4 can be considered as “custom synthesized chemicals” according to ICH Q11 and ICH Q11 Q&A guideline principles.
1. Specifications of starting material CP-4 has been well defined to ensure adequate quality of starting material used in the synthesis of Sakuramil drug substance (refer to [[2.3.4.DS.C Control (Sakuramil) [IROHA-corp]]] ).
1. Discussion on potential impurities of CP-4, their origin as well as fate and purge are presented within [[2.3.4.DS.C Control (Sakuramil) [IROHA-corp]]].
1. Multiple chemical transformation steps are available between CP-4 and final drug substance.
1. In line with all general principles of ICH guideline Q11 on development and manufacture of drug substances (chemical entities and biotechnological/biological entities) and Q&A document.

Figure 1-1           Reaction scheme (CP-4, IROHA-corp.)

4-Brom-benzotrifluorid (CP-1) reacts with (3R)-3-Aminohexanenitrile (CP-2) to form in situ intermediate CP-3 in presence of Pd catalyst/ligand as well as base and toluene (Step A). In Step B, Starting Material CP-4 is formed by reacting with concentrated sulphuric acid solution, toluene and heptane.
Figure 1-2           Reaction scheme (CP-4, HETO-corp.)
[IMAGE:  Untitled.png]
4-Brom-benzotrifluorid (CP-1) reacts with (3R)-3-Aminohexanenitrile (CP-2) to form CP-3 in presence of Pd catalyst as well as ligand and toluene during temperature heating up to 70°C. In the next step, Starting Material CP-4 is formed by reacting with concentrated sulphuric acid solution and toluene.

CP-8 is a bis-trifluoromethyl benzene side chain incorporated in the structure of the Sakuramil.
1. It is a substance of defined chemical properties and structure.
1. Starting material CP-8 can be “custom synthesized chemicals” according to ICH Q11 and ICH Q11 Q&A guideline principles.
1. Specifications of starting material CP-8 has been well defined to ensure adequate quality of starting materials used in the synthesis of Sakuramil drug substance (refer to [[2.3.4.DS.C Control (Sakuramil) [IROHA-corp]]] ).

Impurities that are defined to impact the impurity profile of Sakuramil do not originate from earlier steps than of the starting materials. Manufacturing steps upstream of CP-8 are simple.
1. Only one chemical transformation step is available between CP-8 and final drug substance. CP-8 is controlled in the drug substance to the level of NMT 0.10%.
1. In line with all general principles of ICH guideline Q11 on development and manufacture of drug substances (chemical entities and biotechnological/biological entities) and Q&A document.

# 2.3.4.DP.D.1 Components of the drug product

## 1 Compatibility of the drug substance with excipients
For the development of Sakura Bloom 20 mg Film-coated tablet, standard pharmacopoeial excipients, commonly used in pharmaceutical formulations, were utilized. The concentration of each excipient is within the usual range of administration for a solid oral dosage form. The excipients utilized in the clinical formulation of Sakura Bloom 20 mg Film-coated tablet and their functions are listed in Table 1 below. 

### Table 1 Excipients used in Sakura Bloom 20 mg film-coated tablet
| Excipient | Function |
| Lactose monohydrate/ Lactose hydrate | Diluent |
| Cellulose, microcrystalline/ Microcrystalline cellulose | Diluent |
| Croscarmellose sodium | Disintegrant |
| Hydroxypropyl cellulose | Binder |
| Magnesium stearate | Lubricant |
| Hypromellose | Film-forming agent |
| Macrogol (type 6000)/ Polyethylene glycol (6000)/ Macrogol 6000 | Polishing agent |
| Titanium dioxide (E 171)/ Titanium oxide | Opacifier |
| Iron oxide, red (E 172)/ Ferric oxide/ Red Ferric oxide | Colorant |
The choice and ratio of the excipients used in the film-coated tablet formulation was based on compatibility studies as well as on pharmaceutical experience gained from the development of Sakura Bloom 20 mg film coated tablet in laboratory and pilot scale trials.

### 1.1 Excipients screening and selection
Excipients for formulation development were selected based on the excipient compatibility results, functionality of excipients (e.g., binder, diluent,  disintegrant, lubricant etc.), the selected manufacturing process and available stability data. Excipient screening was conducted using different mixtures of diluent, binder, disintegrant and lubricant and these mixtures representing excipient blends suitable for wet granulation technology were blended with drug substance and stored for 6 weeks at open and closed conditions at 40°C/75%RH.
A discussion on rationale for selection of each excipient is summarized in the following sections.
Diluent / filling agents
Several diluents (filling agents) including lactose hydrate, D- mannitol and microcrystalline cellulose were evaluated for dissolution and hardness. The results showed that a combination of lactose hydrate and microcrystalline cellulose produced a formulation with the highest dissolution rate and appropriate hardness, therefore lactose hydrate and microcrystalline cellulose were selected as diluents.
Disintegrant
To select a disintegrant, croscarmellose sodium, crospovidone, carmellose calcium and low substituted hydroxypropyl cellulose were evaluated for dissolution. Croscarmellose sodium proved to be the most effective disintegrant because of its rapid dissolution and was added to the inner phase of the granulate only.
Binder 
Hydroxypropyl cellulose was selected as a binder to aid the wet granulation process. It was selected over other binders based upon functional performance and preferable final drug product stability.
Lubricant
Magnesium stearate is a commonly used and effective lubricant. The selected levels have been proven to provide good physical characteristics of the tablets.
Film-coating 
Hypromellose, macrogol and titanium oxide are commonly used coating components which have been shown not to interfere with the stability of the drug substance and to provide a smooth and glossy film coat.  To give an appearance of a pale red color, red ferric oxide was added as coloring agent.
Summary
The range of amounts of excipients evaluated in the tablet core, the final amount selected, and the role of the excipient in the formulation of Sakura Bloom 20 mg film-coated tablets are provided in Table 2.
Table 2 summarizes excipients tested and indicates the final formulation of Sakura Bloom 20 mg film-coated tablets.

## 2 Excipient compatibility studies
A six-week compatibility study using standard solid oral excipients in sample formulations at stress conditions of 40°C/75%RH was performed. The formulations used and the corresponding summary of results are provided in table below and detailed results in [[22940ba1-bbd1-8132-8c60-c2cb979b0a03]] . 
The results showed neither a change in appearance, an increase in related substances nor a decrease in assay. Based on the results of the compatibility study, Sakuramil is compatible with all the excipients used to manufacture Sakura Bloom 20 mg Film-coated tablets. 
Registration stability data for the film-coated tablet confirm that the excipients and levels selected provide good stability which meet quality attributes at long-term 25°C/60 % RH, 30°C/75% RH and accelerated 40°C/75% RH storage conditions.

## 3 Key physicochemical properties of drug substance influencing the performance of the drug product
Polymorphism
Only one drug substance polymorph was found to be obtained by the manufacturing process of the drug substance. The polymorphic form was monitored by X-ray powder diffraction method during drug product manufacturing. The polymorphic form was shown to be stable after wet granulation and fluid bed drying process. No change to the polymorphic form was identified during long-term storage in the intended primary packaging configuration of the drug product.  Diffractograms  to confirm the polymorphic form stability in the drug product are provided in [[3.2.DP.D.1 Components of the drug product]]   
XRPD analysis of Sakurabloom 20 mg FCT across stability time points till end of Shelf-life (initial, 3 months, and 6 months, 24 months) under ICH conditions (25°C/60% RH, 30°C/75% RH and 40°C/75% RH) showed consistent diffraction peaks at 2θ values of 12.3°, 18.7°, 22.5°, 27.1°, 29.8 ° confirming the retention of the same crystalline polymorph. No peak shifts, broadening, or new peaks were observed, indicating polymorphic stability.
Particle size
The particle size for the drug substance is determined by laser light diffraction and the requirements are as follows: d (0.1) 26 nm, d (0.5) 40 nm and d (0.9) 66 nm. The drug substance with the same particle size distribution has been used throughout the drug product development and will be used in the commercial drug product manufacturing.
Water content
Sakuramil drug substance is non-hygroscopic. Water content (Loss on drying) test is routinely performed on the drug substance.
Sakuramil drug substance was subjected to stress testing at 40°C/75% RH for 30 days. Gravimetric analysis showed a negligible weight gain of <0.05%, and Karl Fischer titration confirmed moisture uptake below 0.1%. No physical changes (e.g., clumping, discoloration) were observed, supporting its classification as non-hygroscopic.
BCS classification
Based on the solubility profile across the physiological pH and based on the measured permeability across Caco-2 cell membranes ([[3.2.DP.D.1 Components of the drug product]]) , Sakuramil is considered to have low solubility and high permeability according to the Biopharmaceutics Classification System (BCS). Sakuramil is therefore classified as BCS Class 2 compound.

# 2.3.4.DP.D.2 Formulation development

## 1 Formulation development strategy
A systematic Quality by Design (QbD) approach was employed for formulation development of Sakura Bloom 20 mg Film-coated tablet. With the prior knowledge on the drug substance and drug product and manufacturing experiences, Design of Experiments (DoE) and quality risk management were used. This enhanced approach to formulation and process development, enabled identification of Critical Quality Attributes (CQAs) and Critical Process Parameters (CPPs) of the drug substance and the drug product, and Real Time Release Testing (RTRT), supporting continual improvement throughout the product lifecycle.
Approach
Following approaches were employed to support definition of the control strategy for the final manufacturing process and quality assurance of Sakura Bloom 20 mg Film-coated tablet.
1. Establishment of the Quality Target Product Profile (QTPP) and initial risk assessment
1. Identification of the product CQAs that ensure desired quality, safety and efficacy
1. Assessment of the effects of the potential critical material attributes (p-CMA) on CQAs, and identification of critical material attributes (CMA)
1. Assessment of the effects of potential critical process parameter (p-CPP) like inlet air volume, inlet air temperature, spray rate and tableting rotation speed on CMAs, and identification of critical process parameters (CPP)
1. Construction of the control strategy
1. Review of the risk assessment after implementation of the control strategy
1. Overall evaluation of risk assessment
According to the approach described above, Preliminary Hazard Analysis (PHA) was used in the initial risk assessment, and Failure Mode and Effects Analysis (FMEA) was used in the risk assessment of the manufacturing process and in the risk assessment after implementation of the control strategy. More information related to manufacturing is available at: [[1.2. Determination of CMAs affecting each CQA]] 
A risk assessment based on the results of formulation development with Sakura Bloom 20 mg Film-coated tablet indicated that drug substance particle size, granule particle size, uncoated tablet hardness, uncoated tablet weight, uncoated tablet weight variation, and granule segregation impacted the drug product CQAs of dissolution, uniformity of dosage units, and assay. These attributes were therefore identified as CMAs. In the final control strategy, drug substance particle size was included in the specifications of the drug substance, granule particle size and uncoated tablet hardness were to be controlled within the design space to ensure the dissolution, and uncoated tablet weight and the weight variation were to be controlled by in-process control. To confirm that the granule segregation is within the acceptable range, the drug substance concentrations in uncoated tablets are periodically monitored with near infrared spectrophotometry (NIR). CPPs in each unit operation were to be feedback-controlled with Process Analytical Technology (PAT) for granule particle size in the granulation process, and for uncoated tablet hardness, uncoated tablet weight, uncoated tablet weight variation and drug substance concentrations in uncoated tablets in the tableting process. Application of the above control strategy, including supporting models enables real time release testing for the drug product CQAs of dissolution, uniformity of dosage units, and assay.

## 2 Overages 
No overage of Sakuramil is used in the formulation and manufacture of Sakura Bloom 20 mg Film-coated tablets.

# 2.3.4.DP.D.3 Comparability during formulation and product development
As Sakuramil has properties of high metal adherability and poor flowability, Sakura Bloom 20 mg Film-coated tablet used for clinical studies were manufactured using a fluid bed granulation process (one of the wet granulation methods).  A part of a Design of Experiments (DoE), uncoated tablets were prepared containing 3 levels of each of disintegrant, binder, and lubricant, and were assessed for dissolution and hardness to determine the final formula.
Based on the output of the DoE, disintegrant was set at 5% w/w, binder at 3%w/w, and lubricant at 1%w/w. The dissolution and uncoated tablet hardness were found to be met with a wide range of excipient levels, including the optimum solution levels chosen, thus the chosen formulation was confirmed to be robust for drug product CQAs. The amount of coating agent was set at 3%w/w of the formulation, based on the relationship between the amount of coating agent and photostability.
Table 3 shows the composition of 5 mg tablet, 10 mg tablet, and 20 mg tablet used for clinical studies, as well as the composition for the 20 mg tablet for commercial production. For the proposed 20 mg tablet included in this submission, the uncoated tablets had the same formula from the clinical development stage to commercial production. However, the tablet color was white during the clinical development stage but was changed to pale red at the registration stage, with no impact on dissolution.

# 2.3.4.DP.D.4 Physicochemical and biological properties of drug product

## 1 Homogeneity
Homogeneity of the final tablets has been demonstrated by blend and content uniformity testing performed by blend and stratified content uniformity testing performed during process development and will be continued to be monitored during process validation. The values show that both the blend and content uniformity of tablets are achieved with selected process parameters.
Detailed results are provided in [[3.2.DP.D.4 Physicochemical and biological properties of drug product]] 

## 2 Performance testing

### 2.1 Dissolution testing
Sakura Bloom 20 mg Film-coated tablet is an immediate release dosage form. Consequently, the performance testing during release activities is based on dissolution testing.
‘Dissolution testing is conducted for release analysis as well as during stability using the paddle apparatus, 50 rpm, in 900 mL of 0.01 M HCl (pH 1.2), a diluted McIlvaine buffer (pH 4.0) and pH 6.8 phosphate buffer with UV detection. The current requirement for the dissolution test is Not Less Than 80% (Q in 30 minutes) of the declared content according to acceptance table 1 of harmonized Ph. Eur., USP and JP.
As shown in Figure 1, dissolution profiles reflect the solubility, and the dissolution rate was decreased with the increase in pH. Based on the dissolution profile of the drug product used in the phase III clinical studies, the dissolution in the diluted McIlvaine buffer (pH 4.0) with a low dissolution rate (among the dissolution media in which 85% or more was dissolved in a specified time), was used as a discriminatory dissolution method to support manufacturing process development.

# 2.3.4.DP.D.5 Microbiological attributes
Sakura Bloom 20 mg Film-coated tablet is a standard solid oral dosage form. Controls necessary for the manufacture and control of Sakura Bloom 20 mg Film-coated tablet are conducted in accordance with cGMPs to prevent microbial contamination.
MET is proposed to be performed as frequency test (periodic quality indicator test). The risk of microbial contamination of the drug product is considered low due to the manufacturing process, environmental monitoring, and cleaning procedures in place. The analysis of historical MET data supports this assessment. During development, microbial limit testing was performed on more than 10 clinical batches. For all batches tested to date, the results met requirements (Table 5). No microbial growth was observed within 12 month registration stability testing. Furthermore, growth inhibitory properties of the drug substance were observed during method validation (alternatively, discuss water activity levels, if available). Therefore, the proposal to perform MET as frequency test is consistent with the ICH guideline Q6A (Decision tree #8). The microbial enumeration tests will be performed at release on the first 5 consecutive production batches. If the requirements are met testing frequency may be reduced to every 10th batch. At least one batch will be tested in each calendar year in which the product is manufactured.

# 2.3.4.DP.M.1 Development of manufacturing process and process controls

# 1. Manufacturing process development
The same manufacturing process was used from the early development stage through to commercial supply. The process consists of the following steps:
Process 1 (granulation): granulation and drying using a fluid bed granulator
Process 2 (blending): mixing the granules and lubricant
Process 3 (tableting): compressing the blend to produce tablets,
Process 4 (coating),
Process 5 (inspection) and
Process 6 (packaging).
The equipment used for each process was identical to or the same principle as the equipment to be used for commercial production. Drug substance milling was performed as part of the manufacturing process of the drug substance.
To ensure the desired quality, safety, and efficacy of the product, an initial risk assessment of the critical quality attributes (CQAs - description, identification, uniformity of dosage units, assay, dissolution, impurity) was undertaken, and the CQAs (uniformity of dosage units, assay, and dissolution) that were considered high risk were identified.
All the Material Attributes (MAs) that had the potential to affect the high risk CQAs were identified. Potential critical material attributes (p-CMAs) were identified through risk assessment and experimental studies based on the development knowledge from this product and the final CMAs were identified by further increasing knowledge and understanding. Next, all the Process Parameters (PPs) that have the potential to affect the CMAs were thoroughly clarified. Potential critical process parameters (p-CPPs) were identified through risk assessment and experiments, and the CPPs were identified by increased knowledge and understanding. Management of the CPPs to ensure control of the CMAs within an appropriate range (using process analytical technology (PAT) feedback system in this case) makes it possible to continue to assure the CQAs throughout the product life cycle.
For the CQA of dissolution, the “appropriate ranges” of the CMAs were defined by a design space. In general, process parameters are equipment specific. Considering the equipment specific parameters, in order to continually assure the CQAs to achieve the QTPP, it may be more important to appropriately control CMAs such as uncoated tablet hardness, rather than to control PPs such as compression force within an appropriate range. To meet a “target CMA value,” the feedback control of CPPs, which affect CMAs with PAT, makes it possible to continuously ensure the CQA throughout the product life cycle, and supports the concept of ‘ongoing process verification’, which enables continual improvement. Use of CMAs as input factors makes it possible to manufacture the product to ensure it continually satisfies the QTPP, even when we make changes in manufacturing equipment which have the same operating principle.

## 1.1 Initial risk assessment and Justification
Description, identification, uniformity of dosage units, assay, impurities and dissolution were identified as CQAs that may need to be controlled to meet the QTPP for Sakura Bloom 20 mg Film-coated tablet, based on the physicochemical properties, the knowledge and information gained through the formulation development and manufacturing experiences. An initial risk assessment assessing the quality of Sakura Bloom 20 mg Film-coated tablet was performed for these CQAs using preliminary hazard analysis. The results are shown in Table 1.
Based on the QTPP [[2.3.2.1 Quality Target Product Profile]] for Sakura Bloom 20 mg Film-coated tablet and the results of the initial risk assessment, the uniformity of dosage units was considered high risk, because it is affected by the change in drug substance particle size, blend uniformity, uncoated tablet weight/weight variation, and segregation, and may affect the efficacy and safety in patients.
Assay is considered high risk, because it is affected by the change in uncoated tablet weight and may affect efficacy and safety.
Dissolution was considered high risk, because it is affected by the change in drug substance particle size, physical property of lubricant, granule particle size, lubricity of lubricant at blending, compression force/uncoated tablet hardness, and amount of coating film, and may affect the efficacy and safety.
Among the CQAs, the description is only affected by the coating process, which was confirmed to be acceptable during clinical development and at the process development stages. Due to the low risk of affecting efficacy and safety in patients, description was decided to be controlled as per the specifications. Identification is not affected by variable factors in manufacturing and was considered to have a low risk of affecting efficacy and safety in patients. Thus, identification was decided to be controlled as per the specifications.
It was shown that there was no increase in related substances in formulations during the manufacturing processes, from the excipient compatibility tests and results of clinical tablet manufacturing in the formulations of each strength at the development stages. Therefore, it is considered that drug related impurity content has a low risk of affecting efficacy and safety in patients, provided that the impurities in the drug substance are controlled within the specifications.

### Table 1 Summary of initial risk assessment
| CQA | Drug substance | Excipient | Granulation | Blending | Compression | Coating | Rationale |
| Description | Low                 | Low          | Low              | Low           | Low               | Low        | Granulation, blending and compression steps will not impact the description of the drug product. Only the coating process may affect the description but based on experiences gained at the development stages and during manufacture of clinical drug products there is a low risk of affecting efficacy and safety |
| Identification | Low                 | Low          | Low            | Low       | Low             | Low        | Identification is not affected by manufacturing process variables and has a low risk of affecting the efficacy and safety. |
| Uniformity of dosage units | High            | Low          | Low            | High        | High            | Low        | The drug substance particle size, blend uniformity at the blending process, uncoated tablet weight/weight variation following tableting, and segregation influence the uniformity of dosage units and may affect efficacy and safety. |
| Assay | Low                 | Low          | Low            | Low          | High            | Low        | The blend uniformity at blending step and uncoated tablet weight at compression step has an affect on the content of drug substance and may affect the efficacy and safety. |
| Dissolution | High            | High        | High            | High        | High            | High       | The drug substance particle size, physical property of lubricant, granule particle size, lubricity of lubricant during blending, compression force/uncoated tablet hardness, and amount of coating film has an effect on the dissolution and may affect the efficacy and safety. |
| Impurity | Low                 | Low          | Low              | Low           | Low               | Low        | Impurity content was not increased during manufacturing processes and has a low risk of affecting the efficacy and safety, as long as the drug substance impurities are controlled within the specifications. |
The assessment of each CQA of stability samples showed no change in the product quality and confirmed there is no change on storage if the initial quality is assured.

## 1.2. Determination of CMAs affecting each CQA

### 1.2.1 Identification of p-CMAs
Material attributes that can potentially affect the CQAs of Sakura Bloom 20 mg Film-coated tablets are listed in Table 2. p-CMAs were identified for CQAs (uniformity of dosage units, assay, dissolution) which were considered high risk in the initial risk assessment utilizing knowledge gained through the formulation development up to the formulation for phase III clinical studies. p-CMAs identified include drug substance particle size, blend uniformity, segregation, uncoated tablet weight, uncoated tablet weight variation, lubricant surface area, granule particle size, lubricity of lubricant, and uncoated tablet hardness.
The amount of film coating listed in the initial risk assessment, was confirmed not to affect dissolution across a wide range, and thus, not included as a p-CMA.
For implementation of risk assessment, the relationship between QTPP, CQA, and p-CMA was summarized in Figure 1 in the form of an Ishikawa diagram. Risk assessment was performed for these p-CMA using Failure Mode and Effects Analysis (FMEA). The definition of risk priority number (RPN) was defined as follows: ≥ 40 is high risk, ≥ 20 and < 40 is medium risk, and < 20 is low risk. Consequently, as shown in Figure 2 and Table 3 all the p-CMAs identified for each CQA were medium risk or high risk.

### Table 2 Material attributes possibly affecting CQA
|  | Factor |
| Drug substance | Adherability, flowability, water content, agglomeration properties, hygroscopicity, solubility, melting point, physical stability (deliquescent, efflorescent, sublimation, etc.), chemical stability, particle shape, particle size (distribution), residual solvent, wettability, specific surface area, and physical change |
| Excipient | Adherability, flowability, coning properties, polymorphism, water content, agglomerating properties, hygroscopicity, solubility, melting point, physical stability (deliquescent, efflorescent, sublimation, etc.), manufacturer (supplier, site, etc.), grade, origin, purity of ingredient, manufacturing methods, surface condition, compatibility with drug substance (adsorption etc.), interaction between excipients, compression properties, particle size, wettability, and surface area |
| Granulation | Particle distribution (particle size), binder (concentration, viscosity, grade), water content of granules after drying, water content of granules during granulation, surface conditions on granules (wettability), chemical change by moisture, degradation by heating, particle shape, specific volume, drug substance content in each fraction, flowability, granule physical strength, and material of equipment |
| Blending | Flowability, particle size, particle shape, blend uniformity, specific volume, lubricity of lubricant, granule physical strength, and material of equipment |
| Compression | Granule particle size, dispersibility of lubricant in granules, chemical change by moisture, degradation by heating, segregation, uncoated tablet weight, weight variation, disintegration, uncoated tablets hardness/density/thickness, uncoated tablet dissolution, presence or absence of score line/imprint, and material of equipment |
| Coating | Chemical change by moisture, degradation by heating, tablet weight (amount of coating film), hardness, disintegration, coating agent (concentration, viscosity, grades), strength of coating film, water content in coating, water content after drying, presence or absence of score line/imprint, friability/ cracking/chipping, and material of equipment |

### 1.2.2 Identification of CMA
The effect of p-CMAs on CQAs was experimentally studied.
Effect of drug substance particle size on CQA (uniformity of dosage units and dissolution)
As shown in Figure 3 (a), changes in drug substance particle size did not affect the blend uniformity of granules for tableting, and the uniformity of the dosage units. Therefore, it was confirmed that the drug substance particle size did not affect the uniformity of dosage units (CQA), and its severity risk score was decreased.

### Figure 3 Effects of the drug substance particle size on CQA (uniformity of dosage units and dissolution)
[IMAGE:  Untitled.png]
Figure 3 (b) shows a dissolution profile of Sakura Bloom 20 mg Film-coated tablet (Dissolution using Apparatus II (Paddle), pH 4.0 acetate buffer at 50 rpm (n=12)) in which the drug substance particle size was changed. The dissolution rate decreased with increasing drug substance particle size, as shown in the figure, and the drug substance particle size was confirmed to affect the dissolution (CQA). Therefore, the risk score was not decreased. Results are provided in [[3.2.DP.M.2 Development of manufacturing process and process controls]] 
Effects of blend uniformity /granule segregation / uncoated tablet weight/ uncoated tablet weight variation on uniformity of dosage units (CQA)
In the fluid-bed granulation process for Sakura Bloom Film-coated tablet, changes in granulation parameters (such as spray rate) lead to a high drug substance concentration in the small granules using operating condition A, where granulation did not proceed completely, i.e., different drug substance concentrations in different granulation sizes (see Figure 4 (a)). As shown in Figure 4 (b) ‘Granule particle size distribution’, high or low drug substance concentrations were found in about 10% of the granules for condition A. Thus, granule segregation due to differences in granule particle size could be a potential risk causing drug substance content segregation in tablets. When granules for tableting were prepared using these granules, rapid blend uniformity was obtained for both granulation conditions, as shown in Figure 5. Therefore, although the risk score of severity that blend uniformity has on uniformity of dosage units remained unchanged, the risk score of probability of blend non-uniformity decreased in FMEA.

### Figure 4 Effects of granulation conditions on granules
[IMAGE:  Untitled.png]

### Figure 5 Blend uniformity profile
[IMAGE:  Untitled.png]
As the uncoated tablet weight and granule segregation clearly affect the uniformity of dosage units, the severity risk score did not decrease. Also, as shown in Figure 6 weight variation increased with increasing press speed, thus, the probability risk score did not significantly decrease. Similarly, as shown in  (a), when the granules prepared under the condition A were tableted, there was a difference between tablet weight variation and granule segregation with increasing tablet rotation speed, and it was confirmed that there is a risk that granule segregation can occur during tableting. Based on these findings, continuous tableting was performed using two grades of granules shown in Figure 4 at a tableting rotation speed of 50 rpm when there was a difference between tablet weight and drug substance content. As a result, the drug substance content in tablet was the highest under the condition A at the end of tableting. Although the probability risk score decreased as the granule segregation did not occur across a wide range of tableting rotation speeds, it was considered that there was a risk that granule segregation could lead non-uniformity of dosage units.

### Figure 6 Effects of tableting rotation speed
[IMAGE:  Untitled.png]
Effects of the mass of uncoated tablet weight on content (CQA)
It is obvious that the uncoated tablets weight during tableting affects the content (CQA). Therefore, risk score of severity did not decrease as the risk assessment proceeded. On the other hand, as shown in Figure 7  in a total of 6 batches, 3 clinical batches and 3 primary stability batches, the drug substance content in uncoated tablets during tableting over time was almost constant at a mean of 3 tablets, when the target value of the uncoated tablets weight was specified and the tableting was performed under appropriate conditions. Therefore, the risk score of probability that the uncoated tablet weight affects the content was considered to be low.

### Figure 7 Drug substance content at tableting over time (mean of 3 tablets)
[IMAGE:  Untitled.png]
Effect of lubricity of lubricant/granule particle size/ uncoated tablet hardness on dissolution (CQA)
The effects of lubricity of lubricant on dissolution were assessed at a range of blending times with 3 grades of lubricant (magnesium stearate) with different specific surface areas (SSA). As shown in Figure 8 (a), there were no differences in the dissolution profiles between tablet with “small specific surface area and short blending time (small lubricity of lubricant) and tablet with “large specific surface area and long blending time (large lubricity of lubricant).” Therefore, the significance of the risk was low. On the other hand, in uncoated tablets with large granules size (granules shown in Figure 4 are used) or hard uncoated tablets, the dissolution rate was significantly slower as shown in  Figure 8 (b). Because the granule particle size and uncoated tablets hardness affect dissolution, the severity risk score was not decreased. Regarding the probability risk score of changing granule particle size and uncoated tablet hardness, the risk was not significantly reduced, based on the manufacturing history of the clinical tablets.

### Figure 8 Effect of lubricant/granule particle size/lubricity of lubricant/uncoated tablets hardness on dissolution
[IMAGE:  Untitled.png]

- Assay – Uncoated tablet weight
- Uniformity of dosage units – Granule segregation, uncoated tablet weight and tablet weight variation
- Dissolution - Drug substance particle size, granule particle size and uncoated tablet hardness

## 1.3. Process controls

###  1.3.1 Extraction of potential CPPs (p-CPPs)
Table 5 lists the process parameter that could potentially affect each identified CMA of Sakura Bloom 20 mg Film-coated tablet in [[1.2. Determination of CMAs affecting each CQA]]. Particle size of drug substance is a CMA for dissolution CQA, but the control of particle size of drug substance is performed during the drug substance process, thus it is not described in this section. The uncoated tablet weight is a common CMA for assay and uniformity of dosage units, thus the risk assessment was performed as a CMA for assay.
From the listed process parameters, p-CPPs were identified utilizing the knowledge gained through pharmaceutical development up to the phase III clinical studies. Identified p-CPPs included inlet air volume, inlet air temperature, spray rate, tableting rotation speed, and compression force. Risk assessment was performed for these p-CPP using FMEA. The details of FMEA are shown in [[1.2. Determination of CMAs affecting each CQA]]. As for the definition of risk priority number (RPN), ≥ 40 was high risk, ≥20 to < 40 was medium risk, and <20 was low risk. As a result, as shown in Figure 10 and Figure 7  every p-CPP extracted for each CMA was medium risk or high risk. The relation among QTPP, CQA, CMA and p-CPP was summarized in Figure 11 in the form of an Ishikawa diagram.

## 1.4 Construction of the control strategy
The relationship between each CMA/CPP, QTPP, and CQA of Sakura Bloom 20 mg Film-coated tablet, which was defined in Section 1.2 and Section 1.3, is summarized in Figure 11 in the form of an Ishikawa diagram.
The control strategy to assure each CQA is shown below.

### 1.4.1 Uniformity of dosage units (CQA)
For the three CMAs affecting uniformity of dosage units (CQA), uncoated tablet weight and uncoated tablet weight variation are determined by in-process control, and granule segregation is monitored by determining drug substance concentrations of the uncoated tablet by an NIR method. If the results exceeded the threshold, Process Analytical Technology (PAT) feedback control, which controls the rotation speed (CPP) is to be employed. As the drug substance concentration of uncoated tablets is determined in 200 or more tablets per batch, RTRT is to be performed in principle.

### 1.4.2 Assay (CQA)
The CMA of uncoated tablet weight which affects assay (CQA) is to be controlled by in-process control. Because Sakura Bloom 20 mg Film-coated tablet specific CPPs are not present, online monitoring control was employed for the compression force of every tablet through the tableting process, as generally performed. A compression force controller allows correction of the amounts of filled blended powder (filling depth) and removal of tablets out of the acceptable range from the system based on the information of compression force measured. In addition, a correcting system that adjusts the amounts of filled blended powder (filling depth) and compression force control equipment by means of the average weight information periodically measured by automatic sampling and fed back to the tableting machine by weight control equipment is also used. As is the case in uniformity of dosage units, the drug substance concentration of uncoated tablets is determined in 200 or more tablets; thus, RTRT is to be performed using the mean data in principle.

### 1.4.3 Dissolution (CQA)
The granule particle size is controlled within a certain range in the following ways: 1) Particle size (CMA) of drug substance affecting dissolution (CQA) is a specification item for drug substance, 2) Uncoated tablet hardness (CMA) is controlled by feedback of CPP compression force, 3) Granule particle size (CMA) is monitored using Focused Beam Reflectance Measurement (FBRM), and 4) CPP of spray rate that mostly affects the granule particle size is controlled by PAT feedback.
Regarding uniformity of dosage units and content of drug substance, RTRT is to be performed by determining the drug substance content in uncoated tablets after tableting in principle. On the other hand for dissolution, because a factor controlling CMA covers two or more unit processes, feedforward control can be employed from the upstream to the downstream in the manufacturing process. Thus, dissolution prediction formula can be constructed using three CMA values, and the dissolution is controlled by establishing design space consisting of these three CMA to make feedforward control easy.

### Figure 19 Dissolution DoE, central composite design
[IMAGE:  Untitled.png]
Dissolution test was performed for the drug product manufactured under the conditions allocated by DoE, and the effect of each factor on the dissolution rate were investigated. The test results were subjected to multidimensional analysis. For the formula for the sum of each factor which is multiplied by a coefficient, the coefficients that make the residual sum of squares minimum were calculated (the formula is shown below).
Dissolution rate = A – B x particle size of drug substance – C x granule particle size – D x uncoated tablet hardness – E × particle size of drug substance × uncoated tablet hardness
To verify the validity of the formula, each CMA (particle size of drug substance, granule particle size, uncoated tablet hardness; refer to Table 11) of the formulation produced at pilot scale (20 kg) and at commercial scale (200 kg) was input into the formula, and the predicted values and the actual values were compared. As a result, as shown in Figure 20, error in prediction, i.e., Root Mean Square Error of Prediction (RMSEP) was 1.6%, showing good agreement. Based on the above results, the formula for dissolution prediction, which was established by DoE at a laboratory scale, was found to be applicable at pilot scale or commercial scale.

[IMAGE:  Untitled.png]
Based on this formula, the response surface is shown in Figure 21. The cuboid, defines an area that satisfies 80% or more of the dissolution rate (predicted value), specification, was employed to define a design space to assure the dissolution of Sakura Bloom 20 mg Film-coated tablet.
A feedforward control will be used in commercial production to ensure that the dissolution rate is about 90%.
In other words, a control to keep the predicted dissolution value constant is established made by appropriately determining the target value for ‘granule particle size (CMA)’ and ‘uncoated tablet hardness (CMA) within this design space, according to the particle size of drug substance obtained in the drug substance process. The overview is shown in Figure 22.

### 1.4.4 Specifications except for CQA
For identification, it is considered possible to apply an alternative test, by applying an NIR method as an in-process control in the inspection process, and by using a discriminating model constructed by a spectrum in the wavenumber domain indicating the specific peaks of the drug substance. Furthermore, for the description (appearance) it is also considered possible to apply an alternative test as an in-process control in the inspection process.

### 1.4.5 Review of the risk assessment after implementation of control strategy
By applying the above control strategy, the risk of each CMA (Figure 23, Table 10) and CPP (Figure 24, Table 12) was as follows, and all CMA/CPPs were found to be low risk.
1.4.5.1 Risk assessment of Critical Material Attributes (CMA)
Granule segregation
The risk score of probability was decreased and the detectability was improved as well, by establishing an appropriate acceptable range for the tableting rotation speed (CPP), by measuring the content of uncoated tablets with an NIR method during tableting in real time, with a feedback loop to the CPP tableting rotation speed.
Uncoated tablet weight/weight variation
The detectability was improved by establishing in-process control. Although the tableting rotation speed affected the uncoated tablet weight/weight variation during the laboratory scale test, rotation speed did not affect uncoated tablet weight/weight variation using a commercial production machine, resulting the risk score of probability decreasing.
Particle size
The detectability was improved by establishing an appropriate acceptable range for rotation speed of milling equipment and setting a specification for particle size of the drug substance.
Granule particle size
The risk score of probability was decreased and the detectability was improved as well, by establishing an appropriate acceptable range for spray rate (CPP), by measuring the granule particle size at granulation in real time, with the feedback loop to CPP spray rate, and by defining a design space including granule particle size.
Uncoated tablet hardness
The risk score of probability was decreased and the detectability was improved as well, by establishing an appropriate acceptable range for compression force (CPP), with the feedback loop to CPP compression force during tableting in real time, and by defining a design space including uncoated tablet hardness.

1.4.5.3 Overall evaluation of risk assessment
As part of the risk assessment after applying the control strategy, we verified the items that were considered to be low risk at initial risk assessment (Table 1), for those items, no more examination was made.
Description and identification
As shown in sections of [[2.3.4.DP.C Control (Sakura Bloom)[APM][FCT][20 mg]]] and [[2.3.4.DP.S Storage - Bulk (Sakura Bloom )[APM][FCT][20 mg]]], differences in production scale, batch of drug substance, batch of excipients, or manufacturing conditions did not affect the description (appearance) and identification, from the stability test results of clinical tablets and formulations for the pilot scale and the results of manufacture in commercial scale production. It was thus concluded that the effect of manufacturing processes on these attributes was minimal and they have a low risk.
Impurity
For impurity, as shown in sections [[2.3.4.DP.C Control (Sakura Bloom)[APM][FCT][20 mg]]] and  [[2.3.4.DP.S Storage - Bulk (Sakura Bloom )[APM][FCT][20 mg]]], related impurities in the drug product were not produced/increased during formulation and storage (including stress testing). It was thus found that the effect of the manufacturing processes on impurity was minimal and they have a low risk.
Uniformity of dosage units and assay
The items that were considered to be low risk at initial risk assessment shown in Table 1, were verified.
- To assess the effect of drug substance on content, we examined the content of the drug product having drug substance with different particle sizes, as shown in Figure 3. As a result, the particle size of drug substance was confirmed not to affect the content.
- To assess the effect of excipients on uniformity of dosage units and assay, the uniformity of dosage units and assay were examined in the drug products manufactured by DoE at each experimental point. As a result, it was confirmed that there were no differences in uniformity of dosage units and assay at all experimental points. Since the formulations for the NDA, which were prepared with even different batches of excipients, and the manufacturing experience on a commercial scale did not matter, it was confirmed that excipients do not affect the uniformity of dosage units and assay.
- The effect of the granulation process on uniformity of dosage units and assay was examined. As shown in 1.2.2 Identification of CMA’ and ‘1.3.2 Identification of CPP,’ it was found that only inappropriate tableting affects the uniformity of dosage units and assay, under the granulation conditions where the drug substance content in each fraction is non-uniform. Since it is obvious that these risks can be controlled by applying the control strategy, they were confirmed to be low risk.
- With respect to the effect of the blending process on content, the blending process was confirmed to have a low risk, because there was no content reduction such as loss of drug substance in the blending process, in any of the drug products shown in this section.
- As for the risk that the coating process affects the uniformity of dosage units and assay, a case was considered where damage or degradation of tablets affects the content in the coating process. However, none of the two cases was observed through the manufacturing experiences and the coating process was confirmed to have a low risk.
Based on the above results, it was verified that the items that were considered to be low risk in the initial risk assessment, following an overall evaluation of the risk assessment, had a low risk.

# 2.3.4.DP.M.4 Summary of process validation or evaluation studies
The manufacturing process of Sakura Bloom 20 mg Film-coated tablets has been validated using three production-scale batches which have been processed in the same manufacturing facilities, using the same process and the same equipment as for the batches intended for marketing.
All three batches consistently meet the quality control specifications. The results of routine and extended in-process control (IPC) testing have demonstrated that the manufacturing process is robust and consistently yields a product capable of meeting the pre-defined quality characteristics.

Conclusions
The data gathered during the process validation show that the manufacturing process of Sakura Bloom 20 mg Film-coated tablets is robust and consistently yields drug product which meets the predetermined quality characteristics. Moreover, the chosen in-process tests have been shown to be suitable for monitoring the manufacturing process.
The conclusion from the presented data is that the process conditions and values chosen for the processing parameters are acceptable to support the commercial manufacture of the product.
CQAs of Sakura Bloom Tablets are ensured by CMAs that are maintained by routine production. The control strategy in production of Sakura Bloom Tablets operates the following maintenance program to verify the model.
Daily check:
- Trend analyses of CQA and CMA are performed for every batch produced, and the changes are confirmed to be within an acceptable range.
- If the trend is out of the acceptable level, a comparison is made between the model and conventional testing methods. If the model has some problems, it should be revised. If the model has no problems, the relationship between CPP and CMA is considered to be broken. Thus, control of CPP is reviewed so that CMA has an appropriate value.
Periodical check:
- A comparison is made between the values calculated by the model and those obtained by the conventional testing methods at a certain production interval. If the difference between the two is out of the acceptable level, the model should be revised.

# 2.3.4.DP.C.1 Control of impurities
This section addresses potential drug product related impurities and provides characterization information on those impurities that appear as drug product related impurities or degradation products during release and/ or stability testing using the selected analytical procedure. Impurities present in the drug substance that do not increase on storage or during production and storage of the drug product are addressed in section Sakuramil drug substance [[2.3.4.DS.C Control (Sakuramil) [IROHA-corp]]] . Impurities addressed in this document are controlled in line with ICH Q3B. Please refer to [[2.3.3.DP.C Control (Sakura Bloom)[APM][FCT][20 mg]]] for specifications and [[2.3.4.DP.C.3 Justification of specifications]]  for justification of limits for impurities.

### Risk evaluation of Nitrosamine impurities in Sakura Bloom 20 mg Film-coated tablet
The risk evaluation for the potential presence of Nitrosamine impurities, belonging to the mutagenic impurity cohort of concern (CoC) according to the ICH M7 guideline, has been performed.
The risk evaluation for Nitrosamine impurities follows the guidelines indicated below and is also
aligned with the requirements of further National Competent Authorities globally:
•	Assessment report Article 5(3) of Regulation EC (No) 726/2004 ‘Nitrosamine impurities
in human medicinal products’ (EMA/369136/2020) and ‘Questions and answers for
marketing authorization holders/applicants on the CHMP Opinion for the Article 5(3) of
Regulation (EC) No 726/2004 referral on nitrosamine impurities in human medicinal
products’ (EMA/409815/2020, current revision).
•	FDA Control of Nitrosamine Impurities in Human Drugs, Guidance for Industry, current
version
The contribution of the following factors to the potential presence of Nitrosamine impurities in
medicinal product are evaluated regarding:
The materials and their quality:
•	Drug substance 
•	Drug product manufacturing process;
•	excipients;
•	primary packaging material(s).
Drug substance
The risk evaluation for the potential presence of Nitrosamine impurities due to the drug substance
(DS) process is documented in the drug substance risk evaluation  [[2.1.2 Nitrosamine impurities]] 
 CP-6, which contains a secondary amine moiety, is included in the final API specification with a limit of NMT 37.5 ppm.
Excipients
The excipients used in the drug product were evaluated for their potential contribution to the
presence / formation of Nitrosamine impurities in the drug product. Table 2 below assesses the
excipients based on their structure and the potential contribution that they can have on formation
of N-nitroso compounds in the drug product.
Table 2 : Drug Product Excipients and Potential Contribution to Nitrosamine impurities presence / formation in the Drug Product Manufacturing Process
| Description | Excipient |
|  Excipients that neither have a structural alert for the presence or formation of N-nitrosamines, nor have risk for presence of vulnerable amines, but for which the presence of the nitrosating agent nitrite cannot be excluded. Based on available data on nitrite levels in excipients, the levels of reactive impurities such as nitrite are generally expected to be less than 10 ppm. These excipients can contribute to the risk of N-nitrosamine formation. These excipients have to be considered, in cases the API is reactive to trace amounts of nitrite and the nitrosation reaction is possible under the DP process conditions. | Lactose monohydrate Microcrystalline cellulose Croscarmellose sodium Hydroxypropyl cellulose Magnesium stearate |
| Excipients that do not have a structural alert for the presence or formation of N-nitrosamines. | Coating premix red |
Drug Product Manufacturing Process
No nitrosating reagents  are used in the process on drug
product equipment at the manufacturing site facility. No recycled or recovered materials are
used. The drug product equipment is not passivated with nitric acid or cleaned with chlorine or
chloramine. There are no nitrosating agents or nitrosamines that could be in contact with the
product during the manufacturing process.
There is a theoretical potential risk of nitrosamine impurity formation in the wet
granulation/drying process, where the API is initially suspended in water and afterwards the
wet granulated mass is dried by heating. Nonetheless, heat introduced during the drying phase
drives water evaporation, and the process is controlled to stop drying upon achievement of loss
on drying (LOD) limit.
Although CP-6 is controlled in the drug substance at tight limit of 37.5 ppm, during drug product manufacturing in presence of nitrosating agent precursors (e.g. nitrites from the excipients) there exists a potential theoretical risk for conversion to the  respective Nitrosamine impurity N-Nitroso-CP-6 . Testing performed on three recent representative, production-scale and commercial batches (including samples of three batches stored under accelerated stability conditions) applying a quantification limit down to 10% of the acceptable intake (AI) limit however confirmed the absence.  
Primary packaging material(s).
The current drug product primary packaging material consists of a HDPE bottle with desiccant
with polypropylene (PP) child resistant closure cap (or) PA/AL/PVC blister. There is no risk of Nitrosamine impurities formation / contamination of the drug product from the primary packaging material and process. There is also no risk from interaction of the solid dosage form with the primary packaging.
Risk of Increase/Formation of N-nitroso compounds during Storage
Based on 6 months accelerated stability at 40°C/75% RH available for 6 batches, there is no risk of increase/formation of Nitrosamine impurities during stability
 Based on this evaluation, there is no risk for the presence of N-nitroso compounds (N-Nitroso-CP-6) in Sakura Bloom 20 mg film-coated tablet. The detailed risk evaluation including vendor assessments risk evaluation for Sakura Bloom 20 mg film-coated tablet is provided in [[3.2.DP.C.2 Justification of specifications]] .

# Tests not included in specifications

## Water content
During manufacture of tablets, drying of the granulate is controlled to a limit 1 - 2% . This was shown during development to yield a product of appropriate quality. Loss on drying (LOD) of tablets was performed as an in-process control. The microbiological test is performed to verify the effectiveness of moisture control. Water content is therefore not tested on the finished product.

# PAT (Process analytical technology) - RTRT strategy justification
This document provides a scientific and regulatory justification for the implementation of Real-Time Release Testing (RTRT) for Sakura Bloom 20 mg Film-coated tablet. The proposed RTRT strategy complements end-product testing with in-process controls and predictive models, ensuring consistent product quality and compliance with regulatory expectations.
---

### 1. RTRT Scope and Strategy
---
RTRT will be applied to the following critical quality attributes (CQAs). The other CQA remains subject to conventional end-product testing.
| CQA | RTRT Methodology | Traditional Method Replaced |
| Identification | NIR spectroscopy during compression | HPLC |
| Content Uniformity | NIR spectroscopy during blending | Uniformity of dosage units |
| Dissolution | Predictive model based on process data | USP dissolution test |
 In case of RTRT unavailability or model failure, conventional methods will be applied as a fallback approach.
---

### 2. Scientific Justification

### 2.1 Process Understanding
Extensive development studies have established a robust design space for blending, granulation, and compression. Critical process parameters (CPPs) are tightly controlled and correlated with CQAs. Risk assessments (ICH Q9) confirm confirm that the RTRT approach is commensurate with the level of process knowledge established during development.

### 2.2 Analytical Technology
- NIR Spectroscopy: Validated for quantitative assay and uniformity.
- Compression Force Sensors: Provide real-time feedback on tablet hardness and weight.
- Multivariate Models: Chemometric models predict dissolution profiles with high accuracy.
Calibration, maintenance, and data integrity measures are implemented to ensure robustness of PAT tools and multivariate models.

### 2.3 Validation
- RTRT methods have been validated against conventional release tests.
- Comparative studies demonstrate equivalence or superiority in detecting out-of-specification conditions.
- Model lifecycle management includes periodic revalidation and performance monitoring.
Cross-reference: Details on the development of RTRT methods are presented in section [[(Sakura bloom)[APM][FCT][20 mg] ]]  

### 3. Lifecycle management and Change control
RTRT models and PAT tools are managed under the Pharmaceutical Quality System (ICH Q10). Ongoing lifecycle activities include continuous monitoring, periodic review, and predefined acceptance criteria for recalibration. All updates are subject to formal change control, with regulatory reporting where applicable.
---

### 4. Regulatory Reference
This approach is aligned with ICH Q8, Q9, Q10, Q14, and the EMA Guideline on Real Time Release Testing and Parametric Release (EMA/CHMP/QWP/811210/2009 Rev1)

# 2.3.4.AP.3 Analytical Procedure Development
1. Objective
To develop a Near-Infrared (NIR) spectroscopy method for the identification and assay of Excipient A and API B in a solid oral dosage form.
2. Product Description
The product is a solid tablet containing API B (50 mg) and Excipient A (filler), along with other excipients.
3. Instrumentation
FT-NIR Spectrometer equipped with an integrating sphere or fiber optic probe.
4. Method Parameters
Wavelength Range: 1000–2500 nm
Resolution: 8 cm⁻¹
Number of Scans: 64 scans per sample
5. Sample Preparation
For Identification: Direct scan of intact tablet or powder.
For Assay: Powdered blend homogenized before scanning.
6. Reference Standards
Certified reference standards of Excipient A and API B, and a placebo blend.
7. Calibration Model (Assay)
Partial Least Squares (PLS) regression using known concentrations of API B.
8. Preprocessing Techniques
Multiplicative Scatter Correction (MSC), First derivative, and Smoothing (Savitzky-Golay).
9. Validation Parameters
Specificity, Linearity, Accuracy, Precision, Robustness, LOD/LOQ, and System Suitability.
10. Identification and Assay Criteria
Identification: Correlation coefficient ≥ 0.95 with reference spectrum.
Assay: Recovery 98–102%; R² ≥ 0.99 for calibration model.
11. System Suitability
Signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) ≥ 100:1; consistent spectrum of standard.
12. Software Used
Chemometric software such as OPUS, Unscrambler, or TQ Analyst.
13. Challenges Addressed
Overlapping peaks of excipients, moisture interference, and tablet surface variability.
