# 2.3.4.AP.1 Analytical Procedure Justification
The requirements are set in accordance with the harmonised monographs of Ph. Eur. 5.1.4 ‘Microbiological quality of non-sterile pharmaceutical preparations and substances for pharmaceutical use’, USP <1111> ‘Microbiological examination of nonsterile products: acceptance criteria for pharmaceutical preparations and substances for pharmaceutical use’ and JP <G4> ‘Microbial Attributes of Non-sterile Pharmaceutical Products’.
Total aerobic microbial count (TAMC) and total combined yeasts/ moulds count (TYMC) are assessed by the plate count method in accordance with the harmonized method Ph. Eur. 2.6.12 “Microbiological examination of Non-Sterile Products: Microbial Enumeration Tests”, USP <61>: “Microbiological examination of Nonsterile Products: Microbial Enumeration Tests” and JP <4.05> “1. Microbiological Examination of Non-Sterile Products: Microbial Enumeration Tests”.
The absence of specific microorganism Escherichia coli is assessed according to Ph. Eur. 2.6.13 “Harmonized Method: Microbiological Examination of Non-Sterile Products: Tests for Specified Micro-Organisms”, USP <62> “Microbiological Examination of Non-sterile Products: Tests for Specified Microorganisms” and JP <4.05> “2. Microbiological Examination of Non-Sterile Products: Tests for Specified Micro-Organisms”.
MET is proposed to be performed as a frequency test (periodic quality indicator test). The risk of microbial contamination of the drug product is considered low due to the manufacturing process, environmental monitoring, and cleaning procedures in place. The entire process is a dry granulation, blending and compression, and does not use any water or other microbial-growth supporting solvents, except during the coating step.
Water activity results of less than 0.2 for the final blend, uncoated and coated tablets  (Table 1 and Table 2), as well as the historical MET data supports this assessment  (Table 3 and Table 4). During development, microbial enumeration testing was performed on 3 pilot-scale/registration stability batches (i.e., ABC123, ABC456 and ABC789). For all batches tested to date, the results met the proposed requirements. Furthermore, no microbial growth was observed at 6-month registration stability testing point in either blister packaging under accelerated conditions (Table 4).
Therefore, the proposal to perform MET as frequency test is consistent with the ICH guideline Q6A (Decision tree #8). The microbial enumeration tests will be performed at release on the first 5 consecutive production batches. If the requirements are met, testing frequency may be reduced to every 10th batch. At least one batch will be tested in each calendar year in which the product is manufactured.

# 2.3.4.AP.1 Analytical Procedure Justification
The content uniformity testing by NIR is performed on tablet cores using a large sample size of at least 100 units. The content of the individual tablet cores is determined by transmission NIR. The results have to meet the requirements of the Ph. Eur. 2.9.47 (Alternative 1), acceptance value 
(AV) ≤ 15.0 and none of the individual dosage units is outside the range of (1 ± 25.0×0.01)M .
The NIR method has been fully validated according to the EMA guideline on ‘The use of near infrared spectroscopy by the pharmaceutical industry and the data requirements for new submissions and variations’ as well as to the FDA Guidance for Industry (Draft) on ‘Development and Submission of Near Infrared Analytical Procedures’. Due to the application to a large sample size, the test method provides a comprehensive data base to evaluate the content uniformity of the batch.
The acceptance criteria are in line with the requirements of the harmonized Ph. Eur., USP and JP for Uniformity of dosage units.

# 2.3.4.AP.2 Analytical Procedure Validation/Qualification

# 2.3.4.AP.3 Analytical Procedure Development
1. Objective
To develop a Near-Infrared (NIR) spectroscopy method for the identification and assay of Excipient A and API B in a solid oral dosage form.
2. Product Description
The product is a solid tablet containing API B (50 mg) and Excipient A (filler), along with other excipients.
3. Instrumentation
FT-NIR Spectrometer equipped with an integrating sphere or fiber optic probe.
4. Method Parameters
Wavelength Range: 1000–2500 nm
Resolution: 8 cm⁻¹
Number of Scans: 64 scans per sample
5. Sample Preparation
For Identification: Direct scan of intact tablet or powder.
For Assay: Powdered blend homogenized before scanning.
6. Reference Standards
Certified reference standards of Excipient A and API B, and a placebo blend.
7. Calibration Model (Assay)
Partial Least Squares (PLS) regression using known concentrations of API B.
8. Preprocessing Techniques
Multiplicative Scatter Correction (MSC), First derivative, and Smoothing (Savitzky-Golay).
9. Validation Parameters
Specificity, Linearity, Accuracy, Precision, Robustness, LOD/LOQ, and System Suitability.
10. Identification and Assay Criteria
Identification: Correlation coefficient ≥ 0.95 with reference spectrum.
Assay: Recovery 98–102%; R² ≥ 0.99 for calibration model.
11. System Suitability
Signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) ≥ 100:1; consistent spectrum of standard.
12. Software Used
Chemometric software such as OPUS, Unscrambler, or TQ Analyst.
13. Challenges Addressed
Overlapping peaks of excipients, moisture interference, and tablet surface variability.

# 2.3.4.AP.1 Analytical Procedure Justification
The acceptance criteria for content uniformity by HPLC are set to meet the requirements of Ph. Eur. 2.9.40, JP and USP <905> (harmonized procedure). This test is performed only for batch release to assure the content uniformity of the dosage units for Sakuramil. The uniformity of dosage units of Sakuramil is determined by content uniformity by means of an isocratic HPLC method with UV detection at 218 nm using external standards.
The results must comply with the harmonized Ph. Eur., USP and JP requirements for Uniformity of dosage units.
Uniformity of dosage units by content uniformity by HPLC for Sakuramil is used as alternative to the primary release method Uniformity of dosage units by content uniformity for Sakuramil by NIR spectroscopy. This method is also the reference method which may be used by Official Medicines Control Laboratories.

pages.text:
# 2.3.4.AP.1 Analytical Procedure Justification
Dissolution testing is performed in accordance with the Ph. Eur. 2.9.3 “Dissolution test for solid dosage forms”, Acceptance Table 1 of USP <711> “Dissolution”, or JP <6.10> “Dissolution test” (harmonized method), using the paddle method (apparatus 2) at 50 ± 2 rpm and 900 mL of 4.0 N McIlvaine buffer as the dissolution medium. The USP apparatus 2 (paddle) method was chosen based on the dosage form.
Sakura Bloom 20 mg Film-coated tablet is an immediate release product. The speed of 50 rpm is considered standard for the paddle apparatus to provide agitation for an immediate release product. The setting of Q-value and Q-time is based on the release and stability data obtained for batch ABC123 used in registration stability. It was established to ensure that sufficient in vitro release can be achieved. No other batches of Sakura Bloom 20 mg film-coated tablet were used in clinical trials in support of this marketing authorization application. Nevertheless, the requirements previously mentioned are also supported by the dissolution data obtained for the registration stability batches ABC123 and ABC456. The specifications follow the Acceptance Table 1 of USP <711> “Dissolution”, Ph. Eur. 2.9.3 “Dissolution test for solid dosage forms”, JP <6.10> “Dissolution test” (harmonized method) for S1 and S2 testing for release and for stages 1, 2 and 3 for stability. This test is performed at release and during stability.
A detailed discussion on the choice of the dissolution method as well as dissolution profile data for these batches are provided in [[2.1 Dissolution testing]].

# 2.3.4.AP.2 Analytical Procedure Validation/Qualification

### Table 2 Analytical Method Validation Summary
| Validation Parameter | Test Description | Acceptance Criteria | Results | Conclusion |
| Specificity | Evaluate interference from excipients and degradation products | No interference at detection wavelength | No interference observed | Pass |
| Linearity | Standard solutions at 50–150% of expected concentration | R² ≥ 0.999 | R² = 0.9992 | Pass |
| Accuracy | Recovery study at 80%, 100%, and 120% of label claim | Recovery 98–102% | Recovery = 98.5%–101.7% | Pass |
| Precision | Repeatability of 6 dissolution vessels | %RSD of % release ≤ 5.0% | %RSD = 2.8% | Pass |
| Intermediate Precision | Different analyst, day, and instrument | %RSD ≤ 5.0% | %RSD = 3.5% | Pass |
| Robustness | Vary paddle speed, temperature, and filter type | No significant change in % release | All results within ±5% | Pass |
| LOD/LOQ (if applicable) | Lowest concentration reliably detected/quantified | LOD: S/N ≥ 3; LOQ: S/N ≥ 10 | LOD = 0.5 µg/mL; LOQ = 1.5 µg/mL | Pass |
Detailed Validation is available in [[3.2.AP.2 Analytical Procedure Validation/Qualification ]] 

# 2.3.4.AP.3 Analytical Procedure Development
Comparative testing using USP Apparatus I (Basket) and II (Paddle) was performed. Apparatus II (Paddle) at 50 ± 2 rpm provided consistent and reproducible results with minimal variability. 
During the development phase, sampling timepoints of 5, 10, 15, 20, 30, and 45 were set to adequately characterize the ascending and plateau phases of the dissolution curves. More than 85% of the drug is released within the duration of the dissolution test.
Medium deaeration was evaluated and showed no impact on dissolution. Batches with original formulation, medium with deliberate formulation (e.g. (such as higher magnesium stearate) and process variation (such as larger API particle size) were tested, showing distinct dissolution behaviors under different conditions. Therefore, The method’s discriminatory capability was demonstrated. 
The finalized dissolution method for Sakura Bloom 20 mg as depicted in [[2.3.3. AP Analytical Procedures (Dissolution/UV)[Performance][Sakura Bloom 20 mg]]] is scientifically justified, robust, and compliant with international pharmacopoeial standards. It demonstrates reproducibility, discriminatory power, and suitability for routine quality control, comparative dissolution studies, and regulatory submissions. The incorporation of UV detection and McIlvaine buffer at pH 5.0 ensures reliable performance and sensitivity across batches, supporting product quality throughout its shelf life.
For details and raw data of method development, please refer to [[3.2.AP Analytical Procedures (Dissolution/UV)[Performance][Sakura Bloom 20 mg]]].

pages.text:
# 2.3.4.AP.1 Analytical Procedure Justification
A feedforward control will be performed as an operation in commercial production so that the dissolution rate is about 90%. In other words, a control to keep the predicted dissolution value being always constant will be made by appropriately determining the target value for a granule particle size and uncoated tablet hardness within this design space according to the particle size of drug substance.
The particle size of drug substance is measured as a specification testing in the process of drug substance, by a laser diffraction-scattering type particle size distribution measuring device. Without preparing samples for measurement, the powder of drug substance is measured for particle distribution by the dry method (specification testing of drug substance). Regarding the particle size of the granulation, the particle size at the end of granulation, which is obtained by a FBRM method is used. The uncoated tablet hardness is measured in 200 tablets (10 tablets over 20 time points) sampled over time.

# 2.3.4.AP.2 Analytical Procedure Validation/Qualification

### Table 2 Analytical Method Validation Summary
| Validation Parameter | Test Description | Acceptance Criteria | Results | Conclusion |
| Specificity | Evaluate interference from excipients and media in UV/NIR detection | No interference at detection wavelength | No interference observed | Pass |
| Linearity (Model) | Evaluate linearity of predicted vs. actual dissolution values | R² ≥ 0.95 | R² = 0.976 | Pass |
| Accuracy (Model Prediction) | Compare predicted vs. actual % dissolved at each time point | RMSEP ≤ 5% | RMSEP = 3.2% | Pass |
| Precision (Repeatability) | Repeatability of model predictions across 6 units | %RSD ≤ 5.0% | %RSD = 2.7% | Pass |
| Intermediate Precision | Different analyst, day, and equipment | %RSD ≤ 5.0% | %RSD = 3.4% | Pass |
| Robustness | Evaluate under varied paddle speed, temperature, and media composition | No significant change in model prediction | All results within ±5% | Pass |
| Model Validation | Cross-validation and external validation of predictive model | R² ≥ 0.95, RMSEP ≤ 5% | R² = 0.972, RMSEP = 3.5% | Pass |
| System Suitability | %RSD of standard absorbance or spectral response | %RSD ≤ 2.0% | %RSD = 1.1% | Pass |
| Acceptance Criteria (Q value) | % of label claim dissolved in 30 minutes | Q ≥ 80% | 91% dissolved in 30 minutes | Pass |

## 2.3.4.AP.3 Analytical Procedure Development
The development of a Real-Time Release Testing (RTRT) method using UV spectroscopy for dissolution monitoring demonstrates a robust, efficient, and science-based approach to pharmaceutical quality assurance. By leveraging in-line or on-line UV absorbance measurements, this method enables real-time prediction of dissolution performance, reducing reliance on traditional, time-consuming offline testing.
The integration of UV spectroscopy with appropriate calibration models and process controls ensures consistent product quality and supports continuous manufacturing initiatives. This RTRT strategy aligns with regulatory expectations for Process Analytical Technology (PAT) and Quality by Design (QbD), offering enhanced process understanding, faster batch release, and improved operational efficiency.
For further details, refer to [[3.2.AP Analytical Procedures (Dissolution/RTRT)[Performance][Sakura Bloom 20 mg]]]

# 1 Introduction
The HPLC method for the identification of Sakura Bloom 20 mg Film-coated tablets was validated according to the method validation protocol VP_SB_21_2021.  Test method for identity by HPLC, employs the identical chromatographic conditions stipulated in Analytical procedure document. Hence, the validation of identification method was performed simultaneously with the validation of the assay and related substances method.
This document reports the validation results which show that the method is suitable for the identification of Sakura Bloom and Sakuramil in Sakura Bloom Film-coated tablets.  The method has been shown to be specific for the identification of Sakura Bloom Film-coated tablets.

# 2 Reference standard and materials
The reference standard and materials used in the validation of test method are described in Analytical procedure document.

# 3 Results and discussion
Identification by HPLC was evaluated by preparing and injecting blank, placebo, reference standard and placebo spiked with Sakura Bloom and Sakuramil at 100% level (20 mg strength) solutions into an HPLC system according to assay/related substances method.  A validation protocol, VP_SB_21_2021 was prepared for the identification method, the necessary validation data are extracted from validation report of assay and related substances method, VR_SB_21_2021 addendum as these two methods are identical.
Representative chromatograms of blank (diluent and extraction solvent), placebo solution, reference standard and spiked placebo solution with Sakura Bloom and Sakuramil at 100% level (20 mg strength) are illustrated in Figure 4-1 and Figure 4-2.  These chromatograms indicate that there is no interference from the blank and placebo injections with the Sakura Bloom and Sakuramil peaks.  Therefore, the test method identity by HPLC, is suitable for its intended use.

### Figure 4-1           Example chromatograms for identity by HPLC (210nm)
[IMAGE:  Untitled.png]
| A | Placebo spiked with Sakura Bloom and Sakuramil (at Sakura Bloom target concentration) |
| B | Reference standard solution (at Sakura Bloom target concentration) |
| C | Placebo solution |
| D | Diluent |
| E | Extraction solvent |

### Figure 4-2           Example chromatograms for identity by HPLC (218nm)
[IMAGE:  Untitled.png]
| A | Placebo spiked with Sakura Bloom and Sakuramil (at Sakuramil target concentration) |
| B | Reference standard solution (at Sakuramil target concentration) |
| C | Placebo solution |
| D | Diluent |
| E | Extraction solvent |

# 4 Conclusions
The validation data indicated that there is no interference with the Sakura Bloom and Sakuramil peak from the blank and placebo injections.  Therefore, analytical method identity by HPLC, is suitable for its intended use.

# 5 Deviations to protocol
The method validation protocol only included the active strengths of Sakura Bloom tablets.  This report includes placebo tablets, to match the corresponding test method.  Placebo tablets, however, are covered under this validation based on the results from the placebo and spiked placebo solutions.

# 6 References
SB TRD 3246/074 MZ.

# 2.3.3.DP.M.1 Batch Formula

| Ingredients | Reference to standards | Amount per batch (kg) |
| Tablet core |  |  |

| Lactose monohydrate/Lactose hydrate | Ph. Eur., USP/NF, JP | 353.600 |
| Cellulose, microcrystalline/ Microcrystalline cellulose | Ph. Eur., USP/NF, JP | 52.000 |
| Hydroxypropyl cellulose | Ph. Eur., USP/NF, JP | 15.600 |
| Croscarmellose sodium | Ph. Eur., USP/NF, JP | 26.000 |
| Magnesium stearate | Ph. Eur., USP/NF, JP | 5.200 |
| Core batch weight |  | 504.400 |

No overages are applied during manufacturing; all ingredients are added in the quantities specified in the batch formula.

# 2.3.3.DP.M.2 Description of the manufacturing process
The flow diagram, manufacturing process of Sakura Bloom 20 mg Film-coated tablets are provided below.

### Figure 1 Flow diagram for the manufacturing process of Sakura Bloom 20 mg Film-coated tablet
[IMAGE:  Untitled.png]

## 1 Manufacturing process
The Sakura Bloom 20 mg Film-coated tablet manufacturing process involves pre-blending, granulation, blending, compression, coating, inspection and packaging. Detailed information, e.g. all process parameters, is provided in [[3.2.DP.M Manufacture (Sakura Bloom) [APM][FCT][20 mg]]].

### Pre-Blending
1. Blend 52.000 kg of cellulose, microcrystalline, 26.000 kg of croscarmellose sodium, 353.600 kg of lactose monohydrate/Lactose hydrate and 52.000 kg of Sakuramil drug substance into a diffusion mixer (bin blender).
1. Dissolve 15.600 kg hydroxypropyl cellulose in purified water using a vessel with stirrer to prepare a granulation liquid free from lumps.

### Granulation and blending
1. Load the pre-blended material from Step 1 into a fluid bed granulator and add granulation liquid from Step 2 using an inlet air volume of 40-45 m³/min, an inlet air temperature of 75-85°C and a spray rate of 900 – 1100 g/min,  to achieve wetting of pre-blended material and formation of granules. 
1. Dry the obtained granules using dryer integrated within the fluid bed granulator unit. until loss on drying of 1 - 2% is achieved.
1. Sieve the dried granules from Step 4 using a screening mill.
1. Sieve 5.200 kg of magnesium stearate through a screen and add it to the granules from Step 5.
1. Blend the mixture from step 6  using a diffusion mixer (bin blender) to obtain the final blend.

### Tablet compression
1. Compress the final blend from step 7 using a tablet press at 20-30 revolutions with a compression force of 6-14 kN to obtain the tablet cores.

### Film-coating
1. Prepare a homogeneous suspension of the Basic coating premix, red in purified water in a suitable sized vessel.
1. Film-coat the tablet cores from Step 8 using the film coat suspension from Step 9 in a coating pan to achieve desired film-coat weight gain, followed by drying. Collect the film coated tablets in a suitable container.

### Inspection
1. Collect 10 tablets to perform Description test method with RTRT and Identification Test method with RTRT.

### Packaging
1. The film-coated tablets are primary packaged.
1. The  primary packaged product  is then packed in a cardboard based secondary pack.

## 2 Manufacturing equipment
Table 2 provides an overview of the equipment SUPAC class and subclass used in the manufacture of Sakura Bloom 20 mg Film-coated tablets. For each step, the unit operation, equipment class and, where appropriate subclass, capacity and automation are provided.

| Step | Process | Equipment |
| 1 | Pre-blending | SUPAC Class: diffusion mixer SUPAC Subclass: bin blender Capacity: 500 L Automation: Yes |
| 3 | Granulation | SUPAC Class: wet granulator SUPAC Subclass: fluidized bed granulator Capacity: 750 L Automation: Yes |
| 4 | Drying | SUPAC Class: granulator SUPAC Subclass: fluidized bed granulator dryer (dryer integrated within granulator) Capacity: 750 L Automation: Yes |
| 5 | Screening | SUPAC Class: screening mill SUPAC Subclass: oscillating bar Capacity: 30-108 rpm Automation: Yes |
| 7 | Final blending | SUPAC Class: diffusion mixer SUPAC Subclass: bin blender Capacity: 500 L Automation: Yes |
| 8 | Compression | SUPAC Class: rotary tablet press SUPAC Subclass: power assisted Capacity: 10-90 rpm Automation: Yes |
| 9 | Preparation of the coating suspension | Vessel with stirrer Capacity: 750 L Automation: Yes |
| 10 | Film-coating | SUPAC Class: pan coating SUPAC Subclass: perforated coating system Capacity: 300 – 390 L Automation: Yes |

# 2.3.4.DP.S.1 Container closure system
The bulk Sakura Bloom 20 mg Film-coated tablets are packaged in a primary container consisting of a PETP/AL/PE aluminum composite bag, which is tightly sealed to provide an adequate moisture and oxygen barrier. It has demonstrated its suitability for maintaining the chemical and physical stability of the bulk product under the proposed storage conditions. 
The batch analysis results are provided in [[3.2.DP.S Storage - Bulk (Sakura Bloom) [APM][FCT][20 mg]]].

# 2.3.4.DP.S.2 Stability, storage conditions, and shelf life
The stability data generated for Sakura Bloom 20 mg Film-coated tablets stored in PETP/AL/PE composite bags demonstrate that the bulk product remains chemically and physically stable for up to 18 months under long-term storage conditions (25°C/60% RH and 30°C/75% RH). Across both production batches (ABC123 and ABC456), the following results were observed: assay values ranging from 97.4% to 100.9%, total degradation products ranging from 0.2% to 0.4%, unspecified degradation products were consistently reported as <0.2%, and appearance remained unchanged throughout the study period under both conditions. Dissolution after 30 minutes ranged from 92% to 101% (25 °C/60% RH) and 92% to 100% (30 °C/75% RH), meeting the dissolution specification and showing no significant trend. Stability under accelerated conditions (40°C/75% RH) for up to 6 months further supports the stability of the product. Based on these data, a holding time of 18 months is proposed for the bulk product when stored at or below 30°C in tightly sealed PETP/AL/PE bags. These conditions also support intermediate storage and transport under excursions up to 40°C for a limited duration. 
The supportive stability study reports for bulk product are provided in [[3.2.DP.S Storage - Bulk (Sakura Bloom) [APM][FCT][20 mg]]].

## 1 Primary packaging materials
Sakura Bloom 20 mg Film-coated tablet for primary stability studies were packaged in the following packaging type commonly used for solid oral dosage forms and found to be suitably stable.
- PA/AL/PVC blister packs, consisting of a polyamide aluminum and polyvinyl chloride film backed with a heat sealable lacquered aluminum foil.
During development of the tablets, different primary packaging types have been considered and tested. On the basis of the stability data generated during development and registration batches, PA/AL/PVC blisters and HDPE bottles with induction sealing and child-resistant cap were selected as primary packaging of first choice. These container types possess favorable properties resulting in sufficient quality characteristics of tablets during the shelf-life. Suitability of these container closure systems is well established by stability data of Sakura Bloom 20 mg Film-coated tablets.
Microbiological attributes
Sakura Bloom 20 mg Film-coated tablet is a standard solid oral dosage form. Controls necessary for the manufacture and control of Sakura Bloom 20 mg Film-coated tablet are conducted in accordance with cGMPs to prevent microbial contamination.
However, routine microbiological testing is unnecessary as the drug product has no propensity to support microbial growth. Hence, Microbiological Enumeration Testing (MET) is performed as a periodic/skip testing. The control strategy for microbiological attributes is described in  [[2.3.4.DP.C Control (Sakura Bloom)[APM][FCT][20 mg]]].
The detailed information on primary packaging materials selected for commercial supplies, is provided in [[2.3.3.DP.S Storage - Blister (Sakura Bloom)[APM][FCT][20 mg] ]]

## 1    Stability Summary and Conclusions
The stability program for Batches 123, 456, and 789 was designed to comprehensively evaluate the product's performance under various environmental conditions to support its registration and commercialization. The study encompassed long-term stability assessments at 25°C/60% RH and 30°C/75% RH over a 36-month period, accelerated stability testing at 40°C/75% RH for up to 6 months, and photostability evaluations to determine sensitivity to light exposure.  All data were collected using validated analytical methods and monitored for critical quality attributes such as assay, impurities, dissolution and physical appearance.

### 1. Assay (% Label Claim)
Across all conditions (25°C/60% RH, 30°C/75% RH, 40°C/75% RH), assay values remain within a tight range: 98.1% to 101.4%. Slight upward trend at 40°C/75% RH, especially in batch ABC789 (up to 101.4%). 
While some variability in assay data was reported no stability trend was observed.
Assay remains well within acceptable limits across all conditions. No significant degradation or potency loss observed, even under accelerated conditions.
---

### 2. Degradation Products (%)
CP-9-1:
Results consistently < 0.10% across all conditions and batches. Occasional detection at 0.10%, but still within specification.
Individual Unspecified Impurities:
- Mostly Not Detected (ND) or < 0.10%.
Total Impurities:
- Slight increase with temperature:
  - 25°C/60% RH: up to 0.11%
  - 30°C/75% RH: up to 0.14%
  - 40°C/75% RH: up to 0.17%
Impurity levels are low and stable.  Slight increase in total impurities at higher temperatures is expected and within acceptable limits.
---

### 3. Dissolution (% in 30 minutes)
All batches show dissolution between 94% to 106%. Slight increase in dissolution at 40°C/75% RH, possibly due to enhanced solubility.
Dissolution performance is robust across all conditions. No adverse impact from storage conditions.
---
Parameters such as appearance remained unchanged through the shelf-life 
Based on the available drug product stability data provided in  [[3.2.DP.S Storage - Blister (Sakura Bloom) [APM][FCT][20 mg]]] , the proposed packaging is considered protective and compatible with Sakura Bloom 20 mg Film-coated tablet and was stable for not less than 36 months. # Start of shelf life
The calculation of the expiration period of a batch complies with the requirements as stated in the EU guideline NfG on Start of Shelf-Life of the Finished Dosage Form (CPMP/QWP/ 072/96).
The following approach is taken in practice:
The expiration period of a production batch is calculated from the date of production of that batch. The date of production of a batch is no later than the step in the manufacturing process where the active ingredient is combined with other ingredients.

# Introduction
This report presents all data that are referred in the summary part RSR1234 Summary-1G. This report follows protocol RSP1234-1G and updates with 36 months data for all batches accordingly.

# 1 Analytical procedures and requirements
The samples were tested against the specifications cited in the current version of specification sheet.  The current requirements are as follows:

### Table 1-1 Tests and requirements
| Test code | Title of test | Requirements | Test performed for |  |
|  |  |  | Batch release | Stability testing |
| AM10001C | Appearance by visual examination | Pale red colored, round, biconvex film-coated tablet, debossed with ‘SB’ on one side and ‘20’ on the other side | + | + |
| AM50101E | Dissolution by UV | Not less than 80 % (Q) in 30 min | + | + |
| AM54001C | Assay by HPLC | Assay: 95.0 to 105.0% | + | + |
|  | Degradation Products, by HPLC Specified CP‑9‑1* Any unspecified impurity Total degradation products |       Not more than 0.5 %   Not more than 0.2 %   Not more than 1.0 % | + | + |
| AM58001E | Microbial enumeration test | Meets harmonized USP, Ph. Eur. and JP requirements:  Total aerobic microbial count: <= 103 CFU/g   Total yeasts and molds: <= 102 CFU/g   Specific microorganisms:  - Escherichia coli: Not detectable in 1 gram. | +* | + |
- Skip testing performed at 12 months, 24 months and 36 months on all registration stability batches and thereafter every 12 months and end of shelf life
